name: pinneapple_tools

children.name: pinneapple_tools.aero_coefficients
children.doc:
Shared aerodynamic-coefficient utilities (Cp, surface-force integration, CL/CD/CM).

Plain numpy in / numpy out -- no framework lock-in, so both PINN surrogates
(which typically hand back predictions as numpy arrays after `.detach()
.cpu().numpy()`) and non-PINN solvers (analytical, LBM, panel methods, ...)
can share one implementation instead of every example re-deriving the same
algebra inline.

Sign / axis conventions
------------------------
The pressure-coefficient definition (``Cp = (p - p_inf) / q_inf``) is the
standard aerodynamics convention and matches the inline computation in
``examples/benchmark_suite/15_naca0012_aerodynamic_surrogate.py`` (which uses
the incompressible Bernoulli special case ``Cp = 1 - |V|^2 / U_inf^2``, i.e.
``p - p_inf = q_inf * (1 - |V/U_inf|^2)``).

The wind-axis rotation used by :func:`force_to_coefficients` mirrors the
normal/axial -> lift/drag transform in
``examples/use_cases/missile_aero/missile_aero_pipeline.py``
(see the module docstring there, and lines ~262-267 of
``solve_aero()``)::

    CN = normal-force coefficient   (body axis, perpendicular to axis of symmetry)
    CA = axial-force coefficient    (body axis, along axis of symmetry)
    CL = CN * cos(alpha) - CA * sin(alpha)
    CD = CN * sin(alpha) + CA * cos(alpha)

That pipeline works in a single meridional plane, so "normal" and "axial"
map directly onto two coordinate axes. This module generalizes the same
rotation to a full 3D force vector by picking a 2D "aero plane" out of the
3D force via a ``(drag_axis, lift_axis)`` pair and rotating within that
plane by ``alpha``; any component of the force orthogonal to both (e.g. a
sideforce) is reported separately and is NOT folded into CL/CD.

The default convention is a 2D-in-3D setup consistent with the rest of the
repo's LBM/PINN CFD tooling (x = streamwise/free-stream direction, z =
"vertical"/lift direction, y = spanwise): alpha rotates the force from the
*body axes* (x = axial, z = normal) into *wind axes* (drag along the
free-stream direction, lift perpendicular to it) within the x-z plane,
using exactly the CN/CA -> CL/CD sign convention above with
``CN -> F_normal`` (the lift-axis component of body force) and
``CA -> F_axial`` (the drag-axis component of body force)::

    CL = CN * cos(alpha) - CA * sin(alpha)
    CD = CN * sin(alpha) + CA * cos(alpha)

Callers with a different body-axis layout (e.g. a wing with span along x)
should pass an explicit ``drag_axis`` / ``lift_axis`` pair.

classes.name: AeroCoefficients
classes.doc:
Non-dimensional aerodynamic coefficients about the wind axes.

Attributes
----------
CL : lift coefficient (along ``lift_axis``, wind-axis rotated).
CD : drag coefficient (along the free-stream direction, wind-axis rotated).
CM : moment coefficient about ``moment_axis`` (default: perpendicular to
     the drag/lift plane, i.e. the standard pitching-moment axis).
CY : sideforce coefficient -- component of the force orthogonal to both
     the drag and lift axes, non-dimensionalized the same way as CD/CL.
     Zero for a purely 2D-in-3D problem.

functions.name: compute_cp
functions.sig: (p: np.ndarray, p_inf: float, q_inf: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Pressure coefficient ``Cp = (p - p_inf) / q_inf``.

Parameters
----------
p     : array_like, static pressure at each sample point.
p_inf : float, free-stream static pressure.
q_inf : float, free-stream dynamic pressure (``0.5 * rho_inf * U_inf**2``).
         Must be nonzero.

Returns
-------
np.ndarray, same shape as ``p``.

functions.name: integrate_surface_forces
functions.sig: (vertices: np.ndarray, faces: np.ndarray, face_normals: np.ndarray, face_pressure: np.ndarray, face_shear: Optional[np.ndarray] = None, moment_center: Optional[np.ndarray] = None) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Integrate per-face pressure (and optional shear) into a net force and
moment over a triangulated surface.

The pressure contribution on face ``i`` is
``-face_pressure[i] * area[i] * face_normals[i]`` (pressure acts INTO the
surface, i.e. opposite the outward normal -- the standard convention for
aerodynamic surface-pressure integration). If ``face_shear`` is given, it
is added directly (already a vector traction per face, force = shear *
area, no normal-vs-tangent decomposition is imposed on the caller -- pass
the wall-shear-stress vector already projected tangent to the surface).

Parameters
----------
vertices      : (N, 3) float array of mesh vertex coordinates.
faces         : (M, 3) int array of triangle vertex indices.
face_normals  : (M, 3) float array of OUTWARD unit normals, one per face.
face_pressure : (M,) float array of static pressure at each face.
face_shear    : (M, 3) float array of wall-shear-stress vectors, optional.
moment_center : (3,) float array, reference point for the moment.
                Defaults to the origin.

Returns
-------
force  : (3,) net aerodynamic force vector.
moment : (3,) net aerodynamic moment vector about ``moment_center``.

functions.name: force_to_coefficients
functions.sig: (force: np.ndarray, moment: np.ndarray, q_inf: float, ref_area: float, ref_length: float, alpha_deg: float, *, drag_axis: str = 'x', lift_axis: str = 'z', moment_axis: Optional[str] = None) -> AeroCoefficients
functions.doc:
Convert a net body-axis force/moment into wind-axis CL/CD/CM.

Rotation convention (matches
``examples/use_cases/missile_aero/missile_aero_pipeline.py``,
``solve_aero()``, lines ~262-267)::

    CN = force component along ``lift_axis``   (body axis)
    CA = force component along ``drag_axis``   (body axis)
    CL = CN * cos(alpha) - CA * sin(alpha)
    CD = CN * sin(alpha) + CA * cos(alpha)

where ``alpha`` is measured positive rotating the body's ``drag_axis``
toward its ``lift_axis`` (i.e. increasing angle of attack tilts the body
axis toward the lift direction, exactly as in the missile pipeline where
increasing alpha increases the leeward body angle -- see
``body_angle_distribution()`` in that file).

Parameters
----------
force, moment : (3,) arrays, e.g. from :func:`integrate_surface_forces`.
q_inf         : free-stream dynamic pressure.
ref_area      : reference area for force normalization.
ref_length    : reference length for moment normalization.
alpha_deg     : angle of attack in degrees.
drag_axis, lift_axis : one of "x", "y", "z" (default 3D-in-2D convention:
    x = free-stream/axial direction, z = "up"/normal direction). Must be
    distinct.
moment_axis   : axis about which CM is reported. Defaults to whichever
    of "x", "y", "z" is neither ``drag_axis`` nor ``lift_axis`` (the
    standard pitching-moment axis for a 2D-in-3D problem).

Returns
-------
AeroCoefficients(CL, CD, CM, CY)

pinneapple_tools.automation.adapters.base
children.doc:
What every adapter implements, and the context a step runs in.

An adapter wraps one application (FreeCAD, OpenFOAM, ParaView, a web UI) and offers named actions. Each action
receives its rendered ``params`` and a :class:`StepContext`, does the work, preferably through the application's own
API or command line, and returns an :class:`ActionResult`: outputs for later steps, the files it produced, the
images of what happened and the checks it ran on its own artifacts.

Executors of other runners (the Simulation Workflow Runner) can call the same adapters: ``get_adapter(name)``,
``adapter.available()``, ``adapter.run(action, params, ctx)``.

methods.doc: Run a command, writing stdout+stderr to ``<step_dir>/<log_name>`` and recording both.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.adapters.freecad
children.doc:
FreeCAD and the CfdOF workbench.

Actions run a Python script **inside the FreeCAD GUI** on the run's virtual display (CfdOF needs ``FreeCADGui``;
the GUI also gives real screenshots): the script works through FreeCAD's own API, then the adapter finds the FreeCAD
window with xdotool, captures the screen (``screen`` evidence) and the 3D view region of it (``window`` evidence),
and lets FreeCAD exit.

* ``freecad.open``: open a document, list its objects and spreadsheet parameters, measure a solid.
* ``freecad.macro``: run a macro (``.FCMacro`` / ``.py``) with arguments; the macro gets ``ARGS`` and fills ``RESULT``.
* ``cfdof.setup``: build a CfdOF analysis (laminar steady incompressible, velocity inlet, pressure outlet, walls,
  gmsh mesh) on a solid and write the mesh case and the OpenFOAM case.

functions.name: run_in_freecad_gui
functions.sig: (script: str | Path, args: dict[str, Any], ctx: StepContext, name: str, view: dict[str, Any] | None = None, hold_s: float = 60.0) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], ActionResult]
functions.doc:
Run ``script`` inside the FreeCAD GUI with ``ARGS = args``; returns (RESULT, evidence/commands).

``view`` = {"show": [object names], "hide": [...], "view": "viewIsometric" | "viewFront" | ...} sets what the 3D
view shows when the screenshots are taken.

Raises :class:`ActionFailed` when the script raised (with its traceback) or FreeCAD did not answer.

children.summary: FreeCAD and the CfdOF workbench.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.adapters.openfoam
children.doc:
OpenFOAM through its command line: run the mesh script and the solver script of a case (CfdOF's ``Allmesh`` and
``Allrun``, or any command list), then read what happened from the logs with
:func:`pinneapple_data.simulation_metadata.openfoam.parse_log` (end reached, fatal errors, residual history,
convergence message, checkMesh quality).

* ``openfoam.mesh``: ``Allmesh`` in the mesh case, then ``checkMesh``. Checks: a polyMesh exists, checkMesh says
  "Mesh OK".
* ``openfoam.prepare`` / ``openfoam.post``: the case and the post-processing of the FreeCAD -> OpenFOAM pipeline
  (:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.pipelines.freecad_openfoam`).
* ``openfoam.solve``: ``Allrun`` (or ``commands``) in the case. Checks: the solver reached ``End`` without a fatal
  error or floating-point exception, and either OpenFOAM's residual control stopped it ("SIMPLE solution converged")
  or every initial residual of the last iteration is below ``residual_tol``. Evidence: the residual history plot.

Compatibility with OpenFOAM v1912 (the Ubuntu 24.04 ``openfoam`` package; CfdOF targets newer releases), each
edit recorded as an action of the step:

* CfdOF picks the ``transformPoints`` syntax from ``FOAM_API``, which v1912 does not set, so the mesh would stay in
  millimetres: :func:`patch_cfdof_allmesh` adds the v-numbered (ESI) case to the test in ``Allmesh``.
* CfdOF's velocity inlet (``fixedNormalInletOutletVelocity``) did not hold the prescribed flux on v1912:
  :func:`patch_cfdof_inlet` writes it as ``fixedValue`` (ESI releases before v2006 only).

methods.name: do_prepare
methods.doc: Mesh dictionaries and case of the FreeCAD -> OpenFOAM pipeline (``steps.prepare_step``).

methods.name: do_post
methods.doc: Measured quantities, figures and reference errors of the pipeline (``steps.post_step``).

functions.name: patch_cfdof_allmesh
functions.sig: (mesh_case: str | Path) -> str | None
functions.doc:
Make CfdOF's ``Allmesh`` use the ``-scale`` syntax on v-numbered (ESI) releases that do not set FOAM_API.
Returns a description of the edit, or None when the script needed none.

functions.name: patch_cfdof_inlet
functions.sig: (case: str | Path) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
Replace CfdOF's ``fixedNormalInletOutletVelocity`` inlets in ``0/U`` by ``fixedValue`` with the same normal
velocity. On OpenFOAM v1912 the mixed condition is not assignable, so with the zeroGradient inlet pressure the
pressure equation changed the inlet flux (6 % below U*A on the channel example). Returns the edits made.

functions.name: solver_log
functions.sig: (case: Path) -> tuple[Path | None, dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc: The solver log of a case (log.simpleFoam, log.foamRun, ...) and its parsed content.

functions.sig: (parsed: dict[str, Any], path: Path, title: str) -> Path | None

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.adapters.paraview
children.doc:
ParaView through ``pvpython``: open an OpenFOAM case at its last time, export a cell field to CSV (cell centres
and values) and render it on a slice to PNG (``render`` evidence).

* ``paraview.export``: params ``case`` (folder with a ``.foam`` file or the file itself), ``field`` (default U),
  ``arrays`` (exported, default [U, p]), ``slice_normal`` (default [0, 0, 1]), ``view_up``
  (default [0, 1, 0]). Checks: the CSV has one row per cell
  of the mesh and the image exists.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.adapters.pipeline
children.doc:
Adapters of the FreeCAD -> OpenFOAM pipeline (:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.pipelines.freecad_openfoam`):

* ``freecadcmd.export``: FreeCAD **headless** (``freecadcmd``, no display) sets the document's spreadsheet
  parameters, recomputes, exports STEP and the faces; the patches are named by rule and written to a multi-region
  STL. ``backend: fake`` uses the NumPy stand-in (tests, machines without FreeCAD).

and, on the ``openfoam`` adapter (:mod:`.openfoam`), through :func:`pipeline_call`:

* ``openfoam.prepare``: mesh dictionaries and case (internal: blockMesh + snappyHexMesh / cfMesh, simpleFoam /
  pimpleFoam; external: ``ExternalFlow``), with ``Allmesh`` and ``Allrun`` for ``openfoam.mesh`` / ``openfoam.solve``.
* ``openfoam.post``: measured quantities, figures, derived quantities and reference errors.

The work is done by :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.pipelines.freecad_openfoam.steps`; these classes only turn its
results into an :class:`ActionResult`.

functions.sig: (fn, params: dict[str, Any], ctx: StepContext) -> ActionResult

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.display
children.doc:
The screen GUI applications run on: a virtual X display (Xvfb) on a Linux server or container, screenshots of it,
and the three ways of driving a GUI when an application has no usable API.

* :class:`VirtualDisplay` starts Xvfb on a free display number and captures the whole screen with Pillow
  (``ImageGrab.grab(xdisplay=...)``), so no screenshot utility is needed.
* :class:`XdotoolDriver` finds, raises and types into X11 windows with ``xdotool``.
* :class:`PlaywrightDriver` drives a web UI (a solver's web front end, a licence portal) with Playwright.
* :class:`PywinautoDriver` is the interface for Windows desktop applications (Ansys Workbench, Abaqus/CAE, ...)
  through ``pywinauto``. It runs only on Windows: in the Linux container it reports itself unavailable.

API control (the application's own Python, the solver's command line) always comes first; these drivers are the
fallback and the observer.

classes.name: GuiUnavailable
classes.doc: The GUI driver cannot run here (missing tool, wrong platform, no display).

classes.name: VirtualDisplay
classes.sig: (width: int = 1600, height: int = 1000, depth: int = 24, reuse: bool = False)
classes.doc:
An Xvfb display for the duration of a ``with`` block (or until :meth:`stop`).

If ``DISPLAY`` already points at a running X server and ``reuse=True``, that one is used instead of starting a
new one (a desktop session, or a container that started Xvfb + noVNC itself).

methods.doc: Capture the display (or ``box`` = left, top, right, bottom) to a PNG/JPEG file.

classes.name: PywinautoDriver
classes.doc:
Windows desktop GUIs through ``pywinauto`` (UI Automation backend).

The interface mirrors :class:`XdotoolDriver`: ``start(cmd)``, ``wait_window(title)``, ``click(control)``,
``type(control, text)``, ``screenshot(path)``. It is documented here so a workflow written for a Windows
application has a place to plug in; it is **not runnable in the Linux container** and raises
:class:`GuiUnavailable` there.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.interpret
children.doc:
From a task to a structured workflow.

A task is either a workflow already (a dict, or JSON/YAML text: it is validated and used as is) or a sentence
such as "run the channel case with a 55 mm obstacle". A sentence is matched against a **catalog of committed
workflows**: the words of the task pick the workflow and the numbers next to an input's words set its value (with
unit conversion), then the inputs are checked against their bounds. Nothing in a sentence can add steps or run
code: it only chooses among workflows someone reviewed, and sets their inputs.

An LLM is optional. With ``llm=OllamaClient(...)`` (``pinneapple_data.formfill.llm``; the Ollama service of the
deploy stack) the model answers in a JSON schema with the workflow id and input values, and its answer goes
through the same validation; if the server is not reachable, or the answer is invalid, the rule-based reading is
used and the reason is kept in ``notes``.

functions.name: parse_quantity
functions.sig: (text: str, unit: str) -> float | None
functions.doc: The number in ``text`` converted to ``unit`` ("4 cm" -> 40 for mm); None if there is no number.

functions.name: interpret
functions.sig: (task: str | dict[str, Any], catalog: dict[str, Workflow], llm = None, min_score: float = 0.15) -> Interpretation
functions.doc: Turn ``task`` into a workflow of ``catalog`` and its inputs (see the module docstring).

children.summary: From a task to a structured workflow.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.record
children.doc:
What a run leaves behind: one :class:`StepRecord` per step (state, commands, logs, artifacts with their SHA-256,
screenshots, checks, outputs, error) and the :class:`RunRecord` around them, saved as ``run.json`` in the run folder.

A step is ``passed`` only if its action ran, every check it produced held and every artifact it was expected to
leave exists; nothing else may be reported as passed.

classes.name: Evidence
classes.doc:
An image of what happened. ``kind`` says what it is, so a report never passes a plot off as a screenshot:
``screen`` (capture of the whole virtual display), ``window`` (one application window), ``render`` (the
application's own image export), ``plot`` (a chart drawn from the step's log or data).

functions.name: file_record
functions.sig: (path: Path, root: Path) -> FileRecord
functions.doc: Size and SHA-256 of a file; for a folder, the total size and a hash over its sorted file hashes.

children.summary: What a run leaves behind: one StepRecord per step (state, commands, logs, artifacts with their SHA-256, screenshots, checks, outputs, error) and the RunRecord around them, saved as run.json in the ...

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.report
children.doc:
The evidence of a run, for people and for other tools.

* :func:`write_report`: one self-contained HTML file (images embedded) with the inputs, the tools and versions, a
  timeline of the steps (state, duration, commands, actions, checks, artifacts with SHA-256, logs, screenshots),
  the acceptance criteria and the errors. Print it to PDF from a browser for a PDF.
* :func:`to_study_result` / :func:`write_study_result`: the same facts as a ``pinneapple_data.contracts.StudyResult``
  (the contract the apps share, read by the Evidence Report app): checks, criteria, metrics, files with SHA-256,
  limits and provenance; inputs, decision, step states and images in ``metadata``.

Nothing is inferred: a step is shown as passed only if its record says so, and an image's kind (screen, window,
render, plot) is shown next to it.

functions.name: write_report
functions.sig: (run: RunRecord, path: str | Path) -> Path

functions.name: to_study_result
functions.sig: (run: RunRecord)
functions.doc:
The run as a :class:`pinneapple_data.contracts.StudyResult` (``study_type="runs"``, ``app="guiagent"``).

Checks of every step and the acceptance criteria become ``CheckRecord`` (PASS/FAIL with the measured value, or
the step record as evidence); produced files become ``FileRef`` with SHA-256; numeric step outputs and criterion
values become metrics; the workflow's limits are carried over. Inputs, decision, step states and the images go in
``metadata``.

functions.name: write_study_result
functions.sig: (run: RunRecord, path: str | Path) -> Path

children.summary: The evidence of a run, for people and for other tools.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.runner
children.doc:
Run a :class:`~pinneapple_tools.automation.workflow.Workflow` step by step, observe each step and stop on the
first failure or on the first step that needs a human decision.

For every step, in order:

1. skip it if an earlier run already passed it (a run folder can be resumed);
2. block if a step named in ``after`` has not passed, or if the application it needs is not installed;
3. stop with ``awaiting_confirmation`` if the step falls into a confirmation category (``expensive``,
   ``overwrite``, ``destructive``, ``external``) and was not approved: a step whose expected files already exist
   is an overwrite even if the workflow does not say so;
4. run the action through its adapter, with a virtual display if it drives a GUI;
5. check the artifacts it was expected to leave, hash every file it produced, keep its logs, commands, screenshots
   and outputs; the step passes only if the action returned and every check held.

``run.json`` in the run folder is rewritten after every change, so a UI can follow a run while it executes; when
the run stops, the evidence report (``report.html``) and the StudyResult (``study_result.json``) are written.

    from pinneapple_tools.automation import Runner, Workflow, example_workflow
    wf = Workflow.load(example_workflow("channel_obstacle"))
    run = Runner(wf, "runs/demo", inputs={"obstacle_height_mm": 50}).run()
    if run.state == "awaiting_confirmation":         # the solver step is "expensive"
        run = Runner(wf, "runs/demo").run(approve=["solve"], approver="j.doe")

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.runner_step
children.doc:
The GUI agent as a step of the Simulation Workflow Runner (``pinneapple_core.workflows``).

``register()`` adds the step kind ``guiagent``: one step of a runner workflow runs a whole automation workflow
(FreeCAD, CfdOF, OpenFOAM, ParaView, ...) in the step's directory and returns its verdict as outputs, so a runner DAG
can mesh and solve a CAD variant per case and use the acceptance criteria downstream::

    from pinneapple_core.workflows import Step, Workflow, WorkflowRunner
    from pinneapple_tools.automation.runner_step import register
    register()
    wf = Workflow(name="channel sweep", steps=[
        Step(id="h55", kind="guiagent", params={"workflow": "channel_obstacle",
                                                "inputs": {"obstacle_height_mm": 55}, "approve": ["solve"]})])
    WorkflowRunner("work/runner").run(wf)

Step parameters: ``workflow`` (id of a committed workflow, see :func:`~pinneapple_tools.automation.catalog`),
``inputs`` (checked against the workflow's bounds), ``approve`` (ids of the steps the workflow asks to confirm; whoever
writes the runner workflow approves them, and the record says so). A run that stops for a confirmation that was not
given, fails or is blocked makes the runner step fail with the agent's message. Outputs: ``state``, ``message``,
``passed`` (every acceptance criterion met), ``criteria`` (name -> met), ``metrics`` (the numbers of the
StudyResult), ``report`` and ``study_result`` (paths in the step directory).

Cancelling the runner step stops the agent at its next step boundary (a running solver finishes its step).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.verify
children.doc:
Acceptance criteria on a finished run, computed from the produced files with PINNeAPPle's checks.

=================  ==========================================================================================
kind               what is computed
=================  ==========================================================================================
``mass_balance``   volume flux through every boundary patch of the OpenFOAM result (``pinneapple_check``'s
                   finite-volume reader and :func:`pinneapple_check.fv.fv_mass_balance`, from ``phi`` when written);
                   passes when |inlet + outlet| / |inlet| <= ``tol``
``inflow``         the volume flow through the inlet patch equals ``velocity`` x the patch area of the mesh within
                   ``tol`` (the boundary condition the case asked for was actually applied)
``pressure_drop``  area-weighted mean static pressure on the inlet minus the outlet, times ``density`` for
                   incompressible solvers (kinematic p); passes when ``min_pa`` <= dp <= ``max_pa``
``converged``      the named step ran and its "solver converged" and "solver finished" checks held
``artifact``       a file or folder of the run exists and is not empty
``metric``         a numeric ``output`` of a passed ``step`` lies within [``min``, ``max``] (either may be omitted),
                   e.g. a reference error or the largest Courant number
``physics_lint``   ``pinneapple check`` on the case (conservation, divergence, boundary conditions); passes when it
                   reports no error
=================  ==========================================================================================

Each criterion gives one :class:`~pinneapple_tools.automation.record.Check` with the measured value and the
threshold; a criterion whose inputs are missing fails with the reason, it is never skipped silently.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.automation.workflow
children.doc:
The structured workflow an automation run executes: inputs with bounds, steps with preconditions, the artifacts
each step must produce, the confirmations it needs, and the acceptance criteria of the result.

A workflow is plain data (YAML or JSON), so it can be written by hand, produced by :func:`interpret` from a sentence,
reviewed in a pull request and replayed later::

    id: channel_obstacle
    title: Channel with an obstacle, pressure drop vs obstacle height
    inputs:
      obstacle_height_mm: {default: 40, min: 10, max: 80, unit: mm, description: height of the obstacle}
    steps:
      - id: open_project
        action: freecad.open
        params: {document: "{example}/channel_obstacle.FCStd"}
        expects: [{path: "open_project/project.json"}]
      - id: solve
        action: openfoam.solve
        after: [mesh]
        confirm: [expensive]
        params: {case: "{steps.setup.case}"}

Values in ``params`` and ``expects`` are templates: ``{inputs.<name>}``, ``{steps.<id>.<output>}``, ``{workdir}``
(the run directory) and ``{example}`` (the folder of the workflow file). A template that is a whole value keeps the
type of what it refers to (a number stays a number).

classes.doc: The workflow file or the run inputs are invalid; ``errors`` lists every problem found.

classes.doc: A file or folder a step must leave behind. ``path`` is relative to the run directory.

classes.doc: An acceptance criterion on the result, evaluated by the ``verify.criteria`` action.

children.doc:
Engineering GUI agent: run a task in engineering software and deliver the files plus the evidence of what
happened ("Selenium for computational engineering").

* :mod:`.workflow`: the structured workflow (inputs with bounds, steps, preconditions, expected artifacts,
  confirmations, acceptance criteria), loaded from YAML/JSON.
* :mod:`.interpret`: a task (sentence or structured) to a committed workflow and its inputs; Ollama optional.
* :mod:`.adapters`: one adapter per application: FreeCAD and CfdOF (Python API inside the FreeCAD GUI), OpenFOAM
  (command line), ParaView (pvpython), ``verify`` (acceptance criteria with ``pinneapple_check``), ``web``
  (Playwright).
* :mod:`.display`: Xvfb virtual display, screenshots, GUI drivers (xdotool; Playwright; pywinauto for Windows).
* :mod:`.runner`: executes the steps, stops on failure or when a step needs a person's confirmation, records every
  command, log, artifact (SHA-256), screenshot and check.
* :mod:`.report`: self-contained HTML evidence report and the StudyResult JSON.

    from pinneapple_tools.automation import Runner, catalog, interpret
    it = interpret("channel with a 55 mm obstacle at 20 mm/s", catalog())
    run = Runner(it.workflow, "runs/r1", inputs=it.inputs).run(approve=["solve"], approver="me")
    print(run.state, run.message)          # report.html and study_result.json are in runs/r1

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite
pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.api
children.doc:
Arena — high-level API for running PINNeAPPle resolution pipelines.

This module bridges the problem design phase (``ProblemSpec``) with the
resolution pipeline (dataset generation → training → metrics).

Three entry points
------------------
1. From a ProblemSpec (built with ProblemBuilder)::

       from pinneapple_physics.pde_environment import ProblemBuilder
       from pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite import Arena

       spec = ProblemBuilder("heat_1d").domain(x=(0,1), t=(0,1)) ...build()
       result = Arena.from_spec(spec).run(model="VanillaPINN", epochs=5000)

2. From a registered preset::

       result = Arena.from_preset("burgers_1d", nu=0.01).run(...)

3. From a YAML config (existing workflow)::

       result = Arena.from_yaml("configs/experiment_burgers_1d.yaml").run()

Output contract
---------------
All ``.run()`` / ``.compare()`` calls return an ``ArenaResult`` dataclass with:
- ``spec``     : ProblemSpec used
- ``model``    : trained nn.Module
- ``history``  : list of loss dicts per epoch
- ``metrics``  : final evaluation metrics dict
- ``artifacts``: dict of paths to saved files

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.cases
children.doc:
The official benchmark cases and the protocol that makes their table reproducible (#30, roadmap item B3).

A benchmark case is only a benchmark if the same protocol can be applied to the next case without an argument about
what was measured. That is what lives here, in three parts:

* **the protocol** -- ``PROTOCOL``: the seeds, the training budget, the metrics, how the interval is computed, the
  evaluation points, and the tolerance a reproduction is allowed. It is data, so the page, the runner and the tests
  read the same numbers instead of three copies of them.
* **the cases** -- ``CASES``: three transient problems whose exact solution is a closed form, so the reference is not
  another numerical method that can be wrong in the same direction. Each one trains inside a *window* of the domain
  and is scored inside it (in-domain) and outside it (extrapolation): the second number is the one a surrogate user
  actually needs and the one a leaderboard usually omits.
* **the run** -- ``run_case``: one case, every seed of the protocol, the same budget for all of them, returning the
  per-seed metrics, the bootstrap interval and the cost.

Nothing here trains a competitor or claims a ranking; it measures the library against a closed form and publishes
the number it got, including the ones that are bad (all three extrapolate poorly, and the table says so).

Command line: ``python scripts/benchmark_cases.py --run`` writes ``benchmarks/cases/results.json`` and the page;
``--check`` verifies the declaration and the page without training; ``--reproduce`` runs the cases again and
compares them with what is published.

functions.doc:

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.crossframework.evaluate
children.doc:
The one evaluator of the cross-framework benchmark, and the statistics over seeds.

Every runner exports plain arrays (predictions on the shared test points, on the residual stencil, the identified
parameter of an inverse run, the operator predictions on the test split); this module turns them into metrics. A
framework's own reported error is never used.

Metrics (float64):

* ``rel_l2``: ``||u_pred - u_ref||_2 / ||u_ref||_2`` over the test points (:func:`pinneapple_physics.metrics.relative_l2`).
* ``max_abs``: ``max |u_pred - u_ref|`` over the test points.
* ``residual_rms``: root mean square of the PDE residual at fresh interior points, from second-order central
  differences of the exported stencil values (:func:`.problems.residual_from_stencil`); the same formula and step
  for every framework, so it measures the trained function, not the framework's autograd.
* inverse runs: ``nu_rel_err = |nu_hat - nu| / nu`` and the field ``rel_l2``.
* operator runs: mean per-sample relative L2 over the test split (the metric of Li et al. 2021).

functions.name: evaluate_pinn
functions.sig: (problem: PINNProblem, u_test: np.ndarray, u_stencil: np.ndarray | None = None, *, reference: np.ndarray | None = None) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Metrics of a forward run from its exported predictions.

``u_test``: predictions at :func:`.problems.test_points` (N or N x 1). ``u_stencil``: predictions at
``stencil(problem, residual_points(problem)).reshape(-1, 2)`` (5 M values). ``reference``: the reference at the
test points (computed here when omitted; pass it to avoid recomputing it for every run).

functions.name: evaluate_inverse
functions.sig: (nu_hat: float, nu_true: float, u_pred: np.ndarray, u_ref: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Inverse run: relative error of the identified coefficient and the field error on the test points.

functions.name: per_sample_rel_l2
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Per-sample relative L2 over all axes but the first (operator learning).

functions.name: evaluate_operator
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Operator run: mean, median and max of the per-sample relative L2 on the test split.

functions.name: seed_stats
functions.sig: (values: Iterable[float]) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
Median, min, max and n of the finite values; ``n_failed`` counts NaN / inf (failures are not dropped silently:
they are counted, and the median is over the finite values only).

functions.name: paired_ratio
functions.sig: (a: Mapping[int, float], b: Mapping[int, float]) -> dict[str, object]

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.crossframework.problems
children.doc:
The forward and inverse PINN problems of the cross-framework benchmark, with their references.

Every framework gets the same problem definition from here: domain, coefficients, source terms, the exact or
reference solution, the shared training point sets, the test points and the fresh residual points. Nothing in this
module depends on a competitor framework.

Problems (``benchmarks/vs_frameworks/PROTOCOL.md``):

* ``burgers``: ``u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx`` on ``x in [-1, 1]``, ``t in [0, 1]``, ``nu = 0.01 / pi``,
  ``u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x)``, ``u(+-1, t) = 0`` (Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis 2019). Reference: the Cole-Hopf
  solution by Gauss-Hermite quadrature, :func:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.burgers.burgers_sine_exact`.
* ``poisson``: ``u_xx + u_yy = f`` on the unit square, ``u = 0`` on the boundary, manufactured
  ``u = sin(pi x) sin(pi y)``, ``f = -2 pi^2 u``.
* ``helmholtz``: ``u_xx + u_yy + k^2 u = q`` on ``[-1, 1]^2``, ``u = 0`` on the boundary, manufactured
  ``u = sin(a1 pi x) sin(a2 pi y)`` with ``a1 = 1``, ``a2 = 4``, ``k = 1`` (Wang, Teng, Perdikaris 2021, SIAM J. Sci.
  Comput. 43(5), A3055), ``q = (k^2 - (a1 pi)^2 - (a2 pi)^2) u``.
* ``allen_cahn``: ``u_t = d u_xx + 5 u - 5 u^3`` on ``x in [-1, 1]`` periodic, ``t in [0, 1]``, ``d = 1e-4``,
  ``u(x, 0) = x^2 cos(pi x)`` (Raissi et al. 2019, the discrete-time example's data set). Reference:
  :func:`allen_cahn_reference`, Fourier pseudo-spectral in space and ETDRK4 in time
  (:class:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.etdrk4.ETDRK4`), checked by a resolution study in the tests.

The residual used by the neutral evaluator is computed by central finite differences from predictions on a
5-point stencil (:func:`residual_from_stencil`), so the same formula applies to every framework.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.deeponet_ground_truth
children.doc:
The four canonical operator-learning ground-truth solvers from Lu, Jin &
Karniadakis 2019 (DeepONet), arXiv:1910.03193, Section 4: given a GRF-sampled
input function u(x) (`pinneapple_data.grf_sampler.GRFDraw`), each solver
computes the TRUE solution of a different dynamical system driven by u.
Standard, widely-used ground truth for benchmarking any operator-learning
architecture (DeepONet, FNO, or otherwise) — not tied to a specific dataset
or application. Each solver takes a GRFDraw plus query points and operates
on ONE case at a time; a dataset-generation loop over many draws assembles
whatever operator-learning training format the caller needs (e.g. sensor
values + query point + solution at that query point).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.meta_benchmark
children.doc:
Meta-Learning Benchmark for PINNs.

Trains MAML and Reptile meta-models on PDE parameter families (e.g. Burgers
with varying viscosity nu), then evaluates K-shot adaptation against
from-scratch training with the same number of gradient steps.

The central result is a **K-shot error curve**: how quickly each approach
reaches low relative L2 error as K (adaptation steps) grows.

Algorithms
----------
MAML (FOMAML)
    Bi-level: inner loop adapts a copy for K steps on support set, outer loop
    minimises query-set loss w.r.t. the meta-initialization.  First-order
    approximation (FOMAML) is used — gradients through the inner update are
    detached, which scales to deep networks without higher-order overhead.

Reptile
    Per-task: deep-copy model, run K SGD steps, then interpolate meta-weights
    toward task weights by step size epsilon.  Simpler than MAML and often
    competitive in practice.

Scratch baseline
    Start from random Kaiming initialization, run K gradient steps.  Same
    optimizer (Adam) and same data as the meta-adapted models.

Full-scratch oracle
    Train from scratch for the same TOTAL gradient steps as meta-training
    (n_meta_epochs x n_tasks_per_batch x n_inner_steps).  Upper bound on
    what dedicated per-task training can achieve.

classes.name: MetaBenchmarkFamily
classes.doc: A parametric PDE family for meta-learning.

classes.name: MetaBenchmarkPipeline
classes.doc:
Meta-learning benchmark pipeline.

For each family:
  1. Meta-train MAML model on parameter family
  2. Meta-train Reptile model on parameter family
  3. For each eval task and each K in k_shots:
     a. Adapt MAML / Reptile for K steps -> eval
     b. Train from scratch for K steps -> eval
  4. Train from-scratch oracle (same total steps as meta-training)
  5. Report K-shot error curves comparing all approaches

Usage
-----
>>> pipe = MetaBenchmarkPipeline.default()
>>> results = pipe.run(verbose=True)
>>> print(pipe.leaderboard())
>>> pipe.plot_k_shot_curves()

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.physics_pipeline
children.doc:
PhysicsPipeline — standard 6-step PINNeAPPle physics pipeline.

Standard flow
-------------
  Step 1 – Problem selection   : preset registry, built-in list, or custom ProblemSpec
  Step 2 – Geometry & mesh     : GeometrySpec / MeshData / STL / None (use domain bounds)
  Step 3 – Auto-generate       : physics losses compiled + collocation + mesh sampling
  Step 4 – Solver selection    : auto-picks best numerical solver → synthetic reference data
  Step 5 – Models              : user list + physics loss auto-attached per architecture
  Step 6 – Train & export      : auto-metrics, train, visualize, checkpoint (.pt), rank table

Uses:
  - pinneapple_environment.presets  (get_preset, list_presets → ProblemSpec)
  - pinneapple_pinn                 (compile_problem, LossWeights → loss_fn)
  - pinneapple_models               (ModelRegistry.build → any registered model)
  - pinneapple_train.metrics        (MSE, MAE, RMSE, R2, RelL2, MaxError)
  - pinneapple_geom                 (GeometrySpec, MeshData → mesh-based sampling)
  - pinneapple_solvers              (SolverCatalog → numerical reference data)

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite import PhysicsPipeline

    pipeline = PhysicsPipeline(
        problem = "burgers_1d",
        models  = ["vanilla_pinn", "siren", "modified_mlp"],
        epochs  = 3000,
    )
    report = pipeline.run()
    report.save("outputs/burgers_report.json")

    # Show available problems
    PhysicsPipeline.list_problems()

# Backward-compatible alias
PhysicsBenchmarkSpec = PhysicsPipeline

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.runner.run_pipeline
children.doc:
End-to-end pipeline: geometry → solver → dataset → train → predict → report.

Orchestrates the complete workflow:
  1. Load or generate geometry (pinneapple_geom)
  2. Generate mesh (mesher_2d or gmsh)
  3. Run physical solver (OpenFOAM or FEniCS) to generate ground truth
  4. Build training dataset from solver output
  5. Train surrogate model (PINN, GNN, DeepONet, etc.)
  6. Run inference and compute error metrics
  7. Generate report: error plots, field comparisons, loss curves
  8. Save model + all logs + HTML/JSON report

YAML config example
-------------------
pipeline:
  name: my_experiment
  out_dir: results/my_experiment

geometry:
  type: rectangle         # rectangle | sdf | gmsh | mesh_file
  params:
    xlim: [0, 1]
    ylim: [0, 1]
    obstacle: {type: circle, center: [0.3, 0.5], radius: 0.05}

solver:
  backend: openfoam       # openfoam | fenics | builtin
  params:
    solver: simpleFoam
    n_iterations: 500
    n_cores: 4

problem:
  id: ns_incompressible_2d
  params:
    nu: 0.001
    Re: 100

dataset:
  n_collocation: 10000
  n_boundary: 4000
  strategy: lhs           # uniform | lhs | sobol | adaptive

models:
  - id: pinn_mlp
    type: VanillaPINN
    params:
      hidden: [128, 128, 128, 128]
      activation: tanh
    train:
      epochs: 2000
      lr: 1e-3
      device: cuda
      amp: true
      grad_clip: 1.0
      compile: true       # torch.compile()
      grad_accum_steps: 4
    physics_weights:
      pde: 1.0
      bc: 10.0
      data: 5.0

  - id: deeponet
    type: DeepONet
    ...

metrics: [mse, rmse, rel_l2, r2, max_error]

report:
  plots:
    - type: field_2d
      field: u
    - type: error_map_2d
      field: u
    - type: loss_curve
    - type: comparison_table
  format: html            # html | json | both
  save_model: true

functions.name: run_full_pipeline
functions.sig: (config_path_or_dict: Union[str, Path, Dict[str, Any]], *, out_dir: Optional[Union[str, Path]] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run the complete end-to-end pipeline.

Stages
------
1. Geometry — build or load domain geometry / mesh.
2. Solver — run a physical solver to generate ground-truth fields.
3. Dataset — sample collocation/BC/data points for PINN training.
4. Train — train each surrogate model defined in ``config["models"]``.
5. Inference — evaluate each model on a regular grid.
6. Metrics — compute scalar error metrics against labelled data.
7. Report — render error plots and write HTML/JSON summary.

Parameters
----------
config_path_or_dict:
    Either a path to a YAML file (str or :class:`pathlib.Path`) or a
    pre-built config dict following the schema described in the module
    docstring.
out_dir:

    when supplied.

Returns

Summary dict with keys:

- ``"pipeline_name"`` – str
- ``"out_dir"`` – str
- ``"geometry"`` – geometry object or None
- ``"solver_data"`` – dict of field arrays (may be empty)
- ``"models"`` – dict of model_id → result dict
- ``"artefacts"`` – dict of description → file path
- ``"timing"`` – dict of step → elapsed seconds
- ``"success"`` – bool

children.doc:
Navier-Stokes 2D Taylor-Green Vortex benchmark task.

PDE  : u_t + u*u_x + v*u_y = -p_x + nu*(u_xx + u_yy)
       v_t + u*v_x + v*v_y = -p_y + nu*(v_xx + v_yy)
       u_x + v_y = 0  (continuity)

Domain: (x,y) in [0, 2*pi]^2,  t in [0, 1]
Fields: (u, v, p)  (3 outputs)

Exact Taylor-Green Vortex solution:
  u(x,y,t) = -cos(x)*sin(y)*exp(-2*nu*t)
  v(x,y,t) =  sin(x)*cos(y)*exp(-2*nu*t)
  p(x,y,t) = -1/4*(cos(2*x) + cos(2*y))*exp(-4*nu*t)

nu   : 0.01 (default)

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.timeseries_pipeline
children.doc:
TimeSeriesBenchmarkSpec — declarative time-series benchmark pipeline.

Uses exclusively existing PINNeAPPle modules — nothing built from scratch:

  pinneapple_timeseries.datasets.windowed  WindowedTimeSeriesDataset (sliding windows)
  pinneapple_timeseries.spec               TimeSeriesSpec
  pinneapple_train.trainer                 Trainer, TrainConfig  (training loop)
  pinneapple_train.losses                  CombinedLoss, SupervisedLoss
  pinneapple_train.normalizers             StandardScaler
  pinneapple_train.metrics                 MetricBundle + individual metric classes
  pinneapple_data.datasets                 load_dataset  (data loading)
  pinneapple_models / TSModelCatalog       model registry fallback

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite import TimeSeriesBenchmarkSpec

    spec = TimeSeriesBenchmarkSpec(
        source   = "lorenz63",
        models   = ["lstm", "nbeats", "tcn"],
        metrics  = ["mse", "mae", "rmse"],
        horizon  = 50,
        lookback = 100,
        plots    = True,
    )
    report = spec.run()
    report.save("outputs/ts_benchmark.json")

children.name: pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.transfer_benchmark
children.doc:
Transfer Learning Benchmark for PINNs.

Trains a source model from scratch, then fine-tunes it to a family of target
problems using different strategies from ``pinneapple_transfer``.  Compares
each transfer approach against two from-scratch baselines.

Strategies
----------
scratch_budget : train from scratch with same epoch budget as fine-tuning
scratch_full   : train from scratch with source + fine-tune epochs (total budget)
finetune       : transfer all layers, low LR (TransferTrainer strategy="finetune")
partial_freeze : freeze first half of linear layers, fine-tune rest
feature_extract: freeze all except last linear layer
progressive    : frozen backbone for warmup_epochs, then full unfreeze

Key metrics
-----------
rel_l2            : relative L2 error vs exact/reference solution
speedup_factor    : steps_to_threshold(scratch_budget) / steps_to_threshold(transfer)
trainable_ratio   : trainable params / total params
convergence_epoch : first epoch where pde_residual < threshold

classes.name: TransferScenario
classes.doc: One transfer scenario: one source task and N target tasks.

classes.name: TransferBenchmarkPipeline
classes.doc:
Benchmark comparing transfer learning strategies against from-scratch baselines.

For each scenario (source_task → target_tasks):
  1. Train a source model from scratch (n_source_epochs)
  2. For each target task and each strategy:
     a. Clone source model, apply freeze strategy
     b. Fine-tune on target task for n_finetune_epochs via TransferTrainer
     c. Evaluate vs exact/reference solution
  3. Also run scratch_budget (n_finetune_epochs from random init)
     and scratch_full (n_source + n_finetune epochs from random init)
  4. Report and compare all strategies.

Usage
-----
>>> pipe = TransferBenchmarkPipeline.default()
>>> results = pipe.run(verbose=True)
>>> print(pipe.leaderboard())
>>> pipe.save_results("transfer_results.json")

children.name: pinneapple_tools.compute_backends.warp_backend
children.doc:
NVIDIA Warp backend: GPU kernels, ``warp.fem`` weak forms and a differentiable particle step.

`Warp <https://github.com/NVIDIA/warp>`_ (Apache-2.0) compiles ``@wp.kernel`` functions to CUDA (or to the CPU) and
carries a reverse-mode tape (``wp.Tape``) through them, so a step of a simulation written as kernels is differentiable
with respect to its inputs. PINNeAPPle already reaches Warp indirectly through the Newton rigid-body backend
(:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics`); this module is the direct entry point for the three
things that are only possible through Warp itself:

1. **Zero-copy tensors**: ``to_warp`` / ``to_torch`` share memory with PyTorch through DLPack. No copy, no
   serialisation: a tensor built by a PINNeAPPle trainer is the same buffer a kernel reads.
2. **``warp.fem`` weak forms**: assemble a Poisson stiffness matrix and load vector by integrating integrands over a
   grid, and solve it here. :func:`poisson_convergence` measures the error against a manufactured solution at every
   resolution and returns the observed order, which is the check the FEM path is held to.
3. **A differentiable particle step**: :class:`WarpBackend` exposes one symplectic Euler step of the rigid-body state
   used by :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.particle_dynamics` (``RigidBody.step``), recorded on a ``wp.Tape``.
   :meth:`WarpBackend.gradients_against_torch` runs both engines on the same inputs: the state agrees to
   ``1e-16`` and every gradient (position, velocity, force, torque) to ``1e-16`` relative, against the ``1e-6``
   the check asks for. What it took to get there is written next to the kernels: out-of-place writes, the loss as a
   kernel on the tape, and the quaternion in Warp's ``(x, y, z, w)`` order.

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_tools.compute_backends import warp_available, WarpBackend, poisson_convergence
>>> warp_available()                                    # pip install warp-lang
True
>>> rows = poisson_convergence((8, 16, 32))             # manufactured solution, assembled in warpfem
>>> rows[-1]["order"] > 2.0                             # observed convergence order
True

Every function imports Warp lazily: without ``warp-lang`` installed this module imports and
:func:`warp_available` returns ``False``, and the solvers raise :class:`ImportError` with the install line instead of
an obscure ``ModuleNotFoundError``.

Precision: the step kernels exist in **float64 and float32** -- two real kernels, because Warp compiles one per
concrete type. float64 is the default (it is the precision every gradient check in this repository is made at);
float32 is what a consumer NVIDIA GPU is fast at, and `WarpBackend(dim, precision="float32").float32_matches_float64()`
measures how far the two drift apart over a run instead of assuming it is negligible.

Install: ``pip install warp-lang`` (a CUDA build is selected automatically on an NVIDIA machine; ``warp-lang`` also
runs on the CPU, which is what the checks below use).

classes.name: FemPoissonSolution
classes.doc: Result of one ``warp.fem`` Poisson solve on the unit square with homogeneous Dirichlet data.

classes.name: WarpBackend
classes.sig: (dim: int = 2, *, device: str | None = None, precision: str = 'float64')
classes.doc:
One symplectic Euler step of :class:`pinneapple_simulation.particle_dynamics.RigidBodyState`, in Warp.

The step is the same arithmetic as ``particle_dynamics.RigidBody.step`` (``v += dt f/m``, ``x += dt v``, then
the rotation), and the reason to run it in Warp is the tape: :meth:`step_with_tape` records the steps, so
``tape.backward(loss)`` gives ``d loss / d v0``, ``d loss / d force`` and ``d loss / d torque`` for a loss read
off the new state, without a PyTorch graph in the loop. :meth:`gradients_against_torch` runs both engines on the
same inputs and returns the disagreement, which is the check this backend is held to.

``precision`` is ``"float64"`` (default: what every gradient check in this repository is made at) or
``"float32"`` (what a consumer GPU is fast at). Both are real kernels, not a cast: Warp compiles one kernel per
concrete type. ``float32_matches_float64`` measures how far the two drift apart over a run.

:meth:`step` returns a **new** state instead of overwriting the one it is given (see the note on the kernels).
``pos``/``vel``/``omega`` (and ``quat`` in 3-D) are Warp vector types of the chosen precision, ``force`` and
``torque`` are Warp arrays (scalar torque in 2-D), and the mass and inertia are numpy arrays.

methods.name: state_arrays
methods.sig: (*, n_bodies: int, requires_grad: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Zero-initialised state arrays for ``n_bodies`` bodies (identity quaternion in 3-D).

methods.name: step
methods.sig: (state: dict[str, Any], *, force, torque, mass, dt: float, inertia = None, inertia_inv = None) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: One step, **out of place**: returns the new state, leaving ``state`` untouched.

methods.name: position_sq_loss
methods.sig: (state: dict[str, Any], out: Any | None = None, *, rotation: bool = False)
methods.doc: ``sum_i |pos_i|^2`` (plus the rotation when ``rotation``) as a Warp array.

methods.name: step_with_tape
methods.sig: (state: dict[str, Any], *, force, torque, mass, dt: float, n_steps: int = 1, inertia = None, inertia_inv = None, loss: Callable | None = None)
methods.doc: Record ``n_steps`` steps on a ``wp.Tape``; returns ``(tape, state)`` or ``(tape, state, loss_array)``.

methods.name: gradients_against_torch
methods.sig: (*, dt: float = 0.02, n_steps: int = 4, n_bodies: int = 3, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Run the same steps through Warp (with its tape) and through ``RigidBody.step`` (with autograd).

methods.name: float32_matches_float64
methods.sig: (*, dt: float = 0.02, n_steps: int = 20, n_bodies: int = 8, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Run the same steps in both precisions and report how far the state drifts apart.

functions.name: warp_available
functions.sig: () -> bool
functions.doc: ``True`` when ``warp`` imports. Does not initialise a device beyond what ``wp.init`` does.

functions.name: warp_device
functions.sig: () -> str | None
functions.doc: The Warp device kernels will run on: ``"cuda:0"`` on an NVIDIA GPU, otherwise ``"cpu"``.

functions.name: to_warp
functions.sig: (x, *, requires_grad: bool = False)
functions.doc:
A Warp array that shares memory with the PyTorch tensor ``x`` (DLPack, no copy).

``x`` must be contiguous and on a device Warp can see (CUDA tensor on a CUDA build, or a CPU tensor).

functions.name: to_torch
functions.sig: (a, *, requires_grad: bool | None = None)
functions.doc: A PyTorch tensor that shares memory with the Warp array ``a``.

functions.name: manufactured_u
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: The manufactured solution, for a reference plot or a quick check outside Warp.

functions.name: manufactured_f
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``-laplace(u)`` of :func:`manufactured_u`.

functions.name: fem_poisson
functions.sig: (resolution: int, *, degree: int = 2, tol: float = 1e-12) -> FemPoissonSolution
functions.doc:
Solve ``-laplace(u) = f`` on the unit square with ``u = 0`` on all four sides, in ``warp.fem``.

``degree`` is the polynomial degree of the shape functions on the quad grid (``1`` for Q1, ``2`` for Q2).
The Dirichlet data is imposed by projecting the linear system (``fem.project_linear_system``), not by a penalty.

functions.name: poisson_convergence
functions.sig: (resolutions: Iterable[int] = (8, 16, 32, 64), *, degree: int = 2) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
``fem_poisson`` at every resolution, with the error and the observed order against the manufactured solution.

A correct Q1 assembly converges at order ~2 in L2 and Q2 at ~3; an assembly error (a missing Jacobian, a
boundary term left out) shows up as a stuck error and an order near zero, which is what this returns.

children.summary: NVIDIA Warp backend: GPU kernels, warp.fem weak forms and a differentiable particle step.

children.doc:
Multi-backend support for PINNeAPPle: PyTorch (default), JAX and NVIDIA Warp.

Provides a backend abstraction layer so PINN code can run on PyTorch or JAX
without modification.  JAX gives ``vmap``/``jit`` speedups on CPU/TPU; the
default PyTorch backend requires no extra dependencies.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_tools.compute_backends import set_backend, get_backend, JAXBackend

    # Switch to JAX (requires: pip install jax jaxlib)
    set_backend("jax")
    print(get_backend())  # "jax"

    # JIT-compile a PINN. residual_fn receives (u_fn, x), where u_fn is
    # model_fn bound to params (x -> u(x)), so it can take derivatives via
    # jax.grad/jax.hessian -- not a precomputed value, which JAX cannot
    # differentiate.
    compiled = JAXBackend.jit_pinn(model_fn, residual_fn)

    # Vectorise a single-point residual over a batch of collocation points
    batched = JAXBackend.vmap_residual(single_pt_residual)

    # Convert between PyTorch and JAX
    jax_x = JAXBackend.torch_to_jax(torch_tensor)
    torch_x = JAXBackend.jax_to_torch(jax_array)

NVIDIA Warp (``pip install warp-lang``) is a third entry point, for work a PinT/JAX engine cannot do: GPU kernels
with a reverse-mode tape, ``warp.fem`` weak forms and zero-copy torch buffers. It is not a drop-in array engine
(Warp differentiates through an explicit ``wp.Tape``, not through the functions you write), so it has its own
namespace::

    from pinneapple_tools.compute_backends import warp_available, WarpBackend, poisson_convergence

    poisson_convergence((8, 16, 32))          # FEM manufactured-solution order, assembled in warp.fem
    WarpBackend(3).gradients_against_torch()  # d state / d v0 from the tape vs torch.autograd
children.summary: Multi-backend support for PINNeAPPle: PyTorch (default), JAX and NVIDIA Warp.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.dataset_quality
pinneapple_tools.dataset_quality.checks
children.doc:
Generic dataset quality-assessment checks.

Operates on a plain `(coords, fields)` representation of a point-cloud
dataset (`coords`: (N, d) array of sample locations; `fields`: {name: array}
of per-point field values, each array's leading dimension of length N) — the
same shape any PDE/PINN dataset naturally takes, independent of where it came
from. No framework dependency (no orchestration/task-runner coupling).

functions.name: analyze_completeness
functions.sig: (fields: Dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: NaN/missing-value fraction per field, plus an overall completeness score.

functions.name: validate_consistency
functions.sig: (coords: np.ndarray, fields: Dict[str, np.ndarray], monotonic_name_hints: tuple = _MONOTONIC_NAME_HINTS) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Generic cross-field consistency checks:
  - shape consistency: every field array's leading dim must match coords.shape[0]
  - monotonicity heuristic: fields whose *name* suggests a cumulative/
    time-like quantity are checked for (near) non-decreasing behavior.
This is intentionally generic/heuristic — it has no per-problem physical
knowledge (a real physics-residual check is a separate concern).

functions.name: analyze_distribution
functions.sig: (fields: Dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: scipy.stats.describe per field (mean/variance/skewness/kurtosis).

functions.name: detect_outliers
functions.sig: (fields: Dict[str, np.ndarray], random_state: int = 42) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
IsolationForest fit jointly across all numeric fields (stacked as a
feature matrix over points); report the fraction flagged as outliers.

functions.name: field_range_issues
functions.sig: (fields: Dict[str, np.ndarray], ranges: Dict[str, Any]) -> list
functions.doc:
Generic per-field physical-range check, keyed by the field's literal
name: {field_name: (lo, hi)}. Returns a list of human-readable issue
strings (empty if everything is within bounds).

functions.name: build_1d_linear_interpolant
functions.sig: (z: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> 'Any'
functions.doc:
Build a differentiable (torch) piecewise-linear interpolant from a set
of 1D-coordinate samples `z` and corresponding output samples `y`
(shape (N,) and (N, k)). Useful for evaluating a differentiable
PDE-residual function against static point-cloud data when no trained
model is available — the interpolant stands in as a rough, cheap
surrogate. This is an approximation (the true field is only piecewise-
linear between samples), appropriate for a rough consistency signal, not
a rigorous PDE check.

children.summary: Generic dataset quality-assessment checks.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.dataset_quality.vlm_curation
children.doc:
Vision-language-model dataset curation.

Generic engine for curating a synthetic training dataset by running a
vision-language model (VLM) over a short video clip of each sequence and
using its judgment of physical plausibility to filter a raw dataset down
to a "curated" one before training on it.

Ported and generalized from a downstream project (``physcurator``), which
used this exact approach -- clip -> VLM judgment -> JSON label/confidence
-> filter -- to screen synthetic 2D heat-diffusion sequences for
physically-implausible injected anomalies, against a fixed model
(``nvidia/Cosmos-Reason2-2B``) and a hardcoded heat-diffusion prompt.
Nothing in this module is heat2d-specific or Cosmos-specific: the VLM
model name/class, the prompt template (via a caller-supplied physics
description), and the raw-sequence -> clip-path lookup are all parameters
here. ``physcurator`` itself now calls into this module rather than
duplicating the logic locally.

Design, stated plainly (same "no fabricated results" stance as the rest of
this package): this module never invents a curation judgment. Every
label/confidence/reason returned by :func:`curate_sequence` /
:func:`curate_dataset` comes from parsing the VLM's own generated text
(via :func:`extract_json`); a response that is missing or isn't valid,
parseable JSON degrades to a neutral fallback label at confidence 0.5, it
is never silently promoted to a "consistent"/"passed" judgment. Running
:func:`curate_dataset` end to end against a real model requires the
``vlm_curation`` extra (``transformers`` + ``accelerate``) and, for a
hosted checkpoint such as ``nvidia/Cosmos-Reason2-2B``, a real GPU and a
Hugging Face download -- this module has no offline stand-in for the VLM's
judgment itself. :func:`curate_sequence` and :func:`curate_dataset` both
accept an already-loaded ``model``/``processor`` pair, so callers (and
tests) can inject a stub that never touches the network.

classes.name: CurationRecord
classes.doc: One sequence's curation judgment.

functions.name: build_consistency_prompt
functions.sig: (pde_description: str, *, labels: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_LABELS, extra_instructions: Optional[str] = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Build the text prompt asking a VLM to judge a clip's physical
consistency against a stated governing-physics assumption.

Parameters
----------
pde_description : a short, physics-grounded statement of what the clip
    is supposed to show, e.g. ``"governing PDE is dT/dt =
    alpha * Laplacian(T), with constant Dirichlet boundary
    temperature"`` (the exact text ``physcurator`` uses for its
    heat-2D scenario) -- this is the only domain-specific input the
    prompt needs.
labels : the closed label set the VLM must choose from. Defaults to
    ``("consistent", "suspect", "inconsistent")``.
extra_instructions : optional additional free-text appended to the
    task instructions (e.g. dataset-specific caveats).

Returns
-------
The full prompt string, unchanged in structure from ``physcurator``'s
original ``curator/prompts.py::build_prompt`` (same three-part task,
same "JSON only" instruction), just parameterized.

functions.name: extract_json
functions.sig: (text: str) -> Optional[dict]
functions.doc:
Best-effort extraction of the first ``{...}`` JSON object found in
a block of free-form generated text. Returns ``None`` (never raises)
if no valid JSON object is present.

functions.name: normalize_label
functions.sig: (label: Any, *, labels: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_LABELS, fallback: Optional[str] = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Normalize a (possibly malformed) label value onto the closed
``labels`` set: exact match (case/whitespace-insensitive) first, then
substring containment against each candidate label, else ``fallback``
(defaults to the middle label of ``labels``, matching ``physcurator``'s
original "suspect" -- neither pass nor fail -- default).

functions.name: clamp_confidence
functions.sig: (x: Any, *, lo: float = 0.0, hi: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Coerce ``x`` to a float and clamp it to ``[lo, hi]``; a value that
can't be parsed as a float falls back to the midpoint.

functions.name: parse_curation_response
functions.sig: (seq_id: str, text: str, *, labels: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_LABELS, reason_max_chars: int = 300, raw_text_max_chars: int = 1200) -> CurationRecord
functions.doc:
Parse one VLM generation into a :class:`CurationRecord`. Never
raises: a response that fails to parse as JSON yields the fallback
label at confidence 0.5, with an empty reason -- the honest signal
that the model's output was unusable, not a guessed judgment.

functions.name: load_vlm
functions.sig: (model_name: str, *, device: Optional[str] = None, dtype: Optional[Any] = None, model_cls: Optional[Any] = None, attn_implementation: str = 'sdpa')
functions.doc:
Load a Hugging Face vision-language chat model + its processor.

Requires the ``vlm_curation`` extra (``pip install
"pinneapple[vlm_curation]"`` -- ``transformers`` + ``accelerate``);
raises a clear ``ImportError`` naming it if missing, same pattern as
every other optional heavy-dependency bridge in this package (see
``pinneapple_llm.finetune.finetune_lora``).

Parameters
----------
model_name : a Hugging Face model id, e.g. ``"nvidia/Cosmos-Reason2-2B"``.
model_cls : the model class to instantiate. Defaults to
    ``transformers.AutoModelForImageTextToText``, which resolves most
    chat-style VLMs; some checkpoints (Cosmos-Reason2 among them, which
    is a Qwen3-VL-architecture model) are not yet wired into that Auto
    class in every ``transformers`` release -- pass e.g.
    ``transformers.Qwen3VLForConditionalGeneration`` explicitly if the
    Auto class raises for your checkpoint.

Returns
-------
``(model, processor)``

functions.name: curate_sequence
functions.sig: (model: Any, processor: Any, clip_path: str, prompt: str, *, seq_id: str = '', fps: int = 4, max_new_tokens: int = 512, labels: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_LABELS, system_message: str = 'You are a helpful assistant.') -> CurationRecord
functions.doc:
Run one VLM generation over a single clip and parse the result.

``model``/``processor`` are duck-typed to the Hugging Face chat-VLM
contract used by ``processor.apply_chat_template`` +
``model.generate`` + ``processor.batch_decode`` (exactly what
:func:`load_vlm` returns) -- this function itself imports no
heavy dependency, so it can be exercised in tests against a stub
model/processor pair with no ``transformers``/GPU involved.

functions.name: curate_dataset
functions.sig: (index: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]], *, out_dir: str, model_name: str = 'nvidia/Cosmos-Reason2-2B', model: Any = None, processor: Any = None, model_cls: Optional[Any] = None, prompt: Optional[str] = None, pde_description: Optional[str] = None, labels: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_LABELS, id_field: str = 'id', clip_field: str = 'mp4', raw_sequence_loader: Optional[Callable[[Mapping[str, Any]], str]] ...
functions.doc:
Curate every sequence in ``index`` with a VLM and write per-sequence
+ aggregate curation metadata to ``out_dir`` (mirrors
``physcurator``'s ``curator/run_cosmos.py`` orchestration, generalized).

Parameters
----------
index : one entry per sequence, each a mapping with at least an
    ``id_field`` key and whatever the ``raw_sequence_loader`` (or,
    by default, ``clip_field``) needs to locate that sequence's clip.
raw_sequence_loader : ``item -> clip_path``. Defaults to
    ``lambda item: item[clip_field]`` (the common case: the index
    entry already carries a path to a pre-rendered clip, as
    ``physcurator``'s ``data/generate_heat2d.py`` produces).
model, processor : an already-loaded VLM + processor pair (see
    :func:`load_vlm`). If either is ``None``, both are loaded via
    ``load_vlm(model_name, model_cls=model_cls, device=device)`` --
    requires the ``vlm_curation`` extra and, for a real checkpoint, a
    GPU.
model_cls : forwarded to :func:`load_vlm` when ``model``/``processor``
    aren't already loaded -- pass this when ``model_name``'s
    checkpoint needs a specific model class rather than
    ``transformers.AutoModelForImageTextToText`` (e.g.
    ``nvidia/Cosmos-Reason2-2B`` needs
    ``transformers.Qwen3VLForConditionalGeneration`` on at least some
    ``transformers`` releases -- see :func:`load_vlm`'s docstring).
prompt : the full prompt text. If not given, built via
    :func:`build_consistency_prompt` from ``pde_description``
    (required in that case).
resume : skip sequences that already have both a per-sequence JSON
    file in ``out_dir`` and an entry in ``out_dir/curation_index.json``
    -- lets a long curation run be safely re-launched.

Returns
-------
The full list of :class:`CurationRecord` (previously-done + freshly
curated), sorted by id -- also the content written to
``out_dir/curation_index.json``.

functions.name: filter_curated
functions.sig: (index: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]], curation_records: Sequence[Any], *, keep_labels: Sequence[str] = ('consistent',), min_confidence: float = 0.55, id_field: str = 'id', data_field: str = 'npz', out_dir: Optional[str] = None) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
Filter ``index`` down to entries whose curation judgment is in
``keep_labels`` and meets ``min_confidence`` (mirrors ``physcurator``'s
``data/make_curated.py``, generalized off the ``"npz"`` field name and
off filesystem copying being mandatory).

``curation_records`` may be :class:`CurationRecord` instances or plain
dicts with the same keys (as read back from a ``curation_index.json``).

If ``out_dir`` is given, the kept entries' ``data_field`` file is
copied into it (``shutil.copy2``) and the returned entry's
``data_field`` is rewritten to that new path -- matching
``make_curated.py``'s behaviour of materializing a standalone curated
dataset directory. If ``out_dir`` is ``None``, filtering only: no
filesystem I/O, ``data_field`` is left untouched.

Returns the kept entries (each the original index item plus
``label``/``confidence``/``reason``), and, if ``out_dir`` is given,
also writes ``out_dir/index.json`` with that same list.

children.summary: Vision-language-model dataset curation.

children.doc:
pinneapple_tools.dataset_quality — dataset quality assessment.

Two independent ways to vet a dataset before training on it:

``checks``
    Generic, statistical/heuristic checks over a plain ``(coords,
    fields)`` point-cloud representation: completeness (NaN fraction),
    cross-field shape/monotonicity consistency, distribution summaries,
    IsolationForest outlier detection, physical-range issues. No
    framework dependency, no model involved.

``vlm_curation``
    Vision-language-model curation: run a VLM over a short clip of each
    sequence and use its label/confidence judgment (parsed from real
    generated text, never fabricated) to filter a raw dataset down to a
    curated one before training. Ported and generalized from the
    downstream ``physcurator`` project. Requires the ``vlm_curation``
    extra to actually run a model; the parsing/filtering logic itself has
    no heavy dependency.
children.summary: Dataset quality assessment.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.model_evaluation
pinneapple_tools.model_evaluation.metrics
children.doc:
Generic model-evaluation metrics: regression performance, bootstrap
uncertainty, one-at-a-time sensitivity, and calibration — independent of any
particular model storage/registry format. Callers supply plain arrays
(`y_true`, `y_pred`, `coords`) or a plain callable (for sensitivity), not a
framework-specific artifact object.

functions.name: regression_metrics
functions.sig: (y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray, field_names: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
RMSE/MAE/relative-error/R2, overall and per output column.

`y_true`/`y_pred`: (N,) or (N, k) arrays. `field_names`: optional length-k
labels for the per-field breakdown (defaults to "field_0", "field_1", ...).

functions.name: axis_binned_profile
functions.sig: (coord: np.ndarray, field: np.ndarray, n_bins: int = 40) -> Dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Bin ``field`` by one coordinate axis and average within each bin --
the standard way to compare a statistically-homogeneous-in-the-other-
directions field (e.g. a channel/boundary-layer flow's velocity, which
varies with wall-normal distance but is turbulent/scattered in the
other two directions) against a model's prediction: comparing single
(x, z) lines would just compare two different turbulent realizations
at the same y, not the underlying profile.

Parameters
----------
coord : (N,) the binning coordinate (e.g. wall-normal y).
field : (N,) or (N, k) the scalar/vector field to average per bin.
n_bins : number of equal-width bins spanning ``coord``'s range.

Returns
-------
dict with ``"bin_centers"`` (mean ``coord`` actually observed in each
bin, not the bin's geometric midpoint -- matches what the real data in
that bin represents) and ``"bin_means"`` (mean ``field`` per bin, same
trailing shape as ``field``). Empty bins get ``coord``'s midpoint and
NaN respectively.

A model's own prediction should be evaluated by sampling many (x, z)
(or whatever the other axes are) at each returned ``bin_centers``
value and averaging those predictions the same way, then compared
against ``bin_means`` (e.g. via :func:`regression_metrics`) -- not by
evaluating the model once per bin at one arbitrary point.

functions.name: mape
functions.sig: (y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray, eps: float = 1e-08) -> float
functions.doc:
Mean Absolute Percentage Error, as a fraction (multiply by 100 for %).
`eps` guards division by near-zero targets — MAPE dominated by that guard
rather than genuine relative error is a sign `y_true` has values near
zero, not a bug in this function.

functions.name: worst_n_points
functions.sig: (coords: np.ndarray, abs_residuals: np.ndarray, field_names: Sequence[str], n: int = 20) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
Indices/coordinates of the n points with the largest total absolute
error (summed across output fields) — useful for spotting where a model
fits worst.

functions.name: bootstrap_confidence_interval
functions.sig: (residuals: np.ndarray, n_boot: int = 1000, ci: float = 90.0, seed: int = 42) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Bootstrap confidence interval on the mean residual — a simple,
dependency-free uncertainty estimate when no dedicated UQ model is
available.

functions.name: one_at_a_time_sensitivity
functions.sig: (model_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], base_inputs: np.ndarray, param_columns: Dict[str, int], perturb_frac: float = 0.1, default_nominal: float = 1.0) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
First-order, one-at-a-time sensitivity: for each named input column,
perturb it +/- `perturb_frac` around its mean value in `base_inputs` and
measure |model(plus) - model(minus)| / |delta_input|.

This is a simple, hand-rolled approximation — NOT full Sobol/Saltelli
variance-based sensitivity (see `pinneapple_data.parameter_sampling`'s
`saltelli_perturbation_sweep` if that's what's needed instead).

`model_fn`: callable mapping an (N, D) array to an (N, k) (or (N,)) array.
`param_columns`: {display_name: column_index_into base_inputs}.

functions.name: gradient_sensitivity
functions.sig: (model: Callable, x: Any, n_out: Optional[int] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Exact autograd-based sensitivity: mean |d output_j / d input_i| over
the rows of `x`, computed via a single vectorized backward pass per
output channel — not a finite-difference approximation like
`one_at_a_time_sensitivity` above. Requires `model` to be a
differentiable ``torch.nn.Module`` (or any callable built from
differentiable torch ops) and `x` a ``(N, D)`` torch.Tensor.

Complements `one_at_a_time_sensitivity`: use this when the model is
differentiable and you want the exact local gradient rather than a
perturbation-based estimate; use OAT when the model is a black box
(only callable on numpy arrays).

functions.name: calibration_curve
functions.sig: (y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray, residual_std: float, levels: Sequence[float] = (0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95)) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Empirical coverage of a Gaussian(0, residual_std) predictive interval
at each nominal confidence level — compares against the ideal diagonal to
show whether a model's uncertainty estimate is well-calibrated.

children.summary: HTTP front end of the model services (standard library only), with the routes of NVIDIA NIM.

children.doc:
PINNeAPPle Model Services: ready-made PINNeAPPle models as local microservices with the shape of NVIDIA NIM.

Each service is a model with a card (task, inputs, outputs, validity range, measured metrics, references) and a
trust function; every answer carries PINNeAPPle's trust report (decision APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT with its checks),
and a query outside the validity range says so. The HTTP routes follow NIM's: ``GET /v1/health/ready``,
``GET /v1/health/live``, ``GET /v1/models`` (OpenAI list format), ``POST /v1/infer`` (``{"model", "inputs"}``) and,
for language services, ``POST /v1/chat/completions`` (OpenAI format, with ``nvext.guided_json``).

    from pinneapple_tools.model_services import default_registry, serve_in_thread, ModelServiceClient
    server, url = serve_in_thread(default_registry())
    c = ModelServiceClient(url)
    c.models(); c.infer("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", {...})        # outputs + trust
    ModelServiceClient("https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1", api_key=os.environ["NVIDIA_API_KEY"]).chat(...)

``python -m pinneapple_tools.model_services serve --port 8000`` runs the server; ``docker/model_services`` has a
Dockerfile and a compose file. Built-in services: every model of the PINNeAPPle zoo (``pp.zoo``, trust from
``pp.zoo.validate``), physics checks of any field (``pp.trust_card``), and ``pinneapple-intent``, the deterministic
specification extractor of ``pinneapple_design.intent`` behind the chat route (no network, no key: every value it
returns comes with the quote it was read from).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.nvidia
pinneapple_tools.nvidia.brep
children.doc:
Exact geometry with NVIDIA USD BRep (the SMLib NURBS B-rep kernel, ``pip install usd-brep``), measured for
PINNeAPPle: mass properties of the exact solid, curvature of every face, tessellations at several chord tolerances
with their measured deviation from the exact surfaces, and B-rep USD export.

    part = PartRecipe().box("plate", (0, 0, 0), (0.1, 0.06, 0.01)) \
                       .cylinder("hole", (0.05, 0.03, -0.005), 0.01, 0.02).difference("bracket", "plate", "hole")
    rep = evaluate_part(part, chord_tolerances=[1e-4, 1e-5], density=2700.0, usd_brep_path="bracket_brep.usda")
    rep.volume, rep.min_radius, rep.tessellations[-1]["max_deviation"], rep.mesh(-1)   # (V, F) of the finest mesh

A part is a recipe (a list of operations on named solids), so it is data: it can be stored with a result,
regenerated, varied by a design study, or written by a model service. The kernel runs in a worker process
(:mod:`pinneapple_tools.nvidia._brep_worker`) in whichever interpreter has ``usd_brep``: the current one if it
imports, else ``$PINNEAPPLE_BREP_PYTHON`` (the ``usd-brep`` wheel is built for CPython 3.12 only:
``python3.12 -m venv /opt/brep && /opt/brep/bin/pip install usd-brep numpy`` and point the variable at
``/opt/brep/bin/python``).

Checks it gives a trust report: the solid is manifold; mesh volume and area converge to the exact ones; the
largest distance from a mesh triangle to the exact surface (chord error) is below the tolerance asked; the mesh
size resolves the smallest radius of curvature of the part (holes, fillets).
