Architecture diagrams of a PINNeAPPle + NVIDIA pipeline, drawn by code (matplotlib only, no graphviz).

    from pinneapple_tools.nvidia.diagram import Block, architecture_diagram

    blocks = [Block("data", "Darcy solver\n(finite volumes)", "pinneapple", col=0),
              Block("fno", "FNO\nphysicsnemo.models.fno", "physicsnemo", col=1),
              Block("usd", "USD stage\n(OpenUSD, usd-core)", "omniverse", col=2),
              Block("kit", "Omniverse Kit / RTX", "omniverse", col=3, ran=False)]
    architecture_diagram("Cold plate", blocks, [("data", "fno", "a, T pairs"), ("fno", "usd", "T field")], "arch.png")

Each block has an owner (``pinneapple``, an NVIDIA product: ``physicsnemo``, ``omniverse``, ``brep``, ``isaac``,
``cosmos``, ``nim``, or a PINNeAPPle stack: ``robotsim``, ``services``, ``worldmodel``) that sets its colour, a column (left to right is the data flow) and an optional row. ``ran=False`` draws a
dashed, hatched block: the step needs a GPU, an API key or a download and was not executed where the figure was made.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.nvidia.isaac
children.doc:
Isaac Sim-ready robots in OpenUSD (``UsdPhysics``), their checks, and the Isaac Sim script that replays a motion.

Isaac Sim simulates articulations described with the ``UsdPhysics`` schemas (rigid bodies with mass properties,
colliders, revolute joints with drives, an articulation root, a physics scene). This module writes those from a
plain description, so the masses and inertias Isaac Sim uses are the ones PINNeAPPle computed with:

``Link`` / ``Joint`` / ``ArticulationSpec`` (from :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim.spec`)
    links as boxes or cylinders (visual + collider) with mass, centre of mass and principal inertia; revolute
    joints with an anchor point, axis, limits and an angular drive (position or effort).
``author_articulation(stage, spec)``
    adds the robot under ``/World/<name>`` of a :class:`pinneapple_tools.nvidia.omniverse.FieldStage` (or any
    ``Usd.Stage``) with a ``PhysicsScene``, a ground plane, a fixed joint to the world for a fixed base, and the
    articulation root on the robot prim.
``validate_physics(path)``
    :func:`omniverse.validate_stage` plus the physics a simulator will read: ``UsdPhysics.LoadUsdPhysicsFromRange``
    (the USD physics parser) finds every body, joint and articulation; masses positive; inertias physical
    (triangle inequality); every joint between rigid bodies; a gravity direction and magnitude.
``isaac_replay_script(...)``
    a standalone Isaac Sim script (``isaacsim.SimulationApp``, ``isaacsim.core.api.World``,
    ``isaacsim.core.prims.SingleArticulation``) that opens the stage, applies the joint torques PINNeAPPle computed
    (or tracks the positions with the drives), and saves the joint positions and measured efforts to ``.npz``.
    Needs Isaac Sim (RTX GPU); written against the 5.x API, which 6.x still ships (deprecated).
``compare_replay(npz, t, q, tau)``
    tracking and effort errors of an Isaac Sim replay against PINNeAPPle's trajectory.

functions.sig: (stage, spec: ArticulationSpec) -> str
functions.doc: Write ``spec`` under ``/World/<name>``; returns that prim path. ``stage``: a ``FieldStage`` or ``Usd.Stage``.

functions.name: validate_physics
functions.sig: (path: str, *, expect_bodies: int | None = None, expect_joints: int | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc: :func:`validate_stage` plus the ``UsdPhysics`` parse and the mass / joint checks a simulator relies on.

functions.name: isaac_replay_script
functions.sig: (usd_path: str, robot_prim: str, traj_npz: str, out_npz: str, *, mode: str = 'effort', physics_dt: float = 1.0 / 600.0, headless: bool = True) -> str
functions.doc:
Standalone Isaac Sim script (run with Isaac Sim's ``python.sh``). ``traj_npz`` holds ``t``, ``q`` [rad],
``tau`` [N m] (joint order of the USD articulation); ``mode="effort"`` applies ``tau`` open loop, ``"position"``
tracks ``q`` with the drives. Writes ``t``, ``q`` and ``effort`` (``get_measured_joint_efforts``) to
``out_npz``.

functions.name: compare_replay
functions.sig: (npz: str, t, q, tau) -> dict
functions.doc: Max tracking error [rad] and RMS effort error relative to the peak torque, Isaac Sim replay vs PINNeAPPle.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.nvidia.omniverse
children.doc:
PINNeAPPle results as OpenUSD stages for NVIDIA Omniverse (authored and checked with ``usd-core``).

Omniverse apps (USD Composer, Kit, Isaac Sim) open OpenUSD files. This module writes a result as a USD stage with the
physics fields kept as data, not only as colours, and checks the file before anyone opens it:

``FieldStage``
    ``/World`` (Z up, metres) with meshes (``add_mesh``), curves (``add_curves``, pipes, streamlines) and points
    (``add_points``, sensors). Every field is a ``primvars:<name>`` float array (vertex interpolation) with its unit
    in ``pinneapple:unit:<name>``; one field per prim is also baked into ``primvars:displayColor`` so any USD viewer
    shows it. ``add_time_samples`` keys a field (and its colours) over time, so the Omniverse timeline plays a
    transient result. ``set_trust`` stores a trust decision and its checks on a prim (``pinneapple:trust:*``), so the
    scene carries the verdict of the numbers it shows.
``validate_stage``
    re-opens the file and checks it: it opens, up axis and units, every mesh has consistent topology (indices inside
    the points, counts summing to the indices), every vertex primvar has one finite value per point (per time
    sample), extents are set, and the ``UsdUtils.ComplianceChecker`` result.
``render_stage_png``
    a preview: the meshes and curves read back from the file, drawn with matplotlib in their ``displayColor``. It is
    a check that the file holds what was written, not an Omniverse RTX render.
``kit_render_script``
    the script to run inside Omniverse Kit / USD Composer (``omni.usd``, ``omni.kit.viewport.utility``) to open the
    stage and capture an RTX viewport image. Needs an Omniverse install with an RTX GPU.
``grid_surface`` / ``extrude_profile`` / ``tube``
    triangle meshes for the common cases (a plate with a field on it, an extruded section, a pipe along a path).

functions.sig: (path: str, *, required_primvars: Mapping[str, Sequence[str]] | None = None, compliance: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Re-open a USD file and check it. Returns ``{"ok", "problems", "prims", "meshes", "curves", "points",
"time_samples", "up_axis", "meters_per_unit", "compliance"}``. ``required_primvars``: prim path -> primvar
names that must be there.

Every validator OpenUSD registers (``pxr.UsdValidation``: stage metadata, composition, shading, geometry
subsets, and the ``UsdPhysics`` rigid-body, collider, joint and articulation checkers) run on ``stage``, or the
legacy ``UsdUtils.ComplianceChecker`` on builds without ``UsdValidation``.

functions.doc:
Meshes and curves of a USD file as arrays: ``[{"path", "kind", "points", "faces" or "counts", "colors"}]``
(colours from ``displayColor`` at ``time``, a time code; default: the first sample). ``exclude``: prim path

functions.doc:
Draw the meshes and curves of a USD file (read back from disk) in their ``displayColor``; ``colorbar``:
``(label, lo, hi, cmap)``; ``flat``: axes scaled to the data in x, y and a squashed z (long, low scenes such

functions.sig: (usd_path: str, png_path: str, *, frames: int = 60) -> str
functions.doc:
Python to run inside Omniverse Kit / USD Composer (Window > Script Editor, or ``kit --exec``): opens the stage
and writes an RTX viewport capture. Needs Omniverse with an RTX GPU; not runnable with ``usd-core`` alone. Save
it next to the stage: the paths are resolved from the script's own folder.

functions.doc:

``label(t)`` gives each frame's title.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.nvidia.physicsnemo
children.doc:
Small PhysicsNeMo surrogates for tabular physics (a few inputs -> a few outputs), trained and checked the
PINNeAPPle way. Grid operators (FNO, MeshGraphNet) are in :mod:`pinneapple_neural.physicsnemo_bridge`.

``MLPSurrogate.fit(X, Y, budget)``
    ``physicsnemo.models.mlp.FullyConnected`` with inputs and outputs scaled to [-1, 1] by the training box, Adam
    with a cosine learning rate, mini-batches, run until a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget.ComputeBudget`
    is spent (``train_within_budget``, so two models with the same budget got the same compute).
``predict(X)``, ``in_box(X)``, ``save`` / ``load``
    NumPy in and out; the training box is kept so a caller can count extrapolated queries.
``sign_violations(f, grid, axis, output, sign)``
    a physics check on any model: the fraction of grid cells where ``d output / d input[axis]`` has the wrong sign
    (e.g. a wheel's load must grow with sinkage), by finite differences on the grid.
``relative_errors(pred, ref)``
    per-output relative RMS errors.

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (X, Y, budget, *, batch_size: int = 256, lr: float = 0.003, evaluate = None, eval_at = ())
methods.doc: Train on ``X (n, in)``, ``Y (n, out)`` until ``budget`` is spent; returns the ``BudgetRun``.

functions.name: sign_violations
functions.sig: (f, axes: list[np.ndarray], axis: int, output: int, sign: int = 1, *, tol: float = 0.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Fraction of cells of the tensor grid ``axes`` (one 1-D array per input) where the forward difference of
``f(X)[:, output]`` along input ``axis`` has the sign opposite to ``sign`` by more than ``tol``.

functions.name: relative_errors
functions.sig: (pred, ref) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Per-output RMS error relative to the RMS of the reference output.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.nvidia.runinfo
children.doc:
What a run used: versions of the NVIDIA and PINNeAPPle packages, the hardware, and step timings.

    info = RunInfo()
    with info.step("train"):
        ...
    info.mark("Isaac Sim", ran=False, why="needs an RTX GPU")
    info.save("results/run_info.json")

Every example in ``examples/nvidia`` writes one, so each figure can be traced to the machine and the versions that
produced it, and the steps that were *not* executed (GPU, API key) are listed as such.

methods.name: mark
methods.sig: (component: str, *, ran: bool, why: str = '', how: str = '') -> None
methods.doc: Record whether an NVIDIA component was executed here (``ran``) and why not / how.

functions.name: environment
functions.sig: () -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Python, OS, CPU, GPU (CUDA through torch, if any) and the installed versions of the relevant packages.

children.summary: What a run used: versions of the NVIDIA and PINNeAPPle packages, the hardware, and step timings.

children.doc:
pinneapple_tools.nvidia -- PINNeAPPle with the NVIDIA stack (PhysicsNeMo, Omniverse / OpenUSD, Isaac Sim,
Cosmos, NIM).

PINNeAPPle's part is the physics: the problem, the reference solvers and the checks every result must pass before
anyone uses it. The NVIDIA part trains (PhysicsNeMo), shows and simulates (Omniverse, Isaac Sim), generates
(Cosmos) or answers (NIM). This package holds the glue so the examples in ``examples/nvidia`` stay thin:

``diagram``     architecture figures of a pipeline (who does what; which steps need a GPU or an API key)
``omniverse``   results as OpenUSD stages with fields as primvars, a stage validator and a read-back preview
``isaac``       Isaac Sim-ready articulations (``UsdPhysics``), their checks, and the Isaac Sim runner script
``nim``         a client for NIM microservices (OpenAI-compatible, ``nvext.guided_json``) and a physics guard
``cosmos``      clients for Cosmos world foundation models (``/v1/infer``) and Cosmos Reason, and physics
                checks of a video (ballistic fit, conservation of the tracked object)
``physicsnemo`` small PhysicsNeMo surrogates (``FullyConnected``) trained and checked the PINNeAPPle way; grid
                operators (FNO, MeshGraphNet) are in ``pinneapple_neural.physicsnemo_bridge``
``testing``     a local fake server speaking the NIM / Cosmos HTTP contracts, for tests without a key or GPU
``runinfo``     versions, hardware and timings of a run, and which NVIDIA components ran
``figures``     field panels, check charts, curves

Every NVIDIA dependency is optional: ``usd-core`` for USD, ``nvidia-physicsnemo`` for PhysicsNeMo, ``requests``
for the HTTP clients. Isaac Sim, Omniverse Kit and the Cosmos models need an NVIDIA GPU; NIM on build.nvidia.com
needs ``NVIDIA_API_KEY``.
children.summary: PINNeAPPle with the NVIDIA stack (PhysicsNeMo, Omniverse / OpenUSD, Isaac Sim, Cosmos, NIM).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge
pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.client
children.doc:
Thin, honest wrapper around the REA command-line tool.

REA ("Reverse Engineer Anything", https://github.com/morluto/rea, MIT) is a
Node.js CLI / MCP server that inspects software *without its source code* --
JavaScript/Electron bundles, websites, native binaries (through Hopper,
Ghidra or IDA), .NET assemblies, WASM, Android packages -- and returns
**Evidence JSON**: every finding carries the artifact's SHA-256, the
operation that produced it, its confidence/authority and its limitations.

This module only runs that CLI and parses what it prints. It never
interprets, completes or "fixes" REA's results: whatever REA did not
observe stays absent. That matches the rule used by
:mod:`pinneapple_llm.research` (results trace back to a real tool output,
never to an LLM's recall).

Resolution of the executable, in order:

1. ``PINNEAPPLE_REA_BIN`` -- an explicit path (or a command line, split on
   whitespace, e.g. ``"npx -y rea-agents@6.4.0"``);
2. ``rea`` on ``PATH`` (``npm install --global rea-agents``);
3. ``npx -y rea-agents@<PINNED_VERSION>`` if ``npx`` is on ``PATH``.

Nothing is installed implicitly beyond what ``npx`` itself caches.

classes.name: ReaUnavailable
classes.doc: No REA executable could be found (see module docstring).

classes.name: ReaError
classes.doc: REA ran but exited non-zero or printed something that is not JSON.

classes.name: ReaResult
classes.doc:
One REA invocation: the command, the parsed JSON payload and the
progress events REA streamed on stderr (kept for the audit trail).

classes.name: ReaClient
classes.sig: (command: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, *, timeout_s: float = 900.0, cwd: Optional[str] = None)
classes.doc:
Run REA commands and parse their JSON output.

Parameters
----------
command : argv prefix to run REA; resolved with
    :func:`resolve_rea_command` when omitted.
timeout_s : wall-clock limit per invocation.
cwd : working directory for the subprocess (REA itself takes absolute
    target paths, so this rarely matters).

methods.name: analyze_javascript_application
methods.sig: (path: str | os.PathLike, *, analysis_timeout_ms: Optional[int] = None) -> ReaResult
methods.doc: Static reconstruction of a JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR.

methods.name: import_reference_source
methods.doc:
Pin a source tree as *historical reference* (inventory, languages,
root SHA-256, git HEAD). REA has no Python/C++ semantic analyser, so
for such projects this is the provenance record; the study itself is
a direct reading of the source (``Finding.method="manual"``).

methods.name: inspect_binary_layout
methods.doc:
ELF sections, segments, symbols and relocations, without executing
the object. REA delegates to pwntools: set ``REA_PWNTOOLS_PYTHON`` to a
Python with pwntools 4.15 / pyelftools 0.33 / Unicorn 2.1.2.

methods.name: inspect_artifact
methods.doc: Identify one artifact (binary, archive, package) and list next probes.

functions.name: resolve_rea_command
functions.sig: (env: Optional[Dict[str, str]] = None) -> List[str]
functions.doc: Return the argv prefix that runs REA, or raise :class:`ReaUnavailable`.

children.summary: Thin, honest wrapper around the REA command-line tool.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.evidence
children.doc:
Turn REA's JavaScript application Evidence into a compact feature map.

``rea analyze-javascript-application`` returns a large (often tens of MB)
Evidence JSON whose ``normalized_result.semantic_graph`` holds every
function, call site, binding and relation REA recovered from the code, each
with an exact source range. This module keeps only what is useful for
studying *how a feature is implemented*:

- named functions per module with their line ranges;
- the resolved static call graph between them (``calls`` relations from a
  call site to a function, attributed to the call site's enclosing function);
- timers and storage mechanisms the app uses;
- REA's own limitations, copied verbatim.

:func:`locate` then answers "where is feature X?" by matching keywords
against function names and the source lines inside each function's range,
and expands the hits one level along the call graph. Every hit points back to
a file, a line range and the Evidence id, so a finding can always be checked
against the original.

Nothing here infers semantics REA did not record: an unresolved call stays
unresolved, an anonymous function stays anonymous.

functions.name: summarize_js_evidence
functions.sig: (evidence: Dict[str, Any], *, vendor_globs: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_VENDOR_GLOBS, include_vendor: bool = False) -> FeatureMap
functions.doc:
Build a :class:`FeatureMap` from one ``analyze_javascript_application``
Evidence payload (the parsed JSON, not the path).

functions.name: locate
functions.sig: (fmap: FeatureMap, keywords: Iterable[str], *, root: Optional[str | Path] = None, max_hits: int = 20, snippet_lines: int = 40) -> List[FeatureHit]
functions.doc:
Functions whose name or body mentions any keyword (case-insensitive),
most matches first. ``root`` defaults to the analysed directory.

functions.name: exported_functions_from_layout
functions.sig: (evidence: Dict[str, Any]) -> List[str]
functions.doc:
Exported functions recorded by ``rea inspect-binary-layout`` (ELF):
entries of the ``SHT_DYNSYM`` table that are defined, global/weak,
default-visibility FUNC/GNU_IFUNC symbols.

Lets a check done in Python (``fmu_inspect.elf_exported_functions``) be
confirmed against REA's independent parser, with REA's Evidence id.

children.summary: Turn REA's JavaScript application Evidence into a compact feature map.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.harvest
children.doc:
Harvest ledger: what was studied, under which license, and what came of it.

Each :class:`HarvestEntry` records one studied project (URL, commit, license
policy, the REA Evidence id/SHA-256 when REA was used) and its
:class:`Finding` items -- an idea, a technique or a feature, where it lives in
the original, and what PINNeAPPle did with it.

``Finding.status`` values:

``idea``           noted, nothing implemented yet
``adapted``        PINNeAPPle code derived from the original code (needs ``adapt``)
``reimplemented``  written from the published method / observed behaviour
``exists``         PINNeAPPle already had it; the finding only cross-checks
``rejected``       studied and not taken (``note`` says why)

The ledger enforces the license gate: an ``adapted`` finding under a
``clean_room`` or ``reference_only`` policy is refused at construction time,
so the rule cannot be bypassed by editing a JSON file and reloading it.

classes.name: LicenseGateError
classes.doc: A finding claims more reuse than the project's license allows.

classes.name: HarvestLedger
classes.doc: A JSON file of :class:`HarvestEntry` items keyed by project name.

children.summary: Harvest ledger: what was studied, under which license, and what came of it.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.licenses
children.doc:
License gate for anything harvested from another project into PINNeAPPle.

PINNeAPPle is Apache-2.0. What may flow from a studied project into this
repository depends on that project's license, so every harvest is tagged
with one of three policies -- the same "a missing license means all rights
reserved" stance as :mod:`pinneapple_catalog.resources`:

``adapt``
    Permissive and Apache-2.0-compatible (MIT, BSD, Apache-2.0, ISC, Zlib,
    CC-BY-4.0, CC0, Unlicense). Code may be adapted; the original notice
    must be kept (``attribution_required``) -- recorded in the harvest
    ledger and, for copied code, in ``NOTICE``.
``clean_room``
    Copyleft (GPL, LGPL, AGPL, MPL, EPL). Only *behaviour* may be taken:
    equations, algorithms as published in papers, interfaces, observed
    input/output. The PINNeAPPle implementation is written from the
    published method, never from the code, and the ledger refuses an entry
    marked ``adapted`` under this policy.
``reference_only``
    No license, unrecognised license, or a non-commercial / no-derivatives
    term. Read for orientation; nothing is reused.

Detection is deliberately conservative: when a repository carries several
licenses (e.g. VisualPDE: MIT for code, CC-BY-4.0 for HTML/CSS) the most
restrictive one decides, and anything not positively recognised is
``reference_only``.

functions.name: policy_for
functions.sig: (spdx_ids: Iterable[str]) -> LicensePolicy
functions.doc: Most restrictive policy over the given SPDX identifiers.

functions.name: detect_licenses
functions.sig: (root: str | Path, *, max_bytes: int = 200000) -> List[str]
functions.doc:
SPDX ids recognised in the license files at the top of ``root``
(plus ``package.json``/``pyproject.toml``/``setup.py`` declarations).

functions.name: policy_for_path
functions.sig: (root: str | Path) -> LicensePolicy

children.summary: License gate for anything harvested from another project into PINNeAPPle.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.tools
children.doc:
Expose the REA bridge as tools of :class:`PhysicsToolRegistry`, so
:func:`pinneapple_llm.agent_loop.run_agent_loop` can study a reference
implementation the same way it calls a solver: one real tool call, a real
result fed back to the next turn.

The tools are registered only when they can actually run: the license tool
always (pure Python), the REA tools only when an REA executable resolves.

functions.name: register_rea_tools
functions.sig: (registry: Any) -> List[str]
functions.doc: Register the bridge's tools on ``registry``; returns the names added.

children.summary: Expose the REA bridge as tools of PhysicsToolRegistry, so pinneapple_llm.agent_loop.run_agent_loop can study a reference implementation the same way it calls a solver: one real tool call, a real ...

children.doc:
rea_bridge -- study reference implementations with REA, under a license gate.

`REA <https://github.com/morluto/rea>`_ (Reverse Engineer Anything, MIT) is a
Node.js CLI/MCP server that inspects software without its source and returns
Evidence JSON. Within PINNeAPPle it is a third source for the research
pipeline (:mod:`pinneapple_tools.hpo_experiments`): arXiv gives papers,
GitHub gives repositories, REA gives *how a feature is actually built*,
with the artifact's SHA-256 and REA's stated limitations attached.

Modules
-------
client      run the ``rea`` CLI and parse its JSON (no Python dependency)
licenses    license detection and the adapt / clean_room / reference_only gate
evidence    JavaScript Evidence -> compact feature map; keyword ``locate``
harvest     JSON ledger of studied projects and findings, gate-enforced
tools       registration on :class:`pinneapple_worldmodel.PhysicsToolRegistry`

See ``docs/dev/REA_INTEGRATION.md`` for setup and the harvest workflow.
children.summary: Study reference implementations with REA, under a license gate.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.reporting
pinneapple_tools.reporting.datasheet
children.doc:
A technical datasheet: the engineering record of a study, laid out from data -- no LLM anywhere.

A study produces numbers and figures; this module turns them into one self-contained document in the
shape a hardware datasheet has and a review meeting reads:

* a strip of headline numbers (the question the study answers, in six cells);
* numbered sections, each a table beside its figure, every figure captioned with what it shows and
  what to read from it;
* a cost table (how long each step took, on what), a run plan (done / running / queued, with the reason
  each step exists), the items to confirm, and a limitations block.

Nothing here decides content: every string, table and figure is passed in by the study.  The module
owns only layout, so a report can be regenerated from stored results without re-solving.

    from pinneapple_tools.reporting.datasheet import Datasheet, Figure, KPI, Step, Table

    d = Datasheet("3 GHz compact range", subtitle="quiet zone by physical optics", eyebrow="EM / reflector")
    d.kpis([KPI("Focal length", "1.50", "m"), KPI("Quiet zone", "0.60", "m @ 3 m")])
    s = d.section("Reflector geometry", lede="The section and its rolled edge, as modelled.")
    s.row(Table([["Focal length", "1.50 m"], ["Section", "1.20 m square"]], header=["quantity", "value"],
                caption="As modelled."),
          Figure("side.png", "Side section with the rays."))
    d.plan(done=[Step("Geometry", "built from Problem", "done", "0 s")])
    d.build("cr.html", pdf="cr.pdf")

PDF: written by printing the HTML with a headless Chromium/Chrome (``--headless --print-to-pdf``);
playwright is used when it is installed.  Without either, the HTML is still written and the call
returns it -- no PDF toolchain is required to use the module.

classes.name: KPI
classes.doc: One cell of the headline strip: a label, its value, an optional unit and a note.

classes.name: Table
classes.doc:
A two-column (or wider) table.  ``rows`` are sequences of cells; ``header`` names the columns.

``emphasis`` marks rows that carry a conclusion (bold, tinted); ``note`` prints under the caption.

classes.name: Figure
classes.doc: An image with a caption.  ``wide`` takes the full text width, otherwise it shares a row.

classes.name: Note
classes.doc: A callout.  ``kind``: ``info`` (neutral), ``ok``, ``warn``, ``fail`` (a conclusion).

classes.name: Step
classes.doc: One step of the run plan: what it does, why it is in the plan, what it cost, where it stands.

classes.name: Section
classes.doc: One numbered section: a lede, then blocks (paragraphs, callouts, tables, figures, rows).

methods.name: note
methods.sig: (text: str, kind: str = 'info', title: str = '') -> Section

methods.name: figure
methods.sig: (f: Figure | str, caption: str = '', wide: bool = False) -> Section

methods.name: row
methods.doc: Lay blocks side by side (2 or 3 across).

classes.name: Datasheet
classes.doc: A technical datasheet: headline strip, numbered sections, run plan, items to confirm, footer.

methods.name: verdict_box
methods.sig: (text: str, kind: str = 'info', title: str = '') -> Datasheet

methods.name: plan
methods.sig: (*, done: Sequence[Step | tuple] = (), running: Sequence[Step | tuple] = (), queued: Sequence[Step | tuple] = (), blocked: Sequence[Step | tuple] = ()) -> Datasheet

methods.name: to_pdf
methods.sig: (path: str, *, html_path: str | None = None) -> str | None
methods.doc:
Print the datasheet to PDF with a headless Chromium; returns ``path`` or ``None`` if no
browser is available (the HTML is still written next to it).

methods.name: build
methods.sig: (path: str, *, pdf: str | None = None) -> dict[str, str | None]
methods.doc: Write the HTML (and the PDF when a browser is found).  ``path`` is the HTML.

functions.name: find_chrome
functions.sig: () -> str | None
functions.doc:
A Chromium/Chrome executable that can print HTML to PDF, or ``None``.

Order: ``$PINNEAPPLE_CHROME``, ``google-chrome`` / ``chromium`` / ``chromium-browser`` /
``microsoft-edge`` on PATH, the macOS app bundles, then playwright's browser cache.

children.summary: A technical datasheet: the engineering record of a study, laid out from data -- no LLM anywhere.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.reporting.paperkit
children.doc:
Figure style and PDF paper builder for PINNeAPPle technical reports.

Figures: one fixed categorical colour order (never cycled past its 8 entries in a single plot), a
single-hue sequential blue ramp (``SEQ``, registered as ``"seq_blue"``), a blue/red diverging ramp with
a neutral grey midpoint (``DIV``, registered as ``"div_blue_red"``), recessive axes and no top/right
spines. Call :func:`setup_mpl` once, then save each figure with :func:`savefig`.

PDF: :class:`Paper` builds an A4 report with reportlab/platypus in the STIX serif shipped with
matplotlib (full Greek and math glyphs): title block, abstract, numbered sections, equations,
figures, tables with captions, references and page numbers. reportlab is optional and is imported
only when a :class:`Paper` (or :func:`para`) is created::

    pip install "pinneapple[veriphysics]"

Example::

    from pinneapple_tools.reporting.paperkit import CAT, Paper, fmt, savefig, setup_mpl

    setup_mpl()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
    ax.plot(x, y, color=CAT[0])
    png = savefig(fig, "out/fig1.png")

    paper = Paper("Heat conduction in a slab", subtitle="PINN vs. FEM")
    paper.abstract("We compare ...", keywords=["PINN", "FEM"])
    paper.section("Results")
    paper.figure(png, "Temperature along the slab.")
    paper.table([["Method", "rel. L2"], ["FEM", fmt(1.2e-4)]], "Errors against the exact solution.")
    paper.build("out/report.pdf")

Matplotlib's backend is left alone; scripts that run headless and want to be explicit can call
``matplotlib.use("Agg")`` before importing pyplot.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.sandbox
pinneapple_tools.sandbox.custom_solver_runner
children.doc:
Run an untrusted, user-supplied Python solver script out-of-process,
with best-effort resource limits.

SECURITY WARNING -- read this before using this module for anything
------------------------------------------------------------------------
``run_custom_solver`` isolates a script into a *separate OS process* and
applies POSIX resource limits (``resource.setrlimit``) plus a wall-clock
``subprocess.run(..., timeout=...)``. That is **process-level resource
limiting, not a sandbox**, and it does NOT provide a security boundary:

  * No filesystem restriction. The script can read, write, or delete any
    file the calling OS user can touch.
  * No network restriction. The script can open sockets, make HTTP
    requests, exfiltrate data, etc.
  * No syscall/capability restriction of any kind (no seccomp, no
    namespaces, no chroot). It can spawn further subprocesses, load
    arbitrary shared libraries, etc.
  * ``RLIMIT_AS`` bounds *virtual address space*, not resident physical
    memory -- it stops a script that tries to allocate a huge array, but
    is not a general memory-abuse defense (e.g. many small long-lived
    allocations that never trip a single large allocation), and some
    platforms/allocators don't enforce it as tightly as Linux glibc does.
  * ``RLIMIT_CPU`` bounds *CPU time*, not wall-clock time -- a script that
    sleeps, blocks on I/O, or spins a busy network wait can run
    indefinitely without touching its CPU budget. That's why this module
    ALSO enforces the wall-clock ``timeout`` via ``subprocess.run``, which
    is the limit that actually catches an infinite ``while True: pass``
    loop doing real (CPU-bound) work, and the wall-clock timeout is the
    one to rely on for a hang of any kind.

Use this only for scripts you already have some trust in (e.g. generated
by ``pinneapple_physics.codegen`` from a spec you control, or a
cooperative user's code) as a safety net against bugs -- runaway loops,
accidental huge allocations -- never as the only defense against a
genuinely adversarial, untrusted script. For real isolation, put a proper
sandbox in front of this: a container with ``--network=none`` and a
read-only filesystem, or a stronger technology (gVisor, Firecracker,
nsjail). This module does not provide that itself.

Platform support
-----------------
POSIX only (Linux, macOS) -- it relies on the stdlib ``resource`` module
and ``subprocess``'s ``preexec_fn`` (fork-based), neither of which exists
on Windows. ``run_custom_solver`` raises ``RuntimeError`` up front on an
unsupported platform rather than silently running the script with no
limits at all.

Calling convention
--------------------
``script_path`` must define a module-level ``solve(params: dict) -> dict``
function whose returned dict contains at least a ``"coords"`` key -- the
same convention used by every script
``pinneapple_physics.codegen.fdm_script_generator``/
``fenics_script_generator`` produces, so those generated scripts (or any
hand-written script following the same convention) can be run here
unmodified.

functions.name: run_custom_solver
functions.sig: (script_path: str, params: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None, *, timeout: float = 60.0, memory_limit_mb: int = 512) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run ``script_path``'s ``solve(params)`` in a separate, resource-
limited subprocess. See the module docstring's SECURITY WARNING for
exactly what protection this does (and does not) provide.

Parameters
----------
script_path : path to a Python file defining ``solve(params: dict) ->
    dict`` (the dict must contain at least a ``"coords"`` key) — e.g.
    anything produced by ``pinneapple_physics.codegen``.
params : forwarded to ``solve()`` in the child process, JSON-encoded
    for the trip across the process boundary, so it must be
    JSON-serializable (plain numbers/strings/lists/dicts/bools).
timeout : wall-clock seconds before the subprocess is killed. This is
    the limit that actually catches a hang of any kind (an infinite
    CPU-bound loop, a blocked I/O call, ...).
memory_limit_mb : soft cap on the child's virtual address space
    (``RLIMIT_AS``), in megabytes. Bounds virtual memory, not resident
    physical memory -- see the module docstring.

Returns
-------
On success: the ``solve()`` result dict (nested structure preserved),
plus ``"success": True`` and ``"elapsed_s": float``.
On failure (exception raised inside ``solve()``, malformed result,
timeout, or the process being killed outright by the OS/resource
limits): ``{"success": False, "error": <exception class name or
"TimeoutExpired"/"ProcessTerminated">, "message": str, ...}`` -- the
error is always surfaced here, never silently swallowed.

See ``custom_solver_runner`` for the (important, honest) limits of what

not a real sandbox.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.surrogate_policy
children.doc:
pinneapple_tools.surrogate_policy — measured-runtime "does this problem
need a trained surrogate, or can we just call its solver directly?"
policy.

Deliberately measurement-driven, not a dimension-based guess: a 3D solve
is not always slower than a 2D one (a closed-form/analytic 3D solver can
run in microseconds while an iterative 2D CFD solve takes seconds), so a
"3D = always needs a surrogate" heuristic is wrong often enough to be
worth avoiding entirely. The caller supplies a zero-argument thunk that
runs one real solve; this module only handles timing, a small JSON cache
so the same problem isn't re-timed every call, and thresholding.

methods.name: measure_solver_time
methods.sig: (problem_id: str, run_once: Callable[[], Any], *, force: bool = False) -> float
methods.doc:
Runs ``run_once()`` once and caches the elapsed wall-clock
seconds under ``problem_id``. Returns the cached value if already
measured, unless ``force=True``.

methods.name: classify
methods.sig: (problem_id: str, *, run_once: Optional[Callable[[], Any]] = None, has_direct_solver: bool = True, assumed_expensive_geometry: bool = False) -> SurrogatePolicyResult
methods.doc:
Priority order, matching the reasons a sibling internal
project's policy used: (1) no direct solver exists at all -> needs
a model regardless of timing; (2) the geometry step alone is
assumed expensive (e.g. real CAD meshing) -> needs a model without
timing the full solve; (3) otherwise, measure (or reuse a cached
measurement of) the actual solve and threshold on that.

methods.name: recommend_architecture
methods.doc:
A small, honest heuristic — not a learned recommender. Returns
``None`` if no model is needed at all.

children.summary: Measured-runtime "does this problem need a trained surrogate, or can we just call its solver directly?" policy.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.caption
children.doc:
The caption a figure carries: what the field is, in what unit, at what scale (#67).

A rendered field without its unit is a picture of colours. The rule this module enforces is the one the roadmap
states: **a field is not drawn without a unit** -- and a dimensionless field is what ``"-"`` says, so the absence
of a unit has to be declared, never assumed. The second half of the rule is the scale: a deformed shape is an
exaggeration, and an exaggerated deformation that does not say ``x25`` is a lie of proportion.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.caption import figure_caption

    figure_caption("von Mises", "MPa", value_range=(0.0, 512.4), deform=25.0, method="FEM",
                   status="validated").text()
    # 'von Mises [MPa]: 0 to 512.4 MPa, displacement x25, FEM (validated)'

:func:`figure_caption` is what the renderers call; :class:`FigureCaption` is the structured form, so a caller can
put the same facts in a JSON sidecar, an HTML tooltip or a paper's figure list without parsing the sentence back.

classes.name: FigureCaption
classes.doc: The facts a figure must state about itself. Built by :func:`figure_caption`.

methods.name: unit_text
methods.doc: The unit as it goes on the image: ``"-"`` states a dimensionless field, it does not hide one.

methods.name: text
methods.doc: One line: the field and its unit, the range, the exaggeration, the time, the method and its status.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: The same facts as data, for a sidecar file or an application's tooltip.

functions.name: figure_caption
functions.sig: (field: str, unit: str, *, label: str = '', kind: str = 'value', value_range = None, deform: float | None = None, length_unit: str = 'm', time: float | None = None, time_unit: str = 's', method: str = '', status: str = '', source: str = '') -> FigureCaption
functions.doc:
The caption for one field, refusing the two things a figure must not leave out.

``unit`` has no default on purpose: a caller that does not know the unit of the field is drawing a picture of
colours, and ``unit="-"`` is how a dimensionless field says so. ``deform`` is the exaggeration factor the image
used (``25`` for a displacement scaled x25); ``1.0`` means undivided, and is not printed.

Raises
------
ValueError
    When ``unit`` is ``None`` (use ``"-"`` for dimensionless), when ``status`` is not one of
    :data:`STATUSES`, or when ``value_range`` is not an increasing pair.

functions.name: caption_from_figure
functions.sig: (fig, *, filename: str = '', deform: float | None = None, length_unit: str = 'm', method: str = '', status: str = '', source: str = '') -> FigureCaption
functions.doc:
Read the caption back out of a figure that is already drawn, refusing one that declares no unit (#67).

The catalogue saves figures whose caption nobody wrote down, so the figure itself has to be the witness: the
colour bar's label first (it is the field the colours mean), then the y axis, then the x axis, then the title.
A label declares a unit the way this library writes it -- ``"Contact pressure [MPa]"`` -- and the first one that
does wins.

Raises
------
ValueError
    When no label on the figure declares a unit. That is the case the issue is about: the figure is then a
    picture of colours, and the fix is in the drawing code, not here -- so this refuses instead of guessing.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.dashboard.spec
children.doc:
What an animation-centred dashboard shows: an animation (frames), charts synced to its time cursor, KPI tiles, a
parameter panel and a colour bar. Pure data (numpy arrays and strings); the exporters are in :mod:`.html` and
:mod:`.static`.

Charts come in two kinds:

* ``"series"`` -- values along the frames (``x`` has one value per frame: time, distance ...). The cursor is a
  vertical line at the current frame; scrubbing the chart moves the animation.
* ``"phase"`` -- fixed curves (e.g. a testbed curve of drawbar pull versus slip) plus markers that move with the
  frames (e.g. each wheel's current slip and pull).

Units belong in every label: ``Chart(ylabel="Drawbar pull [N]")``, ``Tile(unit="m")``, ``Param(unit="kg")``.

classes.name: Series
classes.doc: A line. ``y`` has one value per frame (series charts) or per ``x`` point (phase-chart curves).

classes.name: Marker
classes.doc: A point that moves with the frames (phase charts): ``x[k], y[k]`` at frame k.

classes.name: Tile
classes.doc: A KPI: a scalar, or one value per frame (the tile follows the cursor).

classes.name: ColorBar
classes.doc:
Colour bar beside the animation; ``saturation`` < 1 shows the colour map muted the way a semi-transparent,
desaturated field overlay draws it (``studio.planetary.SurfaceView.field_saturation``).

PNG and GIF/MP4 exports of a :class:`~.spec.Dashboard`, drawn with matplotlib in the studio's dark style.

Layout (1920 x 1080 by default)::

    title, subtitle                                  KPI tiles
    left charts  |  animation (+ colour bar, time cursor)  |  right charts
    bottom charts ...                                       |  parameters

The figure is drawn once; for every frame only the image, the cursors, the moving markers and the tiles change, so
a video costs a fraction of a second per frame.

functions.name: write_png
functions.sig: (db: Dashboard, path: str, k: int | None = None, size = (1920, 1080), dpi: int = 100, font_scale: float = 1.0) -> str
functions.doc: The dashboard at frame ``k`` (default: the last) as a PNG.

functions.name: write_gif
functions.sig: (path: str, frames, fps: float, colors: int = 255, loop: int = 0) -> str
functions.doc:
Animated GIF of RGB ``frames`` with one shared adaptive palette (octree quantisation of a few frames spread
over the clip, which keeps small areas of distinct colour -- chart lines, a colour bar -- that a median cut
merges away) and frame differencing: after the first frame, pixels whose palette index did not change are written as
one transparent index, so the static parts of a dashboard (and the still areas of the picture) cost almost
nothing.

functions.name: hstack_gifs
functions.sig: (paths_or_frames, out, fps: float = 10, colors: int = 128, background: str = 'white', mismatch: str = 'error', loop: int = 0)
functions.doc:
Several animations side by side in one GIF, frame by frame (e.g. two runs of the same case compared).

``paths_or_frames``: GIF paths, or sequences of RGB frames (arrays or PIL images), left to right. Each output
frame is as tall as the tallest input; shorter inputs are pasted at the top and the rest is filled with
``background``. ``mismatch`` sets what happens when the inputs have different frame counts: ``"error"`` (default,
raise ``ValueError``), ``"hold"`` (the shorter ones stay on their last frame until the longest ends) or
``"loop"`` (the shorter ones start again). Frames are quantised to ``colors`` colours each (median cut) and
written at ``fps``. Returns ``out``.

functions.name: write_video
functions.sig: (db: Dashboard, gif: str | None = None, mp4: str | None = None, *, fps: int = 12, size = (1920, 1080), gif_size = (1280, 720), gif_every: int = 1, dpi: int = 100, frames = None, progress = None, gif_font_scale: float | None = None, gif_colors: int = 255, mp4_quality: int = 8) -> dict

GIF and/or MP4 (H.264, ``size``) of the dashboard over ``frames`` (default all). The GIF keeps every
``gif_every``-th frame at the same playback speed. With ``gif_font_scale`` the GIF is laid out natively at
``gif_size`` with the text scaled by that factor (readable on small screens and social feeds); otherwise its
frames are the video frames downscaled to ``gif_size``.

markers that move with the frames). See ``docs/core_concepts/dashboard.md``.

half filling, so the geometry stays visible on every frame.

functions.name: field_map
functions.sig: (field, extent: Sequence[float], path = None, *, outline = None, vectors = None, title: str = '', label: str = '', cmap: str = 'RdBu_r', symmetric: bool = True, clip: float = 0.995, stride: int = 0, ax = None)

functions.doc: Visualise pointwise |pred - ref| (or relative error) on the domain.

functions.name: field_error_metrics
functions.sig: (reference, prediction) -> dict
functions.doc:
The aggregate error of one field against its reference: ``l2`` (absolute), ``l2_relative`` (the L2 norm over
the reference's RMS -- the number to quote), ``linf``, ``r2`` and ``n`` (the finite points compared).

One definition for the figure and for every benchmark that quotes an error, so two tables cannot disagree.
Non-finite values are left out: a masked wall or an empty patch is not an error of zero.

functions.name: compare_solutions
functions.sig: (x: 'ArrayLike', y: 'ArrayLike', reference: 'ArrayLike', prediction: 'ArrayLike', *, quantity: str = 'field', unit: str = '', labels: Tuple[str, str] = ('Reference', 'Surrogate'), cmap: Optional[str] = None, error_cmap: str = 'magma', percentile: float = 99.0, coord_unit: str = 'm', vmin: Optional[float] = None, vmax: Optional[float] = None, source: str = '', suptitle: str = '', figsize: Option...
functions.doc:
Reference, surrogate and |surrogate - reference| side by side, with the L2 error as a number (#63).

x, y            : coordinates of the values, cell centres or nodes (1-D, or 2-D as a product grid)
reference       : the trusted solution
prediction      : the surrogate's answer on the same points
quantity, unit  : what the colour bars say (``unit=""`` for a dimensionless field); the colour map is the
                  one the house theme registers for that quantity (``cmap=None``), or the one given
percentile      : the error panel runs from 0 to this percentile of the error, and says when it clipped

The two solution panels share one colour scale, computed over both, so the same colour means the same number in
either: comparing them with two scales is what makes a wrong figure look right. The error panel has a scale of its
own from zero (no zero-point is good news: the panel is a magnitude, not a difference in sign), clipped at
``percentile`` and labelled with the true maximum when it is clipped. The aggregate error is in the title and in
the returned :class:`SolutionComparison` -- ``l2`` (absolute, in ``unit``), ``l2_relative`` (the L2 norm over the
reference's RMS, which is the number to quote), ``linf``, ``r2`` and ``metrics`` for a benchmark record.

Non-finite values (a masked wall, an empty patch) are left out of the numbers and out of the scale.

functions.name: write_vtu
functions.sig: (path, points, fields, *, cells = None, title: str = '') -> str
functions.doc:
Write an unstructured grid in VTK XML format: ``points`` plus one data array per field.

``cells`` is omitted for a point cloud (one vertex cell per point, which is what a model evaluated on an arbitrary
domain produces); a mesh passes its connectivity instead, as a sequence of index sequences or as the three arrays
VTK wants (``offsets``, ``connectivity``, ``types``). The file is ASCII so that it diffs and so that no optional
dependency is needed to write it; ParaView, VTK and meshio all read it.

functions.name: render_field
functions.sig: (model, domain = None, *, out: str = 'field', field_names: Sequence[str] | None = None, points = None, title: str = '', cmap: str | None = None, n: int = 4096, dpi: int = 200, image: bool = True) -> dict[str, str]
functions.doc:
Evaluate ``model`` on ``domain`` and write the picture and the VTU of the same numbers.

``model`` is anything with ``predict`` (a ``Solution``, a trained network wrapper) or a callable taking the points.
``domain`` is a ``PhysicalProblem`` (its bounds are used), ``{name: (low, high)}``, ``(lo, hi)`` or an explicit
array of points through ``points=``. ``n`` is the point budget of the grid it builds, shared between the axes. The VTU always carries every field on every point; the picture is drawn for a
2-D grid, and for a 3-D one it is the mid-plane slice in the last coordinate, which is the one a reader can look at
without a 3-D viewer.

Returns ``{"image": ..., "vtu": ...}`` — the same numbers in the two forms the issue asks for.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.headless
children.doc:
Rendering without a display: what this machine has, and the shortest recipe to a frame (#66).

PyVista and VTK open an OpenGL context even for an off-screen render, and on a server with no X or Wayland
display there is nothing to open one against: the render either fails or aborts the process. Three things fix
it, in order of how little they change: a virtual display (``xvfb-run``), an OSMesa build of VTK, or an EGL
context. This module says which of those this machine already has, which one to install, and then actually tries
the render -- VTK can abort the interpreter instead of raising, so the attempt happens in a subprocess.

    python -m pinneapple_tools.visualization.headless      # the diagnosis and a real test render

    import pinneapple as pp
    pp.viz.headless()                                      # the same, as a dict

Run it inside the container in ``docker/headless`` to check that the image is what it claims to be.

functions.name: headless
functions.sig: (size: tuple[int, int] = (320, 240), run_probe: bool = True) -> dict
functions.doc:
Everything about rendering on this machine in one dict, and the commands that would fix it.

``can_render`` is ``None`` when nothing was attempted (``run_probe=False``): pyvista absent, or the caller
only wants the environment. ``recipe`` names the path -- one key of :data:`RECIPES` -- and ``commands``
holds the exact lines from it, so a caller (or a documentation page) never paraphrases them.

children.summary: Rendering without a display: what this machine has, and the shortest recipe to a frame (#66).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.openfoam
children.doc:
An OpenFOAM case, a ``.foam`` pointer or a VTK file, straight into a PyVista grid with the fields of each time (#60).

    import pinneapple as pp

    grid = pp.viz.read_openfoam("case/")                        # every field of the latest time
    pp.viz.render_png(grid, "case/p.png", scalars="p")          # a real case becomes an image in three lines

    pp.viz.read_openfoam("case/", time=0.5, fields=["p", "U"])  # one time, two fields
    pp.viz.read_openfoam("case/", all_times=True)               # one block per time directory, named t=<time>
    pp.viz.read_openfoam_patches("case/")                       # the boundary, one surface per patch
    pp.viz.read_openfoam_patches("case/", include_empty=True)   # also the empty (2-D thickness) patches
    pp.viz.read_grid("case.foam")                               # a .foam file: its folder, no VTK reader needed
    pp.viz.read_grid("results.vtu")                             # VTK files go through PyVista itself
    pp.viz.read_openfoam("examples/physics_check/pass/cases/cavity")   # a case committed in this repository

The case is read by ``pinneapple_data.cae.foam`` (ASCII and binary ``polyMesh``, gzipped or not), so the grid is the
mesh as OpenFOAM wrote it: every cell keeps its own faces (VTK polyhedra, not the hexes of a converted mesh), a volume
field is a cell array and a boundary field is a cell array on the patch surface. That is what ParaView shows, without
requiring VTK's own OpenFOAM reader -- which is missing from some builds and refuses cases that are still readable.

Install: ``pip install "pinneapple[pyvista]"``. Rendering needs an OpenGL context: see
:func:`~pinneapple_tools.visualization.pyvista_bridge.can_render` and ``docs/guides/headless_rendering.md``.

Every face is written once for the cell that owns it and, reversed, for the neighbour cell: a face's node order in
``polyMesh`` is outward from the owner and therefore inward from the neighbour, and VTK wants it outward on both.

``time`` is a time directory (number or name); the latest one by default. ``fields`` keeps only those volume

The boundary of an OpenFOAM case as a ``pyvista.MultiBlock``: one surface per patch, one value per face.

``names`` keeps only those patches; every patch with faces by default. ``empty`` patches -- the two caps that make

and drawn they hide the field behind them (ParaView hides them too). Values come from the boundaryField of the time
directory, so a wall value is the wall value and not the neighbouring cell's. With ``all_times=True`` the result is
one block per time directory, each holding the patches.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.orbit
children.doc:
Turntable animation of a field: the camera orbits while the field advances in time (#64).

    import numpy as np
    import pinneapple as pp

    t = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 40)                     # 40 instants
    x = y = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 60)
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y, indexing="ij")
    field = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (X[None] - t[:, None, None])) * np.cos(2 * np.pi * Y[None])

    pp.viz.turntable(field, "case.gif", t=t, name="u", unit="m/s")    # 1080p GIF, one call
    pp.viz.turntable(field, "case.mp4", t=t, unit="m/s")              # the same as MP4

The frame carries a discreet mark and a caption with the unit and the time, so a clip lifted out of a report still
says what it is. Nothing here needs a display, a GPU or pyvista: the frames are drawn with matplotlib's Agg canvas,
and only the MP4 path needs the ``ffmpeg`` binary on ``PATH`` (the GIF path needs only Pillow).

functions.name: turntable
functions.sig: (field, path: str | Path | None = None, *, x = None, y = None, t = None, name: str = 'u', unit: str = '', time_unit: str = 's', size: Sequence[int] = DEFAULT_SIZE, dpi: int = 100, frames: int | None = None, fps: float = 24.0, cmap: str = DEFAULT_CMAP, clim = None, deform: float = 0.25, elevation: float = 28.0, orbit: float = DEFAULT_ORBIT, azimuth: float = DEFAULT_AZIMUTH, zoom: float = 1.25, b...
functions.doc:
Write a turntable animation of ``field`` to ``path`` (``.gif`` or ``.mp4``), or return its frames.

The camera orbits by ``orbit`` degrees while the field advances from the first instant to the last, so both
the time and the geometry are motion. Every frame is drawn at ``size`` (1080p by default) and carries the
mark and a caption naming the field, its unit and the instant -- a clip that leaves the report still says
what it shows.

Parameters
----------
field : (nt, nx, ny) array-like
    The field at each instant. A single field must be passed as ``field[None]``; a callable or a moving mesh
    is not a turntable input, it is a rendering of one.
path : str or Path, optional
    ``.gif`` (Pillow) or ``.mp4`` (needs ``ffmpeg`` on ``PATH``). When omitted the frames are returned as a
    list of ``(h, w, 3)`` ``uint8`` arrays instead of being encoded, which is what a caller that wants to
    compose them somewhere else needs.
x, y : array-like, optional
    1-D coordinates of the grid axes, ``nx`` and ``ny`` long. Default: the unit square.
t : array-like, optional
    The physical time of each instant, ``nt`` long, shown in the caption. Default: the frame index.
name, unit, time_unit : str
    What the caption says: ``"u [m/s] at t = 1.2 s"`` for ``name="u"``, ``unit="m/s"``.
size : (int, int)
    Pixels per frame, ``(width, height)``. 1080p by default.
frames : int, optional
    Draw this many frames, spread evenly over the run, instead of one per instant. Two frames at least:
    with one there is nothing to animate.
fps : float
    Playback rate of the GIF or MP4.
cmap : str
    A name from :data:`~pinneapple_tools.visualization.style.CMAPS`, or any matplotlib colour map.
clim : (float, float), optional
    Colour limits, held fixed for the whole clip. Default: the range of the whole field, so a colour means
    the same thing in every frame.
deform : float
    Relief height as a fraction of the width of the domain (``0`` leaves the plane flat). The field drives
    the height and the colour; the caption and the colour bar stay readable either way.
elevation : float
    Camera elevation in degrees.
orbit : float
    Degrees the camera sweeps over the clip, spread over the frames drawn. The last frame therefore lands
    one step short of closing the turn, which is what a looping GIF needs: end on the first frame again and
    the loop stutters. ``0`` holds the camera still and lets the time be the only motion.
azimuth : float
    Azimuth of the first frame, in degrees.
zoom : float
    How much of the frame the surface fills. ``1.0`` leaves matplotlib's generous default margin; much more
    than about 1.6 clips the surface at the edges as the camera turns.
background : str
    Figure colour behind the surface.
mark : str
    The discreet mark in the corner; ``""`` draws none.
mark_alpha : float
    Its opacity: the point of a discreet mark is that it is not the subject.
caption, colorbar : bool
    Turn the field/unit/time caption and the colour bar off for a clip that will be annotated elsewhere.
colors : int
    Palette size of the GIF.

Returns
-------
Path, or list of numpy arrays
    The written file, or the frames when ``path`` is omitted.

Raises
------
ValueError
    On a field that is not ``(nt, nx, ny)``, a single instant, a non-finite value, a size under 64 pixels,
    a frame count under 2, an unknown suffix, or ``clim`` that is reversed or empty.
RuntimeError
    When an MP4 is asked for and ``ffmpeg`` is not on ``PATH``.

functions.doc:
Run model inference and immediately plot the prediction panel.

A convenience wrapper that combines :mod:`pinneapple_train` inference
with :func:`plot_pinn_prediction` in a single call.  Handles device

Parameters

y_coords : array-like, shape ``(N,)``

cmap : colormap name (default: CFD rainbow).

Returns

Figure — matplotlib Figure with one or three panels.

Examples
--------

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.pyvista_bridge
children.doc:
PyVista bridge: turn PINNeAPPle meshes and fields into publication-quality 3-D images.

Everything that builds a mesh (``calculix_grid``, ``scene_to_multiblock``, ``grid_from_arrays``) is
plain NumPy + PyVista and runs on any machine. Rendering (``render_png``, ``render_gif``) needs an
OpenGL context: a desktop session, or ``xvfb-run`` / OSMesa / EGL on a headless server. Because VTK
**segfaults** (kills the whole Python process) when no context exists, ``can_render`` probes in a
subprocess first and the render functions raise a ``RuntimeError`` with the fix instead.

Install: ``pip install "pinneapple[pyvista]"``. Headless Linux: ``xvfb-run -a python your_script.py``.
