children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio
pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.animation
children.doc:
Time animation of a :class:`~.scene.Scene`: rigid bodies moving along a trajectory, per-frame arrows, trails,
per-vertex fields and head-up numbers, for the browser viewer (:mod:`.web`) and Blender (:mod:`.blender`).

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import Scene, Surface
    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.animation import Animation
    sc = Scene([Surface("runway", Vr, Fr, "concrete"), Surface("body", Vb, Fb, "paint", group="body")])
    anim = Animation(t)                                   # times (T,) in seconds
    anim.add_track("body", positions, quaternions)        # (T, 3), (T, 4) [w, x, y, z]; body vertices in body frame
    anim.add_vectors("forces", origins, vectors, values=mag, attach="body", label="Force [N]")
    anim.add_trail("path", positions)
    anim.add_hud("V", speed, "Speed", "m/s")
    sc.animation = anim.resample(200)                     # scene.json stays small
    web_viewer(sc, "viewer/")                             # play / pause, time slider, follow camera

The animated axis need not be time: ``Animation(f_ghz, time_label="f", time_unit="GHz", interpolate=False)`` steps
through solved frequencies (the viewer shows only those frames, never a blend), and
``add_surface_shape(surface, vertices)`` moves a surface's vertices frame by frame (a radiation pattern that changes
shape with frequency, a deforming body).

Every array is in the scene's axes (``Scene.axes``, e.g. ``"z_up"``). A track moves the surfaces whose
``Surface.group`` equals its group: their vertices are given in the body frame and sit at frame k at
``p_world = R(q_k) v + positions[k]``. Quaternions are scalar first, ``[w, x, y, z]``, rotating body to scene axes.

classes.name: Animation
classes.doc: Per-frame data on top of a static :class:`~.scene.Scene`; see the module docstring.

methods.name: add_track
methods.doc:
Rigid motion of the surfaces with ``Surface.group == group``: positions (T, 3), quaternions (T, 4)
``[w, x, y, z]`` (None: no rotation).

methods.name: add_vectors
methods.sig: (name: str, origins, vectors, values = None, label: str = '', color_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None, attach: str | None = None, color: str = '#f97316', cmap: str = 'jet') -> Animation
methods.doc:
Arrows per frame: origins and vectors (T, M, 3) already scaled to display length; ``values`` (T, M)
colour them on ``cmap`` ("jet", or the diverging "coolwarm" / "bwr"; range: ``color_range``, else min..max
over all frames for jet and symmetric about zero for a diverging map), otherwise ``color``.
``attach=group``: given in that track's body frame, they move with it.

methods.name: add_trail
methods.sig: (name: str, points, color: str = '#f59e0b', values = None, label: str = '', color_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None, cmap: str = 'jet', radius: float | None = None, alpha: float = 0.8, trail_seconds: float | None = 8.0, fade: bool = True) -> Animation
methods.doc:
A path (T, 3) drawn behind the body up to the current time (e.g. the track's positions): only its last
``trail_seconds`` (None: all of it), its opacity falling from ``alpha`` at the current point to 0 at the
tail when ``fade``. ``values`` (T,) colour it point by point on ``cmap`` (with a colour bar titled
``label``), otherwise it is ``color``. ``radius``: tube radius in Blender (default 0.003 x the tracked
body's size).

methods.name: add_lines
methods.doc: Alias of :meth:`add_trail`: one point per frame, shown progressively.

methods.name: add_surface_field
methods.sig: (surface: str, values, label: str = '', color_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None, cmap: str = 'jet') -> Animation
methods.doc: A per-vertex scalar per frame (T, n_vertices) on the Surface named ``surface``, on ``cmap``.

methods.name: add_surface_shape
methods.doc:
Vertex positions per frame (T, n_vertices, 3) of the Surface named ``surface`` (same vertex order and
count as the surface; its faces stay). The surface's own vertices are what a static view shows.

methods.name: add_hud
methods.sig: (key: str, values, label: str = '', unit: str = '', fmt: str = '{:.1f}') -> Animation
methods.doc: A number per frame (T,) shown in the overlay as ``label: value unit``.

methods.name: pose
methods.sig: (group: str | None = None, k: int = 0) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: 4x4 body-to-scene transform of ``group`` at frame k.

methods.name: frame
methods.doc: The 4x4 transform of every track at frame k.

methods.name: at
methods.sig: (t: float, group: str | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: 4x4 transform of ``group`` at time t: positions linear, rotations slerp (clamped to the time range).

methods.name: transform
methods.doc: Body-frame points (N, 3) of ``group`` in scene coordinates at frame k.

methods.name: vectors_world
methods.doc: Origins and vectors (M, 3) of vector set i at frame k in scene coordinates.

methods.name: trail_window
methods.sig: (i: int, k: int, seconds: float | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
methods.doc:
Indices of the points of trail i shown at frame k (its last ``trail_seconds``, or ``seconds``) and
their opacity factor in [0, 1] (1 at frame k, falling linearly to 0 at the tail end when the trail fades).

methods.name: bounds
methods.doc: Extent of the track and trail points (not the bodies themselves).

methods.name: resample
methods.doc:
The same animation on ``n_frames`` evenly spaced times (positions, vectors, fields and HUD values linear,
rotations slerp). Use it to keep scene.json small, or to get a fixed frame rate for a video.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.sig: (decimals: int = 4, surfaces: Sequence[Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Compact JSON-able dict (floats rounded to ``decimals``; quaternions to 6). ``surfaces``: the scene's
surfaces, to record which glTF nodes (indices, in order) each track moves and where each field goes.

methods.name: from_dict
methods.doc: Inverse of :meth:`to_dict` (up to the rounding).

methods.name: hud_lines
methods.sig: (k: int, time_fmt: str | None = None, keys: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> list[str]
methods.doc:
The overlay text of frame k: the time (:meth:`time_text`, or ``time_fmt``), then ``label: value unit``
per HUD entry (only ``keys``, in that order, when given).

functions.name: matrix_from_quat
functions.sig: (q) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Rotation matrix (3, 3) (or (..., 3, 3)) of unit quaternion(s) ``[w, x, y, z]`` (normalised here).

functions.name: quat_from_matrix
functions.sig: (R) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Unit quaternion ``[w, x, y, z]`` (w >= 0) of a rotation matrix (3, 3) or a stack (..., 3, 3)
(Shepperd's method: the largest of the four squared components is taken first, so it is stable).

functions.name: slerp
functions.sig: (q0, q1, f: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Spherical interpolation between unit quaternions ``[w, x, y, z]`` (shortest arc), f in [0, 1].

children.summary: Time animation of a ~.scene.Scene: rigid bodies moving along a trajectory, per-frame arrows, trails, per-vertex fields and head-up numbers, for the browser viewer (.web) and Blender (.blender).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.api
children.doc:
Three calls a viewer needs, whatever the geometry came from: ``export_gltf``, ``viewer_html``, ``blender_render``.

    import pinneapple as pp

    glb = pp.viz.export_gltf("wing.stl", {"cp": cp})            # bytes: glTF 2.0 binary, field as a vertex attribute
    page = pp.viz.viewer_html(grid, {"cp": cp}, "viewer/")      # index.html + scene.glb: the three.js page
    pp.viz.blender_render("wing.stl", "wing.png", field="cp")   # Blender Cycles, jet scale, colour bar

The input is a mesh in any of the shapes this repository already produces -- an STL/OBJ/glTF/VTK/VTP file, a
``pinneapple_data.cae`` mesh, a PyVista grid (what the OpenFOAM reader of #60 returns), a pair of vertex/face arrays,
or a :class:`~.scene.Scene` -- with per-vertex or per-cell scalar and vector fields. Those are the parts of the
aero_optimizer's 3-D presentation that did not depend on being an aircraft (#281): the aircraft specifics (its parts,
materials, propeller group, axes) stay in ``pinneapple_design.aero.airframe``, which calls the same
:func:`~.scene.write_glb` this module does.

This module is deliberately thin: the work is the ``Scene`` (geometry, materials, fields as vertex attributes), the
page (:func:`~.web.web_viewer`) and the render (:func:`~.blender.render`). What it adds is the input normalisation,
so a caller with a mesh and an array does not have to know which of the five constructors it needs.

functions.name: to_scene
functions.sig: (mesh, fields = None, *, material: str = 'grey', name: str = 'body', axes: str = 'z_up', title: str = '') -> Scene
functions.doc:
A :class:`~.scene.Scene` from ``mesh``, with ``fields`` attached as per-vertex values.

``mesh`` is any of: a path (STL, OBJ, glTF/GLB, VTK/VTP, or anything ``pinneapple_data.cae`` reads), a PyVista
grid or surface, a ``(vertices, faces)`` pair, a ``pinneapple_data.cae`` mesh, or an existing ``Scene``.
``fields``: ``{name: values}`` (per vertex, or per cell -- decided by the lengths) with values that may be vectors
(their magnitude is what a colour map shows) or ``{name: {surface_name: values}}`` for a multi-surface scene.

functions.name: export_gltf
functions.sig: (mesh, fields = None, *, out: Optional[str] = None, materials: Optional[dict] = None, groups: Optional[Mapping[str, Sequence[int]]] = None, generator: str = 'PINNeAPPle', **scene_kw) -> bytes
functions.doc:
The mesh as glTF 2.0 binary, every field a float vertex attribute ``_NAME`` (upper case, what the viewers read).

Returns the bytes; ``out`` also writes them to a file (``.glb``). One mesh per material, PBR materials with
clearcoat and transmission from :data:`~.scene.MATERIALS`, so the same file opens in the browser viewer, in Blender
and in Omniverse. A field's colour range is not baked in: the viewer computes it (``web_viewer`` writes the ranges
in ``scene.json``), because a range baked into the geometry cannot be changed without re-exporting. ``groups``:
node name -> indices of the surfaces to parent under one node (a propeller that spins, a set of parts that moves
together), which is what the airliner viewer needs and why this is not just ``Scene.save``.

functions.name: viewer_html
functions.sig: (mesh, fields = None, out_dir: Optional[str] = None, *, single_file: bool = False, max_faces: Optional[int] = MAX_FACES, title: Optional[str] = None, **scene_kw) -> str
functions.doc:
Write the interactive three.js page for ``mesh``; returns the path of its ``index.html``.

``out_dir`` defaults to a temporary folder (the page is then throw-away until it is served). ``single_file=True``
writes one self-contained page -- the geometry, the viewer and three.js inlined -- which opens from ``file://`` and
can be mailed; without it the folder needs a local server, because browsers do not load ES modules from disk.
Surfaces above ``max_faces`` triangles are decimated for the page (the scene itself is not changed).

functions.name: blender_render
functions.sig: (mesh, out: str, *, fields = None, field: Optional[str] = None, field_range = None, cmap: str = 'jet', samples: int = 64, size: Sequence[int] = (1600, 900), headless: Optional[bool] = None, **scene_kw) -> str
functions.doc:
A Blender Cycles picture of ``mesh`` from the same data as the page; returns the path written.

``field`` picks one of ``fields`` for the colour (the first when omitted), ``field_range`` pins the scale instead
of taking it from the data. ``headless``: run the Blender binary instead of ``bpy`` (None decides: ``bpy`` when it
imports, else the binary, else the reason it cannot). A machine with neither gets a RuntimeError that says so,
never a picture that was not rendered.

children.summary: Three calls a viewer needs, whatever the geometry came from: export_gltf, viewer_html, blender_render.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.bake
children.doc:
Baking the procedural material shaders into texture maps.

A shader (see :mod:`.pbr`) is detail Blender renders and no other tool can read, and it costs evaluation time in every
frame. Baking it once turns the same look into three images, which the Blender renderer, the glTF export and the
browser viewer all read the same way:

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import bake_materials
    maps = bake_materials(scene, "maps/")            # {"painted_steel": {"base_color_map": ..., ...}}
    scene.materials.update({k: {**scene.materials.get(k, {}), **v} for k, v in maps.items()})

The signals come out of Cycles' own bake passes, not out of reading one node of the tree, because a shader such as
``painted_metal`` is two BSDFs mixed: a diffuse bake of it would return only the paint (a metal's diffuse albedo is
black), and the worn-through bare metal would vanish.

- **base colour** -- the DIFFUSE albedo plus the GLOSSY tint, added: the two layers of a mixed shader and the metal
  it exposes, in one image;
- **roughness** -- the ROUGHNESS pass, which Cycles evaluates on the real shader, mixes included;
- **normal** -- the tangent-space NORMAL pass, which picks up the bump nodes.

They are written against the same box-projected UVs the exporters use (:func:`.scene.box_uvs`), so a baked map lands
the same way in the render, in the .glb and in the browser.

functions.name: bake_materials_headless
functions.sig: (scene, out_dir: str, *, exe: Optional[str] = None, timeout: float = 3600.0, **kwargs) -> Dict[str, Dict[str, str]]
functions.doc:
:func:`bake_materials` on a machine where ``bpy`` is not importable: the scene goes to a ``.glb``, the Blender
binary bakes it, and the map paths come back. ``kwargs`` go to :func:`bake_materials` and must be
JSON-serialisable (``materials``, ``size``, ``samples``, ``margin``).

functions.name: unwrap_scene
functions.sig: (scene, *, angle: float = 66.0, margin: float = 0.02) -> 'object'
functions.doc:
Give every surface of ``scene`` its own UV layout (needs ``bpy``): Blender's smart projection, packed into the
square and stored back on ``Surface.uv`` per face corner. This is what a closed or strongly curved body needs --
the box projection of :func:`.scene.box_uvs` folds its islands onto each other -- and the returned scene carries
the layout, so :func:`~.blender.render`, the glTF and the USD all agree with it.

functions.name: bake_materials
functions.sig: (scene, out_dir: str, *, materials: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, size: int = 1024, samples: int = 16, margin: int = 8, uv: str = 'smart', log = None) -> Dict[str, Dict[str, str]]
functions.doc:
Bake every material whose entry names a ``shader`` (or the ones listed in ``materials``) into
``out_dir/<material>_<signal>.png``. Needs ``bpy``. Returns ``{material: {"base_color_map": path, ...}}``, ready
to merge into ``scene.materials``: the entries keep their flat numbers, which stay the fallback and what the
exporters use when a map is missing.

``uv``: "smart" (default) unwraps each material's surfaces with Blender's projection, packed as a group, and
stores the layout on ``Surface.uv`` -- what a curved or closed body needs; "box" keeps the box projection of
:func:`.scene.box_uvs`, which is enough for a plate, a duct or a housing and needs no unwrap pass.

children.summary: Baking the procedural material shaders into texture maps.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.benchmark
children.doc:
A repeatable visual benchmark: the same scenes, cameras and lights every run, so a change to the renderer can be
judged instead of described.

    python -m pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.benchmark --out provas/ --quality preview

Each case pairs a model from the geometry library with the materials, the HDRI and the camera a figure of it would
use. A run writes the PNGs and a JSON record per case with the time, the device and four statistics of the picture:
mean luminance, its spread, the fraction of the frame the subject covers and the edge energy. Those catch what a
regression actually looks like -- a render that went black, blew out, lost its micro-detail or stopped showing the
subject -- without the brittleness of comparing pixels to a golden image across GPUs, drivers and Blender versions.

Pass two records to :func:`compare` (or `--baseline`) to see the deltas; the numbers are the point, not a pass/fail.

functions.name: repository_root
functions.sig: () -> str
functions.doc: The checkout the geometry library and the HDRIs live in.

functions.name: build
functions.sig: (name: str)
functions.doc: The scene of one case, with its materials: ready for :func:`~.blender.render_headless`.

functions.name: picture_stats
functions.sig: (path: str) -> dict
functions.doc:
What the picture looks like, as numbers: mean luminance and its spread, the share of the frame the subject
covers (pixels that differ from the top-left corner by more than a hair) and the edge energy (mean gradient, which
falls when micro-detail disappears).

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (out_dir: str, *, scenes: Optional[list] = None, quality: str = 'preview', device: str = 'auto', samples: Optional[int] = None, size: Optional[tuple] = None, gate: bool = False, log = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Render every case into ``out_dir`` and return the record: ``{case: {seconds, device, picture..., png}}``.

``gate=True`` renders the canonical :data:`GATE` configuration instead of the arguments, so the numbers are the
ones :data:`BASELINE` was recorded with -- a comparison has to be an apples-to-apples render, not whatever preset
the caller happened to use.

functions.name: baseline_of
functions.sig: (record: dict, *, reason: str, blender: Optional[str] = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
What a record keeps when it is committed as the reference: the picture statistics and the configuration they
were measured with, plus a ``_meta`` line saying when, with what and **why** -- a gate whose reference has no date
and no reason is a number nobody can judge.

``reason`` is required on purpose: a baseline moves because somebody decided the pictures should look different,
and that decision is the one piece of the record a machine cannot supply.

The time and the absolute path stay out: one is the machine's, the other is a folder that does not exist anywhere
else.

functions.name: cases_of
functions.sig: (record: dict) -> List[str]
functions.doc: The case names in a record or a baseline: everything but the bookkeeping keys, which start with ``_``.

functions.name: gate
functions.sig: (current: dict, baseline: dict, *, tolerances: Optional[dict] = None) -> List[str]
functions.doc:
The differences between a record and the committed baseline that are too large to be noise.

Absolute tolerances, chosen to pass a CPU render on another machine and to fail a regression: a picture that went
black, blew out, lost its micro-detail or stopped showing the subject moves these by far more than they allow.
The time is not compared -- it is the machine's, not the renderer's.

functions.name: compare
functions.sig: (current: dict, baseline: dict) -> dict
functions.doc: The deltas of one record against another, per case and per statistic (``current - baseline``).

functions.name: main
functions.sig: (argv = None) -> int

children.summary: A repeatable visual benchmark: the same scenes, cameras and lights every run, so a change to the renderer can be judged instead of described.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.bevel
children.doc:
Bevel: the chamfer that a builder cannot add beside a body, because it changes the body itself.

Everything in :mod:`.detail` is a surface put next to the geometry -- a bolt stands on a face, a weld runs along a
seam. A chamfer is not that: it is the same body with its edges cut off, and doing it properly needs the mesh's
topology. So this module is the one place in the studio that edits the mesh instead of adding to it, through the bevel
modifier of the renderer that already draws the scene.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import bevel
    sc = bevel.bevel_scene(sc, angle=35, width=0.0015, segments=2)

A machined edge is never perfectly sharp: at photographic distance the highlight along it is how a viewer tells a
machined part from an extruded one, and it is the first thing that looks wrong in a figure of a casting.

Two limits worth knowing before using it:

* the bevel rebuilds the mesh, so per-vertex fields do not survive it -- do it before mapping a result onto the body,
  or pass ``drop_fields=True`` and accept that they are gone;
* it works on welded geometry, so the surfaces are welded first (``weld``), which is what a mesh that came back from
  glTF needs: the exporter splits vertices at every seam.

functions.name: bevel_scene
functions.sig: (scene, *, angle: float = DEFAULTS['angle'], width: float = DEFAULTS['width'], segments: int = DEFAULTS['segments'], weld: float = DEFAULTS['weld'], clamp: bool = True, drop_fields: bool = False, exe: Optional[str] = None, timeout: float = 3600.0, log = None)
functions.doc:
The same scene with every sharp edge chamfered, as a :class:`~.scene.Scene` you can render and export.

``angle`` is the limit in degrees: only edges sharper than it are cut, so the facets of a curved wall stay flat
surfaces instead of turning into a bead. ``width`` is the chamfer in scene units, ``segments`` how many faces it is
cut into. ``weld`` merges vertices closer than it before the bevel -- without that, the seams the glTF exporter
split would bevel as open boundaries and leave a groove.

children.summary: Bevel: the chamfer that a builder cannot add beside a body, because it changes the body itself.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.blender
children.doc:
Blender Cycles renders of any :class:`~.scene.Scene` (``pip install bpy``, or run inside Blender).

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import Scene, render
    render(scene, "cp.jpg", field="cp")                          # skin coloured by a field, jet scale, colour bar
    render(scene, "flow.jpg", lines=True)                        # streamlines coloured by their values
    render(scene, "slice.jpg", slice="wake", view="back")        # a slice plane (NaN = transparent)
    render(scene, "hero.jpg", background="sky")                  # the materials, under a physical sky

``view``: "iso" (default), "iso_back", "iso_low", "front", "back", "side", "side_left", "top", "bottom", or a
direction (dx, dy, dz) from the centre towards the camera, in scene axes. Names assume x is the object's length
(the flow direction for a CFD scene) and z is up: "front" looks at the x-min end. The colour bar title comes from
``scene.labels[field]`` unless ``title`` is given.

functions.name: hdri_path
functions.sig: (name: str) -> str
functions.doc:
The image behind ``background="hdri:<name>"``: ``name`` itself when it is a file, else ``name`` + ".hdr" /
".exr" / ".png" inside ``$PINNEAPPLE_HDRI_DIR`` (default: ``data/hdri`` of the repository), else a name of
:data:`HDRIS`.

functions.name: render
functions.sig: (scene, out: str, *, field: Optional[str] = None, field_range: Optional[Tuple[float, float]] = None, lines: Union[bool, str] = False, line_range: Optional[Tuple[float, float]] = None, slice: Optional[str] = None, slice_range: Optional[Tuple[float, float]] = None, view: Union[str, Sequence[float], None] = None, distance: Optional[float] = None, lens: Optional[float] = None, background: str = 'st...
functions.doc:
Render ``scene`` (a Scene or a .glb path) to ``out`` (.png or .jpg). Returns ``out``.

field: colour the surfaces by this per-vertex field (surfaces without it are grey). lines: True (all) or the
name of a Lines set, coloured by their values. slice: name of a Slice. background: "studio" (light gradient,
true colours), "dark" (near-black stage, key, rim and fill area lights, AgX: the product-shot look), "sky"
(Nishita sky, filmic) or a lunar preset of :mod:`.lighting` ("lunar_south_pole",
"lunar_low_sun", "lunar_day": black sky, one Sun lamp with the Sun's angular size). ghost: draw the surfaces translucent (default: when a slice is
shown). surface_fields: {surface name: (field, lo, hi, cmap, title)} colours that surface by its own field
on ``cmap`` (one of :data:`.compose.CMAPS`: "jet", or a diverging "rdbu" / "coolwarm" / "bwr") and adds a
second colour bar (bottom left) for it. cmap: the colour map of ``field`` (one of :data:`.compose.CMAPS`).
floor: a glossy floor under the geometry (its reflection; with "dark"). exposure: the AgX exposure in stops
(default: 0 on the light stage, -0.5 on "dark"); lower it when a bright colour map blows out under the key light.
quality: "preview" (24 samples, 960x540, 4 bounces), "production" (96, 1600x900: the default) or "cinematic"
(512, 3840x2160, 16 bounces), used for ``samples`` and ``size`` unless they are given. device: the Cycles compute
device -- "auto" (the first GPU backend this machine exposes), "cpu", "gpu" or a backend name ("metal", "cuda",
"optix", "hip", "oneapi"); an unavailable backend falls back to CPU.
field_alpha: 0..1 draws the field as a translucent layer over the surfaces' own materials instead of replacing
them (a steel pipe keeps its steel and its highlights under the temperature map); None = the map replaces them.
background may also be ``"hdri:<name-or-path>"``: an environment image as the light and as what the metals
reflect (``hdri_strength`` scales it, ``hdri_rotation`` turns it in degrees around z).
camera: a photography preset of :data:`CAMERAS` -- "product" (85 mm on the third line), "hero" (35 mm from
slightly below, shallow), "documentary" (50 mm, everything in focus, centred), "head_on" (100 mm down the main
axis) or "wide" (24 mm establishing shot); it fills ``lens``, ``view``, ``distance``, ``fstop`` and ``composition``
wherever they are not given. composition: "thirds_left", "thirds_right", "thirds_high" or "thirds_low" moves the
subject off centre with a lens shift, which keeps the framing the auto-fit computed. fstop: open the aperture
(depth of field focused on the subject; with "product" and a close camera this is what separates the part from
the background). look: the contrast after the render -- "low", "medium_high", "high", "very_high" or "punchy" (an
S-curve and, for punchy, saturation). post: "bloom", "vignette" or "bloom+vignette". passes: write the Cycles
passes (depth, normal, diffuse, glossy, emission, mist, denoising data) -- with an ``.exr`` output that means a
multilayer file, the input to a grade. film_transparent: no world behind the geometry, an alpha to composite on.

functions.name: blender_executable
functions.sig: () -> Optional[str]
functions.doc:
The Blender executable: ``$BLENDER``, then ``blender`` on ``PATH``, then the usual install locations
(macOS app bundle, ``/usr/bin``, ``/snap``, ``C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation``). ``None`` if there is
none, in which case :func:`render` needs ``pip install bpy`` and :func:`render_headless` cannot run.

functions.name: render_headless
functions.sig: (scene, out: str, *, exe: Optional[str] = None, timeout: float = 3600.0, **kwargs) -> str
functions.doc:
:func:`render` on a machine where ``bpy`` is not importable: the scene goes to a ``.glb``, Blender renders it
from the command line, and ``out`` is written and returned.

``kwargs`` go to :func:`render` (``field``, ``field_range``, ``background``, ``floor``, ``view``, ``lens``,
``size``, ``samples``, ``cmap``, ...) and must be JSON-serialisable. A colour bar needs Pillow, which Blender's
own Python does not ship: draw it afterwards (:func:`~.colormap.colorbar`) or pass ``colorbar_on=False``.
``scene`` is a :class:`~.scene.Scene` or a path ``render`` can read.

functions.name: blender_axes
functions.sig: (axes: str) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Rotation matrix scene axes -> Blender coordinates (what the glTF export + import does to the surfaces).

functions.name: render_animation
functions.sig: (scene, out_dir: str, *, frames: int | Sequence[int] | None = None, size: tuple[int, int] = (960, 540), samples: int = 16, camera: str = 'chase', camera_offset: Sequence[float] | None = None, lens: float = 35, field: str | None = None, hud: bool = True, hud_keys: Sequence[str] | None = None, sparkline: str | None = None, fps: float = 24, gif: bool = False, mp4: bool = True, sun_elevation: float...
functions.doc:
Render ``scene.animation`` (an :class:`~.animation.Animation`) frame by frame with Cycles (CPU, denoised),
burn the HUD into each PNG and encode an MP4 (and a GIF). Returns ``{"frames": [png, ...], "mp4": path | None,
"gif": path | None}``.

frames: None (every frame), an int n (the animation resampled to n evenly spaced frames) or frame indices.
camera: "chase" (behind the tracked body along its direction of travel, or at ``camera_offset`` in the body
frame), "chase_low" (behind and a little aside of the body, the camera kept low over the ground, looking up at it
as it climbs away: a runway shot;
``camera_offset`` in the body frame also works), "follow" (at ``camera_offset`` in scene axes from the body,
default from the 3/4 view), "side" (alongside the path, tracking the body), "tower" (fixed at ``camera_offset``
in scene axes, default beside the middle of the path, looking at the body) or "fixed" (the whole scene and path
in the 3/4 view). ``lens`` in mm.
field: colour the surfaces by this static per-vertex field; animated surface fields and shapes are always shown.
trails: False, True, or ``{"radius": r, "alpha": a, "seconds": s}`` overriding every trail's tube radius,
opacity and time window (defaults: 0.003 x the tracked body's size, ``add_trail``'s alpha and trail_seconds);
a trail is the path of its last seconds behind the body, fading to transparent at its tail.
lines: draw the scene's static Lines as translucent glowing tubes (brighter when there is haze); a sequence of
booleans, one per animation frame, shows them only on those frames (e.g. airflow only once the fans run).
colorbars: True / False, a dict ``{"field": bool, "vectors": bool, "trails": bool, "lines": bool}`` or the
kinds to show; ``colorbar_on=False`` turns them all off.
hud_keys: only these HUD entries in the caption; sparkline: a HUD key drawn as an inset chart (bottom-left).
motion_blur: True (a 1/30 s shutter in scene time) or the shutter in seconds of scene time (not of the clip,
which may run faster than real time); the tracked bodies and the camera are keyframed at every rendered frame,
so the ground blurs in a chase view while the tracked body stays sharp. dof: f-stop, focused on the tracked body each frame.
haze: cloud-like volumetric haze, ``haze`` = optical depth over ten camera-to-body distances (0.5 to 2 reads
as light haze; costs render time). exposure: view exposure (default -0.3 sky, -0.2 studio).
ground: True for a grey plane under the scene and path, or a height (scene up axis) for its level.
background: "sky" (physical sky with its sun disc lighting the scene) or "studio" (light gradient and a lamp).
Materials named "asphalt" and "grass" become procedural (colour patches, roughness variation, bump); surfaces
whose material contains "marking" are lifted (and "grass" lowered) a hair so coplanar paint stays crisp.
smooth: smooth shading with sharp edges above 35 degrees. crf: H.264 quality of the MP4 (higher = smaller).
Materials missing from ``MATERIALS`` and ``scene.materials`` render grey; their names are logged.

functions.name: render_still
functions.sig: (scene, out_png: str, frame: int, *, size: tuple[int, int] = (1920, 1080), samples: int = 64, **kw) -> str
functions.doc:
One high-quality frame of ``scene.animation`` (frame index ``frame``) as a PNG at ``out_png``; takes every
option of :func:`render_animation` (camera, dof, motion_blur, haze, hud_keys, sparkline, trails, lines, ...).
With motion blur the neighbouring frames are keyframed too, so the blur is that of the clip.

children.summary: Blender Cycles renders of any ~.scene.Scene (pip install bpy, or run inside Blender).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.captions
children.doc:
Captions, title cards and narration for rendered stills and videos: the part of a product-style film that is
not the 3-D render itself.

    caption(path, "OpenFOAM k-omega SST, slant 25 deg, 60 m/s", sub="surface pressure coefficient")
    title_card("intro.png", (1280, 720), "Ahmed body", ["From CFD to a digital twin", "and back to the wind tunnel"])
    wav = narrate("Fifty-eight OpenFOAM runs.", "line1.wav")             # eSpeak NG (``espeak-ng`` binary)
    mux_audio("film.mp4", [(0.0, wav)], "film_voiced.mp4")                 # ffmpeg

Style (:data:`STYLE`): a near-black ground, light text and one accent colour (default the green of a dark product
stage, ``#76b900``) used for the title underline, the caption marker and the progress bar; fonts from DejaVu (always
installed with matplotlib). Every function works on PNG or JPEG files in place or to a new path and needs only
Pillow; :func:`narrate` and :func:`mux_audio` need the ``espeak-ng`` and ``ffmpeg`` binaries and say so when they
are missing.

functions.name: caption
functions.sig: (path: str, text: str, *, sub: str = '', out: str | None = None, corner: str = 'top-left', progress: float | None = None, footer: str = '', footer_corner: str = 'bottom-left', style: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Burn a caption (``text`` bold, ``sub`` below it) with an accent marker into the image at ``path``
(``out`` defaults to in place); ``progress`` in 0..1 draws a thin accent bar along the bottom edge and
``footer`` a small line of muted text above it in ``footer_corner`` (the source, a licence, a frame counter;
bottom-left by default, away from a colour bar at the bottom right).

functions.name: title_card
functions.sig: (out: str, size: tuple[int, int], title: str, lines: Sequence[str] = (), *, kicker: str = '', footer: str = '', style: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
A full-frame card on the dark ground: ``kicker`` (small, accent) above a large ``title`` with an accent
rule, then ``lines`` in light text and ``footer`` in muted text at the bottom.

functions.name: narrate
functions.sig: (text: str, out_wav: str, *, voice: str = 'en-us', speed_wpm: int = 165, exe: str = 'espeak-ng') -> str
functions.doc:
Synthesise ``text`` to ``out_wav`` with eSpeak NG (English by default). Raises ``RuntimeError`` naming the
missing binary when it is not installed.

functions.name: audio_duration
functions.sig: (path: str) -> float
functions.doc: Seconds of a WAV file (header only).

functions.name: mux_audio
functions.sig: (video: str, cues: Sequence[tuple[float, str]], out: str, *, gain_db: float = 0.0) -> str
functions.doc:
Lay the WAV files of ``cues`` (``(start_s, wav_path)``) on the video's timeline (silence elsewhere) and write
``out`` (H.264 copied, AAC audio) with ffmpeg; raises ``RuntimeError`` when ffmpeg is missing.

children.summary: Captions, title cards and narration for rendered stills and videos: the part of a product-style film that is not the 3-D render itself.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.colormap
children.doc:
The CFD colour scale (jet: blue = low, red = high), the perceptual magma scale, and a colour bar burnt
into an image.

functions.name: jet
functions.sig: (t: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc: sRGB jet colour for t in [0, 1], as floats in [0, 1].

functions.name: magma
functions.sig: (t: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc: sRGB magma colour for t in [0, 1], as floats in [0, 1].

functions.name: ramp
functions.sig: (t: float, stops = None) -> tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc: sRGB colour of a piecewise-linear scale (default :data:`JET`) at t in [0, 1], floats in [0, 1].

functions.name: decimals
functions.sig: (lo: float, hi: float) -> int
functions.doc: Decimals that tell five ticks over [lo, hi] apart (same rule as studio-core.js).

functions.name: fmt
functions.sig: (v: float, nd: int) -> str
functions.doc: A tick label: fixed with ``nd`` decimals, exponent form beyond 1e4 or below 1e-3 (as JavaScript prints it).

functions.name: ticks
functions.sig: (lo: float, hi: float, n: int = 5, nd: Optional[int] = None) -> List[str]
functions.doc: Evenly spaced tick labels from lo to hi, identical to the browser viewer's.

functions.name: colorbar
functions.sig: (path: str, title: str, lo: float, hi: float, nd: Optional[int] = None, lo_txt: str = '', hi_txt: str = '', corner: str = 'bottom-right', stops = None, dark: bool = False) -> str
functions.doc:
Draw a colour bar (jet, or the scale ``stops`` such as :data:`RDBU`) with 5 ticks and a title in a corner of
the image at ``path`` (overwritten); ``dark``: a near-black panel with light text (for a dark stage).

children.summary: The CFD colour scale (jet: blue = low, red = high), the perceptual magma scale, and a colour bar burnt into an image.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.compose
children.doc:
Colour maps for animations (jet and diverging blue-white-red), colour bars burnt into images, and multi-panel
pictures and videos (a grid of renders with labels and one common colour bar).

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.compose import compose_grid, compose_grid_video
    compose_grid(["a.png", "b.png", "c.png", "d.png"], "grid.png", labels=["A320", "ATR", "Glider", "Jet"],
                 colorbar=("n_z [g]", 0.0, 2.0, "jet"))
    compose_grid_video(["a.mp4", "b.mp4"], "grid.mp4", labels=["A", "B"], ncols=2, crf=28)

Colour maps: ``"jet"`` (CFD convention, blue = low, red = high; the same stops as :mod:`.colormap` and
studio-core.js) and the diverging ``"coolwarm"`` / ``"bwr"`` / ``"rdbu"`` (ColorBrewer RdBu reversed; blue =
negative, neutral midpoint, red = positive), used with a range symmetric about zero (:func:`symmetric_range`).

One picture of ``images`` on a grid of ``ncols`` columns (every image scaled to the first one's size), a

A grid video of ``mp4_paths`` (ffmpeg ``xstack``; every clip scaled to the first one's size, the shorter ones
