children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.detail
children.doc:
Mechanical detail: the fasteners, welds and bosses a figure needs and a solver mesh must not have.

A CFD or FEA mesh is right to be smooth -- every bolt head is a place where a boundary layer goes wrong. A figure is
the opposite: at photographic distance the eye reads scale from exactly those details, and a casing with no seam, no
fastener and no weld looks like a render of a mesh, which is what it is.

These builders stay out of the physics. They take the geometry you already have, put the detail where a fabricator
would have put it, and hand back :class:`~.scene.Surface` objects to add to the scene:

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import detail
    sc.surfaces += detail.bolt_circle(hub_centre, normal=(0, 0, 1), radius=0.11, count=8, head_radius=0.008)
    sc.surfaces.append(detail.weld_bead(root_path, radius=0.004))

Everything is generated, so it is reproducible, parameterised and cheap: a detail level is a number in a script, not a
second CAD model to keep in sync.

functions.name: hex_bolt
functions.sig: (centre, normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), *, head_radius: float = 0.01, height: float = 0.006, washer: bool = True, material: str = 'steel', name: str = 'bolt') -> Surface
functions.doc:
One hex-head bolt standing on ``centre`` along ``normal``: a hexagonal prism with a flat top, and under it a
washer a hair wider and a hair shorter, which is the lip that makes the head read at a distance.

functions.name: bolt_circle
functions.sig: (centre, normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), *, radius: float = 0.1, count: int = 8, head_radius: float = 0.01, height: float = 0.006, washer: bool = True, material: str = 'steel', name: str = 'bolts') -> List[Surface]
functions.doc:
``count`` bolts evenly spaced on a circle of ``radius`` around ``centre``, in the plane of ``normal``, the first
one on the ``u`` axis of that plane (so two runs with the same arguments put them in the same places).

functions.name: weld_bead
functions.sig: (points, *, radius: float = 0.004, material: str = 'steel', name: str = 'weld', segments: int = 12) -> Surface
functions.doc:
A weld along ``points``: cylinders between consecutive points with a sphere at each joint, so the bead reads as
one continuous run rather than a set of tubes. The radius is the bead's, which is how a weld is called out.

functions.name: seam_ring
functions.sig: (centre, normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), *, radius: float = 0.1, thickness: float = 0.004, material: str = 'steel', name: str = 'seam', n: int = 48) -> Surface
functions.doc:
A raised ring where two cast halves meet: a torus of ``thickness`` around a circle of ``radius``. It is what
tells a viewer the part is assembled instead of printed.

functions.name: pad
functions.sig: (centre, normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), *, radius: float = 0.02, height: float = 0.006, chamfer: float = 0.0015, material: str = 'steel', name: str = 'pad', n: int = 40) -> Surface
functions.doc:
A machined pad: a boss that stands proud of a casting so a bolt or a cover has something flat to land on. The
top edge is chamfered, which is the difference between a machined face and an extruded circle.

functions.name: gusset
functions.sig: (a, b, c, *, thickness: float = 0.006, material: str = 'steel', name: str = 'gusset') -> Surface
functions.doc:
A stiffening rib: the triangle ``a``-``b``-``c``, extruded ``thickness`` along its own normal. Two plates at a
right angle and a rib across the corner is how a welded frame gets its stiffness, and the triangle is what a viewer
reads as one.

functions.name: cone
functions.sig: (a, b, r0: float, r1: float, *, name: str, material: str, n: int = 48) -> Surface
functions.doc: A truncated cone from ``a`` (radius ``r0``) to ``b`` (radius ``r1``): a weld neck, a reducer, a handrail foot.

functions.name: pipe_flange
functions.sig: (centre, axis = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), *, pipe_radius: float = 0.035, flange_radius: float = 0.075, thickness: float = 0.018, raised_face: float = 0.002, neck: float = 0.03, bolts: int = 4, bolt_radius: Optional[float] = None, head_radius: float = 0.008, material: str = 'steel', bolt_material: Optional[str] = None, name: str = 'flange', n: int = 64) -> List[Surface]
functions.doc:
A whole connection, not a disc: the plate, the raised face the gasket sits on, the weld neck that tapers into the
pipe and the bolts on the face. This is the item the audit called "conexões" — a flange drawn as one cylinder reads
as a puck, and the three parts together read as a joint.

Returns the surfaces; add them to the scene with ``sc.surfaces += ...``.

children.summary: Mechanical detail: the fasteners, welds and bosses a figure needs and a solver mesh must not have.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.fieldview
children.doc:
Fields on a mesh for the apps' 3-D views: the boundary surface of a ``pinneapple_data.cae`` mesh with several
fields (values and errors), optional deformed shapes and marked regions, as a glTF plus a small JSON description.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.fieldview import field_view
    fv = field_view(mesh, [
        {"name": "fem", "values": vm_fem, "label": "FEM von Mises", "unit": "MPa", "group": "vm", "deform": "fem"},
        {"name": "rom", "values": vm_rom, "label": "ROM von Mises", "unit": "MPa", "group": "vm", "deform": "rom"},
        {"name": "err", "values": abs(vm_rom - vm_fem), "label": "|ROM - FEM|", "unit": "MPa", "kind": "error"}],
        deform={"fem": u_fem, "rom": u_rom},
        markers=[{"name": "clamp", "kind": "bc", "points": mesh.points[clamp]}])
    fv.glb()          # bytes for /shared/fieldview3d.js (GLTFLoader): fields as vertex attributes _F0, _F1, ...
    fv.meta           # fields with their colour ranges, deformations with an automatic scale, markers, sizes

Colour ranges are computed on the surface values that are shown. Fields of one ``group`` share a range (a prediction
and its reference on the same scale). Errors run from 0 to their 99th percentile and say when the scale is clipped.
Above ``max_faces`` triangles the surface is decimated (vertex clustering, fields averaged): see the size guide in
docs/core_concepts/studio.md (interactive up to about 500 k triangles; the default keeps a view light).

functions.name: colour_range
functions.sig: (values, kind: str = 'value') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
``{"lo", "hi", "max", "clipped"}``: values span min..max; errors span 0..99th percentile (``clipped`` when
the maximum is above it).

functions.name: length_factor
functions.sig: (unit: str | None, to: str = 'm') -> float | None
functions.doc: Factor from ``unit`` to ``to`` when ``unit`` is a length (``mm`` -> m: 1e-3), else None.

functions.name: displacement_factor
functions.sig: (name: str, unit: str | None, components: int, mesh_unit: str = 'm') -> float | None
functions.doc:
If a nodal vector field is a displacement, the factor that converts it to the mesh's length unit: its unit is
a length, or it has no unit and is named like one (``D``, ``U``, ``disp``, ``displacement``). Else None.

functions.name: subsample
functions.sig: (points, n: int = MAX_MARKER_POINTS) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: At most ``n`` of the points, evenly spread over the array (markers do not need every node).

functions.name: field_view
functions.sig: (mesh, fields: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]], *, deform: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, markers: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]] = (), max_faces: int | None = VIEW_MAX_FACES, title: str = '', axes: str = 'z_up', notes: Sequence[str] = (), length_unit: str = '') -> FieldView
functions.doc:
Build the view. ``fields``: dicts with ``name``, ``values`` (one per point or per cell, vectors as magnitude,
6-component tensors as von Mises), optional ``where`` ("point" / "cell", from the length), ``label``, ``unit``,
``kind`` ("value" or "error"), ``group`` (shared colour range), ``deform`` (a key of ``deform``) and ``note``.
``deform``: key -> nodal displacement (n_points, 3) in the mesh's length unit. ``length_unit``: the mesh's length unit (shown with the displacements). ``markers``: dicts with ``name``,
``kind`` ("bc", "load", "hotspot", "region"), ``points`` (k, 3), optional ``detail``, ``centre`` (where the label
goes; default: the member nearest the mean), ``label`` (False: points only) and ``fields`` (names of the fields it belongs to; default: shown with every field).

children.summary: Fields on a mesh for the apps' 3-D views: the boundary surface of a pinneapple_data.cae mesh with several fields (values and errors), optional deformed shapes and marked regions, as a glTF plus a ...

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.lighting
children.doc:
Lighting and sky presets shared by the studio renderers (PyVista, Blender Cycles, three.js viewer).

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.lighting import PRESETS, apply_pyvista
    apply_pyvista(plotter, "lunar_south_pole", target=(0, 0, 0), extent=10.0)

Presets
-------
``studio``            the grey-blue gradient and soft three-point light of the CFD renders (Formula car, aircraft).
``lunar_south_pole``  a black sky and one hard, low Sun: at about 86 deg S (the VIPER landing region) the Sun stays
                      within about 5.5 deg of a level horizon (90 - 86 + 1.54 deg lunar obliquity), so shadows are
                      many times longer than the objects. No atmosphere: no sky light, only a faint bounce light
                      from the regolith. The Sun's disc is 0.53 deg across, so shadow edges are sharp.
``lunar_low_sun``     the same black sky with the Sun 12 deg high: still long, hard shadows, but the floors of
                      small craters are partly lit, which keeps data on them readable.
``lunar_day``         the same black sky with the Sun 30 deg high (mid latitudes).

Earth can be added (``earth=True``): a 1.9 deg blue-white disc (Earth's angular diameter seen from the Moon) in the
sky, by default low above the horizon.

methods.name: sun_direction
methods.doc: Unit vector from the scene towards the Sun (z up).

functions.name: get_preset
functions.sig: (preset) -> LightingPreset

functions.name: apply_pyvista
functions.sig: (plotter, preset = 'lunar_south_pole', target = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), extent: float = 10.0, earth: bool | None = None, shadow_resolution: int = 4096) -> LightingPreset
functions.doc:
Set the background, a directional Sun (with shadows when the preset asks for them), a weak fill light and,
optionally, Earth in the sky of a PyVista ``plotter``.

functions.name: add_earth_pyvista
functions.sig: (plotter, preset, target, extent: float)
functions.doc: Earth as a shaded sphere far away, with the right angular size, lit from the Sun's direction.

functions.name: threejs_config
functions.sig: (preset = 'lunar_south_pole') -> dict
functions.doc: The preset as plain data for the browser viewers (background, sun direction and intensity, fill).

functions.name: blender_world
functions.sig: (preset = 'lunar_south_pole', bpy = None)
functions.doc:
Configure the current Blender scene: world colour, one Sun lamp with the preset's angular size and strength,
and (for black-sky presets) no world light. Returns the Sun object.

children.summary: Lighting and sky presets shared by the studio renderers (PyVista, Blender Cycles, three.js viewer).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.manufacture
children.doc:
A body with a manufacturing history.

Everything else in the studio adds detail from the outside: a bolt, a weld, a chamfer. This is the other direction -- a
part that carries the record of how it was made, because that record *is* what a viewer reads as a real part. A
casting has a draft on its walls, a skin with sand grain and a parting line; a machined face on that casting is flat,
bright, cut in one direction, and its edge is a chamfer, not a corner; a bore has a chamfered mouth and a dark throat; a
weld has a bead and the straw-and-blue band beside it. Nothing in that list is visible as "detail" -- the whole surface
changes character.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import manufacture as M
    body = M.cast_blank(radius=0.11, height=0.09, draft=2.0).machine_face([0.11, 0, 0], (1, 0, 0), radius=0.05)                                                      .bore([0.11, 0, 0], (1, 0, 0), diameter=0.03)                                                      .weld(path).finish()
    sc = body.scene
    body.describe()          # the history, in order, as a sentence a figure caption can carry

Each operation appends to :attr:`Body.history` and leaves the scene editable, so the same body can be rendered at any
point of its history -- the blank, three operations in, and finished -- and the pictures are a comparison of the part,
not of three different models.

What this is not: a mesh kernel. A bore here is drawn, not cut -- a dark throat under a chamfered mouth, which reads as
a hole at photographic distance because a hole is a shadow with a bright lip. A boolean would need a real modeller; the
day one is in the stack, ``bore`` is the operation that should call it.

classes.name: Operation
classes.doc:
One step of the history: what was done, the surfaces it left behind, and the numbers it was done with -- the
last one is what lets the history be written down as data and replayed.

classes.name: Body
classes.doc: A scene and the history that made it. Every method returns ``self``, so the operations read as a process.

methods.name: spec
methods.doc:
The body as data: the blank's parameters and every operation with its numbers, in order. ``build`` replays
it, so a route sheet is a file instead of a script.

methods.name: describe
methods.doc: The history as one line, for a figure caption: ``cast blank; machined face 50 mm; bored 30 mm``.

methods.name: materials
methods.doc: The body's own material overrides, ready for a render: the cast skin, the cut face, the oxide and the bore.

methods.name: machine_face
methods.sig: (centre, normal, *, radius: float, height: float = 0.003, chamfer: float = 0.0012, name: str | None = None) -> Body
methods.doc:
Cut a face: a pad standing proud of the casting with a chamfered rim, in the machined material. It is the
contrast that does the work -- the same light that dulls the cast skin runs down the cut.

methods.name: bore
methods.sig: (centre, normal, *, diameter: float, depth: float = 0.02, csk: float = 0.0015, cut: bool | None = None, name: str | None = None) -> Body
methods.doc:
Bore a hole. With a kernel it is **cut**: :mod:`.solid.boolean` subtracts a closed cylinder and leaves an
opening with an interior wall and a silhouette that changes with the camera. Without one -- or on a body whose
shells are open -- it is **drawn**: a dark throat under a chamfered mouth, which is what a hole looks like at
photographic distance, because a hole is a shadow with a bright lip.

methods.name: shell
methods.sig: (*, thickness: float = 0.01, floor: float = 0.01, name: str | None = None) -> Body
methods.doc:
Hollow the casting: subtract an inner volume so the body has a wall of ``thickness`` and a floor of
``floor``. This is the operation a boolean was needed for -- the geometry inside did not exist before, and no
amount of surface detail can stand in for it.

methods.name: weld
methods.sig: (points, *, radius: float = 0.005, tint: float = 1.35, name: str | None = None) -> Body
methods.doc:
Weld along a path: the bead, and the heat-tinted band beside it. The band is what makes a weld look welded
rather than glued -- the metal around the bead is not the metal of the plate.

methods.name: bolt_pattern
methods.sig: (centre, normal, *, radius: float, count: int, head_radius: float = 0.008, name: str | None = None) -> Body
methods.doc: Drill and fit a bolt pattern on a face: the machined face, the bolts and the chamfered mouths.

methods.name: finish
methods.sig: (*, angle: float = 30.0, width: float = 0.0015, segments: int = 2, log = None) -> Body
methods.doc: Break every remaining sharp edge -- the last thing a shop does to a part -- by beveling the whole body.

functions.name: cast_blank
functions.sig: (*, radius: float = 0.11, height: float = 0.09, draft: float = 2.0, base: float = 1.16, running: float = 0.012, material: str | None = None, name: str = 'blank', closed: bool = True) -> Body
functions.doc:
A housing as it leaves the mould: a drum with a drafted wall, a wider base and the as-cast skin.

``draft`` is in degrees and is not decoration -- a casting that has to come out of a mould cannot have a vertical
wall, and the slight taper is one of the cues that says "cast" before any texture does.

``closed`` builds the shell as a solid (a closed drum), which is what a real :meth:`Body.bore` needs; the drafted
wall then lives on the solid's own rings, and there is no visible difference from the shell at render time.

functions.name: build
functions.sig: (spec: dict, *, log = None) -> Body
functions.doc:
A body from its route sheet: ``{"blank": {...}, "operations": [{"op": "bore", "params": {...}}, ...]}``.

The operations are the methods of :class:`Body`, called in the order they appear -- so a history is data a shop can
write down, diff and keep next to the drawing, and the same file renders the same part anywhere.

children.summary: A body with a manufacturing history.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.particles
children.doc:
Particle animations: thousands of spheres coloured by a value (speed, temperature, species), inside glass or steel
equipment that can move (a turning impeller), rendered frame by frame with Blender Cycles; then composed with live
charts that draw themselves as time runs, a colour bar and a clock, into a GIF (and an MP4 when Blender's encoder
is available). Works for any Lagrangian result: stirred tanks, fluidised beds, hoppers, sprays, mixers, DEM.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.particles import render_particle_frames, compose_video
    pngs = render_particle_frames(frames, d=3e-3, equipment=lambda k: tank.surfaces(angle[k]), out_dir="frames",
                                  field_range=(0, 0.3), view=(-1.0, -1.2, 0.55))
    compose_video(pngs, times, out="tank.gif", charts=[("Particles Top [%]", times, 100 * top),
                                                       ("Stirrer Speed [RPM]", times, rpm)],
                  colorbar=("Velocity Magnitude (m/s)", 0, 0.3))

``frames``: a list of dicts with ``x`` (n, 3) positions and ``value`` (n,) (or ``speed``), z up.
``equipment(k)``: the surfaces of frame k as (name, V, F, material) with material in "glass", "liquid", "steel",
"grey".

functions.name: render_particle_frames
functions.sig: (frames: Sequence[dict], d: float, out_dir: str, *, equipment: Callable[[int], Sequence[tuple]] | None = None, field: str = 'speed', field_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None, view: Sequence[float] = (-1.0, -1.25, 0.55), distance: float = 1.0, lens: float = 50, size: tuple[int, int] = (960, 720), samples: int = 24, every: int = 1, floor: bool = True, background: tuple[float, float, float] ...
functions.doc:
Render every ``every``-th frame to ``out_dir/frame_XXXX.png``; the camera frames the equipment (or the
particles) once. Returns the PNG paths. ``device``: the Cycles compute device, as in
:func:`~.blender.render` ("auto" takes the GPU when the machine has one).

functions.name: compose_video
functions.sig: (images: Sequence[str], times: Sequence[float], out: str, *, charts: Sequence[tuple[str, Sequence[float], Sequence[float]]] = (), colorbar: tuple[str, float, float] | None = None, cmap: str = 'viridis', clock: str = 'Time: {t:.1f}', title: str = '', duration_ms: int = 100, width: float = 12.0, dpi: int = 80, mp4: bool = False, frame_dir: str | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
One composed frame per image: the render on the left, the ``charts`` (label, t, y) on the right drawn up to
the current time (full axes from the start, so the line grows), a colour bar over the render and a clock.
Writes a GIF to ``out``; with ``mp4`` also ``out`` with .mp4 through Blender's FFmpeg when available.

functions.name: encode_mp4
functions.sig: (pngs: Sequence[str], out: str, fps: int = 10) -> str
functions.doc: H.264 MP4 of a PNG sequence with Blender's sequencer (no ffmpeg binary needed).

children.summary: Particle animations: thousands of spheres coloured by a value (speed, temperature, species), inside glass or steel equipment that can move (a turning impeller), rendered frame by frame with Blender ...

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.pbr
children.doc:
Procedural PBR shaders for the materials a flat factor table cannot describe on its own.

An entry of ``MATERIALS`` (see :mod:`.scene`) carries the numbers every consumer can use — glTF, USD, the three.js
viewer — and optionally ``"shader": "<name>"``, naming one of the builders registered here that Blender alone runs
at render time. An entry with a shader still exports, everywhere else, as the flat material it declares; the shader
only adds what the export formats cannot carry: micro-bump, wear, spatter and streaks.

    "brushed_steel": {"color": [0.72, 0.73, 0.74], "metallic": 1.0, "roughness": 0.22,
                      "shader": "brushed_metal"}

The recipes are the ones the industrial pump-station example
(``examples/use_cases/physics_data_factory/blender_factory_render.py``) proved out — painted steel that chips to
bare metal, concrete with aggregate, fine manufacturing bump — rewritten against the table's parameters so that any
colour gets the same treatment, with the procedural detail driven by object coordinates (so it stays put when the
body moves, and always has a physical scale in metres).

functions.name: shader
functions.sig: (name: str)
functions.doc: Register a builder under ``name`` (used by ``"shader"`` in a ``MATERIALS`` entry).

functions.name: painted_metal
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc:
Industrial paint with fine manufacturing bump, chipped through to bare metal where it wears (``wear``: the
fraction of the surface, 0..0.4; ``metal_color``: what shows through). The pump casing of the factory example.

functions.name: brushed_metal
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc:
Brushed stainless: streaks along the object's x, a roughness that runs from polished to dull across the
brush, and a bump too fine to see as bumps. ``streak`` stretches the pattern (higher = finer lines).

functions.name: cast_metal
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc: Cast iron or a sand-cast housing: a pitted surface with dull and polished patches, no paint.

functions.name: oxidized_metal
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc:
Bare metal under rust: the entry's colour is the metal, ``rust_color`` the oxide that covers it in patches,
with a soft edge (rust does not chip like paint). ``rust``: 0..1, how much of it there is.

functions.name: concrete
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc:
Cast concrete: aggregate in two shades of the entry's colour, a coarse pit, and the dull roughness a floor or
a wall has. ``aggregate``: the grain size in metres^-1 (higher = finer).

functions.name: galvanized
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc: Hot-dip galvanising: the spangle of zinc crystals, which is a voronoi cell pattern, over the entry's colour.

functions.name: rubber
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc: Rubber, a matte seal or a belt: a fine pebbled bump and a roughness that barely varies.

functions.name: as_cast
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc:
The skin a part has the moment it leaves the mould: a sand grain too fine to see as bumps, a dull roughness that
varies in patches, and no highlight sharp enough to read as machined. ``grain`` is the sand; ``mottle`` how much the
roughness wanders (a casting is never uniform).

functions.name: machined
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc:
A machined face: tool marks in one direction, a roughness that is low and even, and the fine chatter of a
cutter that is never perfectly still. The contrast with :func:`as_cast` on the same part is the point -- it is how
a viewer reads which faces were cut and which were merely cast.

functions.name: heat_tint
functions.sig: (bpy, mat, st)
functions.doc:
The straw and blue a weld leaves beside the bead: the entry's colour is the metal, ``tint`` the oxide, and the
band follows a stretched noise so it is never a painted stripe.

children.summary: Procedural PBR shaders for the materials a flat factor table cannot describe on its own.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.planetary
children.doc:
Renders of a vehicle on a planetary surface with PyVista: heightfield terrain with baked photometry and hard Sun
shadows (:mod:`.shadows`), vehicle parts with their studio materials, rocks, optional field colour maps on the terrain
and on the parts (with a colour bar), Earth in the sky and a title.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.planetary import SurfaceView, render_surface
    view = SurfaceView(X, Y, Z, parts=[(V, F, "white_paint"), ...], rocks=[(V, F)], preset="lunar_south_pole")
    render_surface(view, "frame.png", camera=((-4, -5, 2), (0, 0, 0.8)), title="t = 12.0 s")

``parts`` entries are ``(vertices, faces, material)`` or ``(vertices, faces, material, values)`` where ``values`` (one
per vertex) are coloured with ``cmap`` / ``clim`` instead of the material. ``terrain_field`` (ny, nx) colours the
terrain where it is finite (e.g. normal stress in the ruts), blended over the regolith by ``field_alpha``: the colour
multiplies the regolith albedo before the photometry, so the relief, the shading and the shadows stay visible
through it; ``field_glow`` adds a share of unshaded colour that keeps the map readable inside shadows (0 = a pure
semi-transparent tint); ``field_saturation`` < 1 mutes the colours so the relief dominates. ``far_field`` colours
the far grid the same way.

Horizon: with ``horizon`` > 0 an annulus of terrain runs from the edge of the ``far`` grid out to ``horizon`` metres,
its height following ``far_fn`` near the grid and dropping with the curvature of the body (``planet_radius``,
the Moon by default) further out, so the visible edge of the ground is the real horizon (about 2.6 km for a camera
2 m above the lunar surface) and no mesh border is seen. :func:`border_visibility` checks this for a camera.

functions.name: horizon_distance
functions.sig: (height: float, planet_radius: float = MOON_RADIUS) -> float
functions.doc: Distance [m] to the horizon of a smooth sphere seen from ``height`` metres above it.

functions.name: ring_height
functions.sig: (view: SurfaceView, x, y)
functions.doc:
Height of the horizon annulus [m] at (x, y): ``far_fn`` (or the grid's edge level) blended into the edge
level over ``horizon_blend`` metres, a long-wavelength relief faded in with distance, and the curvature drop.

functions.name: terrain_height
functions.sig: (view: SurfaceView, x, y)
functions.doc: Height of the rendered ground at (x, y): the detailed patch, the far grid, then the horizon annulus.

functions.name: border_points
functions.sig: (view: SurfaceView, n: int = 720) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Points (n, 3) on the outer border of the rendered ground (the annulus rim, else the far grid's edge).

functions.name: border_visibility
functions.sig: (view: SurfaceView, camera, size = (1600, 900), view_angle: float = 35.0, samples: int = 400, margin: float = 0.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
Is the outer border of the ground mesh visible from ``camera``? Every border point is projected through the
camera; a point inside the frame (grown by ``margin`` pixels) counts as visible unless the ground between the
camera and the point hides it (``samples`` steps along the sight line, geometric spacing). Returns the number of
border points tested, inside the frame, and visible, plus the visible points' pixel coordinates.

functions.name: render_surface
functions.sig: (view: SurfaceView, path: str | None, camera, *, size = (1600, 900), view_angle: float = 35.0, title: str = '', subtitle: str = '', plotter = None, return_image: bool = False, shadow_cache: dict | None = None)
functions.doc:
Render ``view`` with ``camera = (position, focal_point[, up])``. Returns the image path or (with
``return_image``) the RGB array.

children.summary: Renders of a vehicle on a planetary surface with PyVista: heightfield terrain with baked photometry and hard Sun shadows (.shadows), vehicle parts with their studio materials, rocks, optional field ...

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.post
children.doc:
Finishing a figure after Cycles writes it: the contrast, the bloom and the vignette.

These are the last steps of a photographic pipeline, and they act on the written file, so they work the same on any
machine and on any Blender version -- the scene compositor and the AgX contrast looks moved between Blender 4 and 5,
and a figure should not depend on which one is installed. They are PNG/JPEG only: an EXR is a set of render passes to
be graded elsewhere, and must not be touched.

    render(scene, "hero.png", camera="product", look="punchy", post="bloom+vignette")

``look``: "neutral" (nothing), "low", "medium_low", "medium_high", "high", "very_high" -- an S-curve on the display
values, so the mid tones keep their shape and only the shoulders move -- or "punchy", the same curve plus a little
saturation, which is what a product shot gets before it ships.

``post``: "bloom" (the highlights bleed, as a bright lamp does on a sensor), "vignette" (the corners fall off) or
both joined by "+".

functions.name: look
functions.sig: (rgb: np.ndarray, name: str) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
An S-curve on the display values (and, for "punchy", a little saturation): the contrast step a colourist would
apply before the figure ships. ``name`` as in :data:`LOOKS`; an unknown one is an error, so a typo never silently
renders flat.

functions.name: vignette
functions.sig: (rgb: np.ndarray, strength: float = 0.55, softness: float = 0.55) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Darken towards the corners: an elliptical falloff that leaves the middle untouched, the way a wide-open lens
does. ``strength`` is how far the corners go down, ``softness`` how wide the transition is.

functions.name: bloom
functions.sig: (rgb: np.ndarray, threshold: float = 0.85, radius: float = 0.02, strength: float = 0.55) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
The highlights bleed into their surroundings: what a bright lamp does on a sensor. ``radius`` is a fraction of
the image's long side, so the same look holds at any resolution.

functions.name: apply
functions.sig: (path: str, *, look_name: 'str | None' = None, post: 'str | None' = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Finish the PNG/JPEG at ``path`` in place: the look, then bloom, then the vignette. Returns ``path``.

Anything else (an EXR, a file another process is still writing) is left alone: a render pass set is the input to
a grade, not something to burn a contrast curve into.

children.summary: Finishing a figure after Cycles writes it: the contrast, the bloom and the vignette.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.pyvista_render
children.doc:
Off-screen renders of a studio :class:`~.scene.Scene` with PyVista (VTK): the Blender-free counterpart of
:func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.render`, for machines without ``bpy``.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.pyvista_render import render_scene
    render_scene(scene, "beauty.png")                                   # materials (paint, carbon, tyre...)
    render_scene(scene, "cp.png", field="cp", cmap="jet", clim=(-2, 1))  # a surface field with a colour bar
    render_scene(scene, "lines.png", lines=True)                         # streamlines coloured by speed
    render_scene(scene, "wake.png", slice_name="wake: vorticity", view="back", slice_crop=(0.25, 0.75, 0, 0.5))

``view``: "front", "back", "side", "top", "bottom", "iso" or a direction (x, y, z) from the target to the camera.

functions.name: render_scene
functions.sig: (scene: Scene, path: str, *, field: str | None = None, cmap: str = 'jet', clim: tuple[float, float] | None = None, lines: bool = False, slice_name: str | None = None, view: str | Sequence[float] = 'iso', size = (1600, 900), background: str = '#11151C', zoom: float = 1.0, ground: bool = False, title: str = '', line_width: float = 2.0, max_lines: int | None = None, hide: Sequence[str] = (), slice...
functions.doc:
``slice_crop``: (s0, s1, t0, t1), the part of the slice to show as fractions of its ``u`` and ``v`` edges.
``wireframe``: a colour (e.g. "#3B82F6") draws every surface as its mesh edges in that colour instead.
``bar_title``: a short colour-bar title with its units (e.g. "Cp"); by default the field's label, which goes
under the title when too long for the bar.

children.summary: Off-screen renders of a studio ~.scene.Scene with PyVista (VTK): the Blender-free counterpart of pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.render, for machines without bpy.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.scene
children.doc:
A 3D scene for any geometry: surfaces with materials and per-vertex fields, streamlines, slice planes.

Build it from an STL/OBJ file, a ``pinneapple_data.cae`` mesh (any CFD/FEA result), plain arrays or an existing list of
parts, map a field onto it (CFD faces, FEA nodes, sensor points), then export it (glTF with the fields as vertex
attributes, OpenUSD, STL), render it in Blender (:mod:`.blender`) or open it in the browser (:mod:`.web`).

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import Scene
    sc = Scene.from_file("part.stl")
    sc.map_field("cp", points, cp)              # nearest-neighbour inverse-distance mapping onto the vertices
    sc.save("part.glb")                          # .glb / .usda / .stl

Coordinates are engineering axes with z up (metres or the model's unit). ``axes="aircraft"`` keeps the convention of
``pinneapple_design.aero`` (x aft, y right, z up) for its viewers.

classes.name: Surface
classes.doc:
One triangulated surface. ``fields``: name -> one value per vertex. ``uv``: optional texture coordinates
(per face corner, or per vertex); when absent they come from :func:`box_uvs`, so a material with a map needs
no unwrap step.

classes.name: Lines
Slice
classes.doc:
A rectangular plane with a value grid: ``origin`` + s*``u`` + t*``v`` for s, t in [0, 1]. ``grid[j, i]``:
row j along v, column i along u; NaN = no value (inside a body).

methods.name: from_file
methods.doc:
STL (binary or ASCII, one surface per solid), OBJ, glTF/GLB (fields from float vertex attributes ``_NAME``),
VTK PolyData .vtp (needs the ``vtk`` package), or any mesh/result ``pinneapple_data.cae`` reads (OpenFOAM
case directory or zip, Gmsh, VTK .vtk/.vtu, CalculiX .frd, Abaqus .inp ...).

methods.name: from_mesh
methods.sig: (mesh, fields: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None, material: str = 'grey', name: str = 'body', **kw) -> 'Scene'
methods.doc:
The boundary surface of a ``pinneapple_data.cae`` mesh (volume or surface elements, polyhedral OpenFOAM
meshes) with its cell or point fields on the vertices: vectors as magnitude, 6-component tensors as von
Mises. ``fields`` defaults to the mesh's own (``mesh.cell_data`` / ``mesh.point_data``).

methods.name: from_parts
methods.doc: From objects with name/vertices/faces/material (e.g. ``pinneapple_design.aero`` parts).

methods.name: map_field
methods.sig: (name: str, points, values, *, k: int = 4, mirror_y: bool = False, surfaces: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, label: str = '') -> 'Scene'
methods.doc:
Put ``values`` known at ``points`` (CFD wall faces, FEA nodes, sensors) on every vertex by inverse-distance
weighting of the ``k`` nearest. ``mirror_y``: the data covers y >= 0 only (half model with a symmetry plane).

methods.name: field_range
methods.sig: (name: str, pct: Tuple[float, float] = (1, 99)) -> Tuple[float, float]

methods.name: add_lines
methods.sig: (points, values = None, name: str = 'streamlines', label: str = '', cmap: str = 'jet', alpha: float = 1.0, radius: Optional[float] = None, color_range: Optional[Tuple[float, float]] = None) -> 'Scene'

methods.name: add_slice
methods.sig: (name, origin, u, v, grid, label: str = '', group: str = '') -> 'Scene'
methods.doc: ``group``: slices with the same group form a stack the browser viewer steps through with a slider.

methods.name: set_lighting
methods.doc: Use a preset of :mod:`.lighting` (e.g. ``"lunar_south_pole"``) in the browser viewer.

methods.name: unknown_materials
methods.doc:
Material names of the surfaces found neither in ``MATERIALS`` nor in ``self.materials`` (they export as
plain grey).

methods.name: decimate
methods.doc:
Reduce the surfaces (in place) to about ``max_faces`` triangles in total, each in proportion to its size,
by vertex clustering; fields are averaged over the merged vertices. Small parts and the surfaces named in
``keep`` (e.g. those carrying an animated per-vertex field) are left alone.

methods.name: save
methods.doc: By extension: .glb (fields as vertex attributes ``_NAME``), .usda, .stl, .json (lines and slices).

methods.name: extras
methods.doc:
Lines, slices and the animation as JSON (scene axes, same as the surfaces), with the field labels and,
when the surfaces have two or more groups, those groups as layers.

functions.name: box_uvs
functions.sig: (vertices, faces) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Texture coordinates by box projection, one pair per face corner (three per triangle): each triangle is
projected on the plane of its dominant normal axis and the extents of that pair mapped to 0..1. No unwrap step and
no external tool, and the same numbers everywhere -- which is what lets a map baked in Blender line up in glTF and
in the browser viewer. Every face gets the whole square, so a seam falls exactly where the projection changes
instead of being averaged across it. An island per axis is what a box-shaped part wants; a closed or strongly
curved body overlaps its islands and is better served by :func:`~.bake.unwrap_scene`.

functions.name: loop_uvs
functions.sig: (s) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
The UVs a surface carries, one pair per face corner (three per triangle, in the order of ``faces.ravel()``): its
own ``uv`` -- given per corner, or per vertex, in which case it is expanded -- or :func:`box_uvs` of its geometry.
A bake stores the layout it used here (:func:`~.bake.unwrap_scene`), so the render and the exports follow it.

functions.name: decimate_surface
functions.sig: (srf: 'Surface', target_faces: int) -> 'Surface'
functions.doc:
Vertex clustering on a uniform grid whose cell size is searched (bisection) to land near ``target_faces``.
Fast and robust for display; thin features below the cell size may close up.

functions.name: scalar_of
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
One value per entry: itself, the magnitude of a vector, the von Mises stress of a 6-component tensor
(xx, yy, zz, xy, yz, zx).

functions.name: sphere_surface
functions.sig: (centre, radius: float, *, name: str = 'marker', material: str = 'led', n_lat: int = 16, n_lon: int = 24) -> Surface
functions.doc:
A :class:`Surface` sphere: a source, a sensor, a probe location. ``led`` emits, so it reads against a dark
stage without a light of its own.

functions.name: rod_surface
functions.sig: (a, b, radius: float, *, name: str = 'rod', material: str = 'metal', n: int = 16) -> Surface
functions.doc: A :class:`Surface` cylinder from ``a`` to ``b``: a ray, a beam axis, a support.

functions.name: disc_surface
functions.sig: (centre, radius: float, *, normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), name: str = 'plane', material: str = 'glass', n: int = 48) -> Surface
functions.doc:
A :class:`Surface` disc of ``radius`` about ``centre``: a measurement plane, a quiet zone, an aperture. Give
it a material with ``alpha`` in ``Scene.materials`` to draw the plane translucent.

functions.name: vertex_normals
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: read_stl
functions.sig: (path: str) -> List[Tuple[str, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]]
functions.doc: (name, vertices, faces) per solid; duplicate vertices merged.

functions.name: read_obj
functions.sig: (path: str) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]

functions.name: read_gltf
functions.sig: (path: str, axes: str = 'z_up') -> List[Surface]
functions.doc:
Triangle meshes of a .glb/.gltf (embedded, data-URI or external buffers), node transforms applied, converted
from glTF's y-up to the scene ``axes``. Float vertex attributes starting with ``_`` become fields (their original
names when the file was written by this module). The material names are kept as written, so a scene saved and
read back renders with its own ``Scene.materials``; a name found in neither that nor ``MATERIALS`` renders grey
(:meth:`Scene.unknown_materials` lists it).

functions.name: read_vtp
functions.sig: (path: str, material: str = 'grey') -> Surface
functions.doc: VTK PolyData (.vtp) with its point and cell data (vectors as magnitude). Needs ``pip install vtk``.

functions.name: write_glb
functions.sig: (surfaces, T: np.ndarray, materials: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]], generator: str = 'PINNeAPPle', groups: Optional[Dict[str, List[int]]] = None) -> bytes
functions.doc:
glTF 2.0 binary with PBR materials (clearcoat, transmission, emissive). Every per-vertex field becomes a
float attribute ``_NAME`` (upper case; three.js reads it back as ``_name``). ``groups``: node name -> indices of
surfaces to parent under one node (e.g. a propeller that spins).

functions.name: write_usda
functions.sig: (surfaces, materials: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]], title: str = 'scene', root: str = 'Scene') -> str
functions.doc:
OpenUSD text: one Mesh per surface with UsdPreviewSurface materials; z up, metres (Omniverse, usdview).
Per-vertex fields become ``primvars:<name>`` (float, vertex interpolation).

functions.name: write_stl
functions.sig: (surfaces, solid: str = 'scene') -> bytes
functions.doc: Binary STL of all surfaces.

children.summary: A 3D scene for any geometry: surfaces with materials and per-vertex fields, streamlines, slice planes.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.shadows
children.doc:
Sun shadows and planetary-surface shading for heightfield terrains, independent of the renderer.

* :func:`terrain_self_shadow` -- cells of a heightfield hidden from the Sun by the terrain itself (horizon march).
* :func:`cast_shadow` -- the shadow of arbitrary triangle meshes (a vehicle) on a heightfield: every triangle is
  projected along the Sun direction onto the terrain and rasterised.
* :func:`lunar_lambert` -- the Lunar-Lambert photometric function of McEwen (1991), ``I = A [(1 - L) mu0 +
  2 L mu0 / (mu0 + mu)]`` (mu0, mu: cosines of the incidence and emission angles; L = 1 is the Lommel-Seeliger law
  of dark regolith), which keeps regolith lit at grazing Sun angles where a Lambert surface turns black.
  McEwen, A.S. (1991). Photometric functions for photoclinometry and other applications. Icarus 92, 298-311.
* :func:`shade_terrain` -- RGB per terrain vertex: photometry x (1 - shadow) + a weak fill, tone mapped.

Shading is baked into vertex colours, so any renderer (PyVista without its shadow pass, three.js, matplotlib) shows
the same hard shadows.

functions.name: terrain_self_shadow
functions.sig: (Z, cell: float, sun_dir, max_distance: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Boolean (ny, nx): True where the heightfield ``Z`` (rows along y, columns along x, spacing ``cell``) hides
the Sun (``sun_dir`` points from the ground to the Sun).

functions.name: points_in_terrain_shadow
functions.sig: (P, X, Y, Z, sun_dir, step: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Boolean per point (N, 3): the heightfield (X, Y, Z) blocks the Sun as seen from the point.

functions.name: cast_shadow
functions.sig: (meshes, X, Y, Z, sun_dir, iterations: int = 3, supersample: int = 1) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Boolean (ny, nx): cells of the regular grid (X, Y, Z) in the shadow of the triangle ``meshes`` [(V, F), ...].

With ``supersample`` > 1 the shadow is rasterised that many times finer and averaged: a float (ny, nx)
shadow fraction, which keeps the shadow edge smooth on a coarse grid.

functions.name: lunar_lambert
functions.sig: (normals, sun_dir, view_dir, L: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
McEwen (1991) Lunar-Lambert reflectance (without the albedo) for unit ``normals`` (N, 3); ``view_dir`` (3,) or
(N, 3) points from the surface to the camera.

functions.name: relief_noise
functions.sig: (X, Y, rms: float, wavelengths = (0.6, 8.0), n: int = 40, seed: int = 7, slope: float = 1.2)
functions.doc:
World-anchored smooth random relief [m] at points (X, Y): a sum of ``n`` plane waves with random directions
and phases, wavelengths log-spaced in ``wavelengths`` and amplitudes ~ wavelength^slope, scaled to ``rms``.
The same (x, y) always gives the same height, so a moving window of terrain does not swim.

functions.name: grid_normals
functions.sig: (Z, cell: float) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: shade_terrain
functions.sig: (X, Y, Z, sun_dir, camera_position, albedo = (0.45, 0.44, 0.42), shadow = None, exposure: float = 1.0, fill: float = 0.04, L: float = 0.6, tint = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
(ny, nx, 3) colours in [0, 1]: Lunar-Lambert photometry, shadows from ``shadow`` (bool grid or 0-1 fraction), a weak
fill light, a filmic shoulder. ``tint`` (ny, nx, 3) multiplies the albedo (e.g. a field colour map).

children.summary: Sun shadows and planetary-surface shading for heightfield terrains, independent of the renderer.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.solid
children.doc:
Solids and a real boolean: cutting a hole instead of painting one.

:func:`~.manufacture.Body.bore` used to draw a throat, because a shadow with a bright lip is what a hole looks like at
photographic distance. This module is the other answer: a closed solid, a cutter, and a kernel that subtracts one from
the other. The difference matters the moment the camera moves -- a drawn hole has no other side, no interior wall and no
change of silhouette.

What the kernel needs, and what this module therefore insists on:

* **closed operands.** A boolean on an open shell does not fail loudly, it produces a plausible mess. :func:`is_closed`
  checks the edge manifold before anything is cut, and the functions here build closed solids by construction.
* **a kernel.** Blender's exact solver, driven headless -- the same route :mod:`.bevel` takes. There is no bundled mesh
  kernel in this package; ``trimesh`` with ``manifold3d`` does this too, and if you have it the shapes here are ordinary
  ``Surface`` objects it can eat.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import solid
    body = solid.solid_drum([0, 0, 0], radius=0.11, height=0.09, n=96)
    cut = solid.boolean(body_scene, [solid.solid_drum([0.05, 0, 0.05], 0.02, 0.2, n=32)], op="difference")

functions.name: is_closed
functions.sig: (surface: Surface) -> bool
functions.doc: True when every edge of the mesh is shared by exactly two triangles -- the manifold a boolean needs.

functions.name: open_edges
functions.sig: (surface: Surface) -> int
functions.doc:
How many edges are not shared by two triangles: zero for a closed solid, and the number to look at when a
boolean goes wrong.

functions.name: solid_drum
functions.sig: (centre, radius: float, height: float, *, radius_top: float | None = None, n: int = 64, axis = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), name: str = 'drum', material: str = 'grey') -> Surface
functions.doc:
A closed cylinder: wall, bottom and top. The workhorse of a real cut -- a boss, a pad, a body in the rough.

``radius_top`` gives the wall a taper, which is how a casting's draft lives on a solid instead of on a shell.

functions.name: solid_box
functions.sig: (centre, size, *, name: str = 'box', material: str = 'grey') -> Surface
functions.doc: A closed box: a cutter for a slot, a flat, a window.

functions.name: circle_profile
functions.sig: (centre, radius: float, *, n: int = 48, normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), phase: float = 0.0)
functions.doc:
One station of a loft: a ring of ``n`` points. Any set of ``(n, 3)`` points is a profile, so a station can also be
a rounded rectangle, a section off a drawing, or the outline of a duct.

functions.name: rounded_rect_profile
functions.sig: (centre, width: float, height: float, *, n: int = 48, roundness: float = 0.35, normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0))
functions.doc:
A station that is not a circle: a rectangle with rounded corners as a superellipse. A duct transition between a
round inlet and a rectangular outlet is the shape no primitive in this package gives, and it is everywhere in
ventilation and in pump casings.

functions.name: loft
functions.sig: (stations, *, caps: bool = True, name: str = 'loft', material: str = 'grey') -> Surface
functions.doc:
The skin through a sequence of profiles: an organic body out of sections, which is how a duct transition, a
volute or a pump casing is drawn -- and the shape no primitive here can make.

Every station is an ``(n, 3)`` array with the same ``n``. The interpolation between stations is linear, which is
honest: a station is a measurement, and a spline through measurements invents the shape in between. Put the stations
where the geometry bends and linear is invisible; ``caps`` closes the two ends so the result is a solid a boolean
can cut.

functions.name: cutter_cylinder
functions.sig: (a, b, radius: float, *, n: int = 48, name: str = 'cutter', material: str = 'cutter') -> Surface
functions.doc: The tool of a bore: a closed cylinder from ``a`` to ``b``, long enough to pass through the part.

functions.name: boolean
functions.sig: (scene, cutters: Sequence[Surface], *, op: str = 'difference', exe: str | None = None, timeout: float = 1800.0, log = None) -> Scene
functions.doc:
``scene`` with every closed ``cutter`` combined into it (``difference``, ``union`` or ``intersect``).

Blender's exact solver does the work, headless, so the result is a real mesh: an opening with an interior wall and a
silhouette that changes with the camera. Open shells are refused before anything runs -- a boolean on them does not
fail loudly, it makes a mess that looks like a result.

children.summary: Solids and a real boolean: cutting a hole instead of painting one.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.solver_view
children.doc:
The result of a solver run as a 3-D view, to check it before its numbers are used: the mesh, its fields, the
deformed shape (CalculiX displacement, with a scale factor) and the regions where the case defines its boundary
conditions and loads.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.solver_view import solver_result_view
    fv, info = solver_result_view("runs/r1/c01.solve")     # a folder with <job>.frd (+ <job>.inp), or an OpenFOAM case
    fv.glb(), fv.meta                                       # for /shared/fieldview3d.js
    info["conditions"]                                      # what was marked, from the deck or the case files

* **CalculiX:** the ``.frd`` (nodes, elements, last increment of each result: DISP, STRESS as von Mises, ...) and,
  from the ``.inp`` next to it, ``*BOUNDARY`` (supports) and ``*CLOAD`` / ``*DLOAD`` (loads) as marked node sets.
* **OpenFOAM:** the polyMesh, the volume fields of the latest time (vectors as magnitude) and every non-empty patch
  with its conditions from the first time directory, all as boundary conditions. A patch with a non-zero fixed vector
  value (a moving wall, an inlet) is the one that drives the flow: its role says so, and a note gives its value next
  to the cell values the colours show (a wall value is not a cell value).

Above ``max_faces`` triangles the surface is decimated (``VIEW_MAX_FACES``, from the size guide in
docs/core_concepts/studio.md); the description says so.

functions.name: find_result
functions.sig: (folder: str | Path) -> tuple[str, Path] | None
functions.doc: ``("calculix", <job>.frd)`` or ``("openfoam", <case dir>)`` for a step folder (or the case itself), else None.

functions.name: solver_result_view
functions.sig: (folder: str | Path, *, max_faces: int | None = VIEW_MAX_FACES) -> tuple[FieldView, dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
View of the CalculiX or OpenFOAM result in ``folder`` (see the module docstring). Raises ``ValueError`` when
there is no result to show.

children.summary: The result of a solver run as a 3-D view, to check it before its numbers are used: the mesh, its fields, the deformed shape (CalculiX displacement, with a scale factor) and the regions where the case ...

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.view_cache
children.doc:
Disk caches of 3-D result views (a JSON description next to its glTF binary).

A web app that shows a solver or model result in 3-D builds the view once (it can take seconds: reading the mesh,
evaluating a model, decimating) and serves it again from disk. Two shapes are used:

- :func:`cached_view`: one view per **key** (a job, a step and its hash, a held-out sample). The first call builds
  it, later calls with the same key read it back;
- :func:`save_view` / :func:`prune_views`: views of one-off results kept under a random id, oldest dropped first.

::

    meta, glb = cached_view(job_dir / "views", f"test_{k}", lambda: prediction_view(...))
    return {**meta, "glb": url}, FileResponse(glb)

functions.name: view_paths
functions.sig: (directory: str | Path, key: str) -> tuple[Path, Path]
functions.doc:
The ``(json, glb)`` paths of ``key`` in ``directory`` (characters outside ``[A-Za-z0-9_.-]`` become ``_``,
so a key cannot leave the directory).

functions.name: cached_view
functions.sig: (directory: str | Path, key: str, build: Callable[[], tuple[Any, dict]]) -> tuple[dict, Path]
functions.doc:
The cached view ``key`` in ``directory``: ``(description, glb_path)``.

When both files exist they are read back; otherwise ``build()`` is called. It returns ``(view, payload)``:
``view`` has a ``glb()`` method (a :class:`~pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.FieldView`) and ``payload`` is
the description (made JSON-safe with :func:`~pinneapple_core.jsonable.to_jsonable`). The glTF is written first and
the JSON last, so an interrupted build is rebuilt on the next call. Exceptions of ``build`` propagate and leave
no description behind.

functions.name: save_view
functions.sig: (directory: str | Path, view: Any) -> str
functions.doc: Write ``view.glb()`` under a new random id (32 hex characters) in ``directory``; returns the id.

functions.name: prune_views
functions.sig: (directory: str | Path, keep: int, pattern: str = '*.glb') -> int
functions.doc:
Keep the ``keep`` newest files matching ``pattern`` in ``directory`` (by modification time), delete the
rest; returns how many were deleted.

children.summary: Disk caches of 3-D result views (a JSON description next to its glTF binary).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.web
children.doc:
Interactive browser view of a :class:`~.scene.Scene` (three.js, shipped with the library; no internet needed).

    web_viewer(scene, "viewer/")       # writes index.html, viewer.js, studio-core.js, scene.glb, scene.json and three.js
    web_viewer(scene, "v/", single_file=True)   # one self-contained v/index.html (three.js, scene inlined): opens from file://
    serve(scene)                       # the same in a temporary folder, served on http://localhost:8000
    screenshot("viewer/", "view.png", frame=10)   # headless Chromium (playwright) picture of the page

Modes: the materials ("Realistic"), each surface field on the jet scale with a colour bar, streamlines coloured by
their values, each slice plane. Browsers do not open ES modules from file://, so open the folder through a local
server (``python -m http.server -d viewer``), use :func:`serve`, or write a single self-contained page
(``single_file=True``: the scene, the viewer and the vendored three.js inlined; it opens from disk and can be mailed). A scene with an ``animation``
(:class:`~.animation.Animation`) gets a bottom bar: play / pause, time slider, speed, head-up values, follow camera.

functions.name: web_viewer
functions.sig: (scene, out_dir: str, title: Optional[str] = None, max_faces: Optional[int] = MAX_FACES, single_file: bool = False, filename: str = 'index.html') -> str
functions.doc:
Write the viewer for ``scene`` into ``out_dir``; returns the path of its index.html. Surfaces above
``max_faces`` triangles in total are decimated for the page (the scene itself is not changed); None keeps all.
``single_file``: write only ``out_dir/filename``, with scene.json, scene.glb, the viewer and three.js inlined
(ES modules as ``data:`` URLs in an import map), so it opens from file:// with no server.

functions.name: serve
functions.sig: (scene, port: int = 8000, open_browser: bool = True, block: bool = True, out_dir: Optional[str] = None, max_faces: Optional[int] = MAX_FACES)
functions.doc:
Write the viewer (to ``out_dir`` or a temporary folder) and serve it on ``port``. ``block=False`` returns the
server (call ``.shutdown()``); otherwise serves until Ctrl+C.

functions.name: screenshot
functions.sig: (viewer_dir: str, out_png: str, frame: int | None = None, size: tuple[int, int] = (1280, 720), setup_js: str | None = None, timeout_ms: int = 60000) -> str | None
functions.doc:
PNG of the viewer written by :func:`web_viewer` in ``viewer_dir`` (or of a single-file page: the path of the
.html, opened from file://), taken in headless Chromium (needs
``pip install playwright``; ``PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM`` or /opt/pw-browsers/chromium is used when the bundled browser
is missing). ``frame``: animation frame to show (``window.studio.setFrame``); ``setup_js``: JavaScript run after
the page is ready (e.g. ``"studio.setMode('real')"``). Returns ``out_png``, or None with a warning when
playwright is not installed.

children.summary: Interactive browser view of a ~.scene.Scene (three.js, shipped with the library; no internet needed).

children.doc:
PINNeAPPle studio: realistic 3D visualisation of any geometry and its physics.

    import pinneapple as pp
    sc = pp.viz.Scene.from_file("result.frd")          # or an STL, an OpenFOAM case, arrays, a CFD result
    sc.save("result.glb")                               # glTF with the fields, also .usda (Omniverse) and .stl
    pp.viz.render(sc, "stress.jpg", field="STRESS")     # Blender Cycles, jet colour scale, colour bar
    pp.viz.render_headless(sc, "stress.png", field="STRESS")   # same, through the Blender binary (no bpy needed)
    pp.viz.web_viewer(sc, "viewer/")                    # interactive three.js page: surfaces, streamlines, slices
    pp.viz.LIGHTING_PRESETS["lunar_south_pole"]         # black sky, low hard Sun (also: studio, lunar_low_sun, ...)
    pp.viz.field_view(mesh, fields, deform=..., markers=...)   # fields, errors and deformed shapes for the apps' views
    pp.viz.export_gltf("wing.stl", {"cp": cp})          # glTF/GLB bytes, the field as a _CP vertex attribute (#281)
    pp.viz.viewer_html(grid, {"cp": cp}, "viewer/")     # the three.js page for any mesh and any field
    pp.viz.blender_render("wing.stl", "wing.png", field="cp")          # Blender Cycles, jet scale, colour bar
    pp.viz.read_openfoam("case/")                       # an OpenFOAM case as a PyVista grid with its fields (#60)
    pp.viz.compare_solutions(ref, pred, ...)           # reference, surrogate and the error map, L2 in the title (#63)

Planetary surfaces (heightfield terrain, Sun shadows, Lunar-Lambert regolith): :mod:`.planetary`, :mod:`.shadows`.

functions.name: bake_materials
functions.doc:
Bake the procedural material shaders into base colour, roughness and normal maps; see
:func:`.bake.bake_materials` (needs bpy).

functions.name: bake_materials_headless
functions.doc: The same through the Blender binary, for a machine without bpy; see :func:`.bake.bake_materials_headless`.

functions.name: bevel_scene
functions.doc:
The same scene with its sharp edges chamfered -- a mesh operation, not a surface beside the body; see
:func:`.bevel.bevel_scene`.

functions.name: hdri_path
functions.doc: The image behind ``render(background="hdri:<name>")``; see :func:`.blender.hdri_path`.

functions.name: turntable
functions.doc:
A GIF or MP4 in which the camera orbits while the field advances in time; see
:func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.orbit.turntable`.

functions.name: figure_caption
functions.doc:
The caption a figure carries: field, unit, range, exaggeration, time, method and status; see
:func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.caption.figure_caption`. A unit is required -- ``"-"`` is how a
dimensionless field says so.

functions.name: headless
functions.doc:
What this machine needs to render without a display, and whether it can; see
:func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.headless.headless`.

functions.name: render_field
functions.doc:
Evaluate a model on a domain and write the picture and the VTU of the same numbers (#61); see
:func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.fields.render_field`.

functions.name: write_vtu
functions.doc:
Write an unstructured grid in VTK XML format (#61); see
:func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.fields.write_vtu`.

functions.doc: Blender Cycles render; see :func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.blender.render`.

functions.doc:
Blender Cycles render from the command line, for a machine without bpy; see
:func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.blender.render_headless`.

functions.name: blender_executable
functions.doc: The Blender executable ``render_headless`` uses (or None); see :func:`.blender.blender_executable`.

functions.doc: Interactive page; see :func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.web.web_viewer`.

children.summary: PINNeAPPle studio: realistic 3D visualisation of any geometry and its physics.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.style
children.doc:
CFD-style colour maps, themes and defaults for PINNeAPPle visualisation.

Two layers live here. ``use_cfd_style`` is the older dark CFD theme and is kept
for the figures that already use it. ``use_theme`` is the house theme described
in #918: one font stack, one colour-blind-safe palette, perceptually uniform
maps, and helpers that make the quantity and its unit part of the figure.

No colour is written down in this module. Every palette entry, colour map stop,
figure size and font comes from :mod:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.theme`, the
one file the studio viewer, the twin3d viewer and the apps read as well (#65), so
a figure in a report and a field in a browser cannot disagree.

functions.name: use_cfd_style
functions.sig: (dark: bool = True) -> None
functions.doc: Apply CFD dark/light theme globally.

functions.name: get_cmap
functions.sig: (name: str = DEFAULT_CMAP)
functions.doc:
Return a matplotlib colormap by PINNeAPPle alias or standard name.

A colormap already in hand is returned unchanged: PyVista accepts either, and a caller passing a
``Colormap`` to ``render_png`` must not find it turned into a missing-name error.

functions.name: make_figure
functions.sig: (nrows: int = 1, ncols: int = 1, **kwargs)
functions.doc: Create a styled figure.

functions.name: use_theme
functions.sig: (kind: str = 'report', dark: bool = False) -> None
functions.doc:
Apply the house theme: one font stack, one palette, one set of maps.

``kind`` is ``"report"`` (read on screen), ``"slide"`` (projected, larger
type) or ``"paper"`` (printed at column width). ``dark`` switches to the
dark background used by the older CFD theme.

``cfd_rainbow`` stays registered for comparison pictures against commercial
CAE, but it is no longer any figure's default: it is not perceptually
uniform, so a reader cannot rank two colours by value.

functions.name: field_cmap
functions.sig: (quantity: str)
functions.doc:
Return the colormap registered for ``quantity`` (e.g. ``"temperature"``).

Unknown quantities raise instead of silently falling back: a fallback is
how two figures of the same quantity end up with different colours.

functions.name: figure_sizes
functions.sig: (kind: str = 'report') -> dict
functions.doc: Figure sizes for 1-, 2- and 3-panel layouts of the given theme kind.

functions.name: make_panel_figure
functions.sig: (ncols: int = 1, kind: str = 'report', **kwargs)
functions.doc: Figure and axes sized by the theme for a 1-, 2- or 3-panel layout.

functions.name: colorbar
functions.sig: (ax, mappable, quantity: str, unit: str, **kwargs)
functions.doc:
Colour bar that always carries the quantity and its unit.

Both are required: an unlabelled colour bar is a number the reader cannot
use. ``unit`` accepts ``""`` only for a genuinely dimensionless quantity,
and the label then says ``[-]``.

functions.name: label
functions.sig: (ax, x = None, y = None, title: str = None)
functions.doc: Axis labels as ``(name, unit)`` pairs, plus an optional title.

functions.name: annotate_verdict
functions.sig: (ax, text: str, ok: bool, xy = (0.02, 0.98), **kwargs)
functions.doc:
Stamp a pass/fail verdict in the corner of an axes.

The colour is not the only signal: the marker and the word carry the same
information, so the stamp survives a grey-scale print.

functions.name: panel_letters
functions.sig: (fig, axes = None, *, start: int = 0, xy = (-0.02, 1.02), **kwargs)
functions.doc: Letter the panels (a), (b), (c) in reading order.

functions.name: source_note
functions.sig: (fig, text: str, *, y: float = -0.01, **kwargs)
functions.doc: Data provenance line under the figure; required on every exported figure.

functions.name: save_figure
functions.sig: (fig, path, *, formats = ('png', 'svg'))
functions.doc:
Save the figure as PNG at 200 dpi plus a vector copy.

The issue asks for both: a raster for review and a vector for the paper and
the report, where a zoomed detail must stay sharp.

children.summary: CFD-style colour maps, themes and defaults for PINNeAPPle visualisation.

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.theme
children.doc:
The one theme file, and the code every renderer reads it through (#65).

``theme.json`` next to this module is the single source of the house colours: the brand inks, the two surfaces a
figure can sit on, the categorical palette, the colour maps with their stops, the quantity -> map registry, the font
stack and the figure sizes. Nothing else in the library declares a colour a reader is meant to recognise.

Three renderers consume it, and none of them keeps a private copy:

``pinneapple_tools.visualization.style``
    the matplotlib/PyVista side -- ``use_theme``, ``field_cmap``, the maps;
``pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.web`` (the apps, and ``pp.viz``'s browser viewer)
    through the generated ``studio/web/theme.js`` that ``studio-core.js`` imports;
``pinneapple_twin3d.viewer``
    through the generated ``viewer/theme.js`` that ``viewer.js`` imports.

The two JavaScript modules and the apps' ``theme.css`` are generated by ``scripts/build_theme.py`` and checked in, so
a browser page needs no fetch to draw; ``scripts/build_theme.py --check`` fails the day one of them drifts from
``theme.json``, which is what keeps "one theme file" true instead of aspirational.

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.theme import theme, colormap, palette, surface

    surface(dark=True)["plot"]        # '#0b1220', the background of every 3-D plot
    palette()[:3]                     # the first three categorical colours
    colormap("cfd_sequential")        # a matplotlib map built from the file's stops

functions.name: theme
functions.sig: () -> dict
functions.doc: The parsed theme file. Cached: it is read by every figure and never edited at run time.

functions.name: brand
functions.sig: () -> dict
functions.doc: The house inks: ``ink`` (near-black), ``blue`` and ``ember``, plus the lifted ember for small marks.

functions.name: surface
functions.sig: (dark: bool = False) -> dict
functions.doc: The surface a figure sits on: ``plot`` (the canvas), ``paper``, ``ink``, ``muted`` and ``line``.

functions.name: palette
functions.sig: () -> tuple[str, ...]
functions.doc: The categorical palette, in order. The first three carry most figures; do not reorder.

functions.name: font
functions.sig: () -> dict
functions.doc: The font stack and the base body size the theme sizes everything else from.

functions.name: figure
functions.sig: (kind: str = 'report') -> dict
functions.doc: Figure sizes for 1-, 2- and 3-panel layouts, plus the type scale and the DPIs.

functions.name: colormap_names
functions.sig: () -> tuple[str, ...]

functions.name: colormap_stops
functions.sig: (name: str) -> list
functions.doc: The stops of a map as ``[(position, (r, g, b)), ...]`` with RGB in 0..1.

functions.name: colormap_kind
functions.sig: (name: str) -> str
functions.doc: ``sequential``, ``diverging``, ``cyclic`` or ``rainbow`` -- what the map is allowed to be used for.

functions.name: colormap
functions.sig: (name: str, n: int = 256)
functions.doc: A matplotlib colormap built from the file's stops. Cached, so the same name returns the same object.

functions.name: field_cmaps
functions.sig: () -> dict
functions.doc: The quantity -> map registry, read from the file rather than guessed at the call site.

functions.name: field_cmap_name
functions.sig: (quantity: str) -> str
functions.doc: The map a quantity always gets; raises for a quantity nobody registered.

functions.name: stops_as_bytes
functions.sig: (name: str) -> list
functions.doc:
The stops in the shape the JavaScript viewers use: ``[[position, [r, g, b]], ...]`` with RGB 0..255.

Bytes and not floats because both viewers already divide by 255, and an integer stop is what a browser page
cached from an earlier version of the theme compares cleanly. The quantisation is 1/255, below what an 8-bit
display can show.

functions.name: hex_of
functions.sig: (rgb) -> str
functions.doc: ``(0.267, 0.005, 0.329)`` -> ``'#440152'``, for an HTML legend that must match the figure.

functions.name: simulate
functions.sig: (rgb, kind: str = 'deuteranopia') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Apply a dichromacy approximation to an ``(n, 3)`` sRGB array; ``kind`` is a key of :data:`VISION`.

functions.name: separation
functions.sig: (colors, kind: str = 'deuteranopia') -> float
functions.doc:
Smallest pairwise Euclidean distance in linear RGB, after simulating ``kind`` colour vision.

Linear RGB and not sRGB because that is where a distance means "how different these look"; the floor the tests
hold the palette to is 0.10, which is about the gap between two neighbouring steps of a sequential map.

functions.name: palette_separation
functions.sig: () -> dict
functions.doc: The palette's worst pair distance under each simulated colour vision.

functions.name: hex_to_rgb
functions.sig: (value: str) -> tuple[float, float, float]

functions.name: as_js
functions.sig: (consumer: str) -> str
functions.doc: The theme as an ES module: the same values, in the shape a three.js viewer needs.

functions.name: as_css
functions.sig: (dark: bool = False) -> str
functions.doc: The theme as CSS custom properties for the apps' shared stylesheet.

functions.name: generated
functions.sig: () -> dict
functions.doc: Every generated artefact, path -> content. ``scripts/build_theme.py`` writes this mapping.

functions.name: viewport
functions.sig: (dark: bool = False) -> str
functions.doc: The background of a 3-D plot: the one colour PyVista, the studio viewer and the twin3d viewer share.

children.summary: The one theme file, and the code every renderer reads it through (#65).

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.trust_panels
children.doc:
Side-by-side field panels with a trust verdict under each model: the figure (and GIF) of "which prediction can I
use, and where does it break the physics".

Each row is a case (a regime, a sample); each panel is a field on a 2-D grid. ``kind="field"`` panels of a row share
one sequential colour scale (blue, light to dark), so the reference and the predictions are directly comparable;
``kind="residual"`` panels show a magnitude on a logarithmic orange scale (the PDE residual, an error). A panel may
carry verdict badges (``verdict``, ``verdicts``), coloured by the first status word in them (APPROVED, REVIEW,
REJECT, PASS, OK, FAIL) and always shown with their text, so the colour never carries the meaning alone.

``trust_panels(rows)`` returns a matplotlib figure; ``trust_panels_gif(frames, path)`` writes one figure per frame
into an animated GIF (Pillow, which matplotlib already depends on).

classes.name: Panel
classes.doc:
One field. ``kind``: ``"field"`` (shared linear scale per row), ``"residual"`` (log magnitude) or ``"error"``
(magnitude on a linear scale from 0 to ``error_max`` of :func:`trust_panels`). ``inset``: draw a dashed square
that many cells inside the border (e.g. the edge of an interior region).

functions.name: trust_panels
functions.sig: (rows: Sequence[Row], *, title: str = '', footer: str = '', cell: float = 2.4, residual_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None, error_max: float | None = None, error_label: str = '', dpi: int = 110)
functions.doc:
Figure with one row per :class:`Row`: its ``"field"`` panels, a colour bar, its ``"residual"`` / ``"error"``
panels and their colour bar (labelled ``error_label``); every row has the same number of panels of each group.

functions.name: trust_panels_gif
functions.sig: (frames: Sequence[Sequence[Row]], path: str | Path, *, duration_ms: int = 1600, **kwargs) -> Path
functions.doc:
One :func:`trust_panels` figure per frame, written as a looping GIF. ``kwargs`` go to ``trust_panels`` (pass
the same ``residual_range`` to every frame for a fixed residual scale).

children.summary: Side-by-side field panels with a trust verdict under each model: the figure (and GIF) of "which prediction can I use, and where does it break the physics".

children.name: pinneapple_tools.visualization.vortex
children.doc:
Vortex identification and flow visualization — Q-criterion, λ₂, vorticity.

Inspired by the Q-criterion iso-surface style used in production CFD post-processing
(e.g. the fastback/Ahmed-body visualisations from OpenFOAM / ParaView).

Functions
---------
Analysis (numpy / torch input):
  compute_vorticity_2d        — ω_z scalar field
  compute_vorticity_3d        — full vorticity vector field (curl u)
  compute_q_criterion_2d      — Q = 0.5(|Ω|²-|S|²) on 2-D structured grid
  compute_q_criterion_3d      — Q on 3-D structured grid
  compute_lambda2_3d          — λ₂ vortex criterion (Jeong & Hussain 1995)
  compute_enstrophy           — 0.5*sum(|ω|²), accepts 2-D scalar or 3-D vector vorticity
  compute_dissipation_rate    — viscous dissipation rate ε = 2ν S_ij S_ij (3-D)

Visualization:
  plot_vorticity              — coloured vorticity map
  plot_q_criterion_2d         — filled Q contour with zero iso-line
  plot_q_criterion_3d         — 3-D iso-surface via marching cubes
  plot_vortex_identification  — one-shot: compute Q from (u, v) and plot
  plot_lbm_flow               — specialised 4-panel dashboard for LBM output
  plot_flow_panel             — pressure + |v| + Q + streamlines (4-panel)

functions.name: compute_vorticity_2d
functions.sig: (u: 'ArrayLike', v: 'ArrayLike', dx: float = 1.0, dy: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
z-component of vorticity: ω_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y.

u, v : 2-D arrays (nx, ny)
Returns ω_z (nx, ny)

functions.name: compute_q_criterion_2d
functions.sig: (u: 'ArrayLike', v: 'ArrayLike', dx: float = 1.0, dy: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Q-criterion for 2-D incompressible flow.

Q = (∂u/∂x)(∂v/∂y) − (∂u/∂y)(∂v/∂x)

Q > 0 → rotation dominates strain → vortex core.
u, v : 2-D arrays (nx, ny).  Returns Q (nx, ny).

functions.name: compute_vorticity_3d
functions.sig: (u: 'ArrayLike', v: 'ArrayLike', w: 'ArrayLike', dx: float = 1.0, dy: float = 1.0, dz: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Full vorticity vector field ω = ∇×u for 3-D flow:
  ω_x = ∂w/∂y − ∂v/∂z
  ω_y = ∂u/∂z − ∂w/∂x
  ω_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y

u, v, w : 3-D arrays (nx, ny, nz).
Returns ω stacked as (3, nx, ny, nz) — components [ω_x, ω_y, ω_z].

functions.name: compute_strain_rate_tensor_3d
functions.sig: (u: 'ArrayLike', v: 'ArrayLike', w: 'ArrayLike', dx: float = 1.0, dy: float = 1.0, dz: float = 1.0) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Symmetric strain-rate tensor S_ij = 0.5(∂u_i/∂x_j + ∂u_j/∂x_i) for 3-D flow.

u, v, w : 3-D arrays (nx, ny, nz).
Returns (S11, S22, S33, S12, S13, S23), each (nx, ny, nz).

functions.name: compute_q_criterion_3d
functions.sig: (u: 'ArrayLike', v: 'ArrayLike', w: 'ArrayLike', dx: float = 1.0, dy: float = 1.0, dz: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Q-criterion for 3-D flow:  Q = 0.5(‖Ω‖²_F − ‖S‖²_F)

u, v, w : 3-D arrays (nx, ny, nz).  Returns Q (nx, ny, nz).

functions.name: compute_enstrophy
functions.sig: (vorticity: 'ArrayLike') -> float
functions.doc:
Enstrophy: 0.5 * sum(|ω|²).

Accepts either a 2-D scalar vorticity field (ω_z, from compute_vorticity_2d)
or a 3-D vector vorticity field stacked as (3, nx, ny, nz) (from
compute_vorticity_3d). No branching is needed: |ω|² at a point is the sum
of its squared components, so summing squared entries over every axis
(including the stacked-component axis, when present) gives the same
total in both cases.

functions.name: compute_dissipation_rate
functions.sig: (strain_rate_tensor_components: Tuple['ArrayLike', 'ArrayLike', 'ArrayLike', 'ArrayLike', 'ArrayLike', 'ArrayLike'], nu: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Viscous/turbulent dissipation rate: ε = 2ν S_ij S_ij (double contraction
of the strain-rate tensor).

strain_rate_tensor_components: (S11, S22, S33, S12, S13, S23), e.g. from
compute_strain_rate_tensor_3d(u, v, w, dx, dy, dz).
Returns ε field, same shape as the S_ij components.

functions.doc:

Vortex core: λ₂ < 0.

doc:
pinneapple_tools — Visualization, model export, HPO, benchmarking, and compute backends.

Sub-modules
-----------
visualization     (was pinneapple_viz)
    CFD-style visualization: scalar/vector fields, streamlines, PINN loss
    histories, vorticity, Q-criterion, mesh plots, animations.

model_export      (was pinneapple_export)
    Model deployment: TorchScript, ONNX, CSV, NPZ export.

hpo_experiments   (was pinneapple_researcher)
    Literature pipeline: discover papers, build knowledge base,
    extract problem-solution pairs, reproduce benchmark results.

benchmark_suite   (was pinneapple_arena)
    Benchmark suite: Arena, PINNArenaBenchmark, TransferBenchmarkPipeline,
    MetaBenchmarkPipeline; task/backend registries.

compute_backends  (was pinneapple_backend)
    Multi-backend abstraction: PyTorch (default) and JAX (jit_pinn,
    vmap_residual, torch↔jax conversion).

dataset_quality
    Dataset quality assessment: statistical/heuristic checks over a
    (coords, fields) point-cloud representation, plus vision-language-
    model dataset curation (run a VLM over each sequence's clip and
    filter on its label/confidence judgment before training).

reporting
    Report figure style and PDF technical-report builder (``reporting.paperkit``;
    the PDF part needs reportlab). Not imported eagerly.

Integration helpers
-------------------
``plot(model, domain, ...)``
    Quick visualization shortcut that auto-selects 1D or 2D plot.
``export_model(model, path, fmt, ...)``
    Format-dispatching export shortcut.
``run_benchmark(models, tasks, ...)``
    PINNArenaBenchmark shortcut for quick model comparison.

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_tools import plot, export_model, run_benchmark
>>> plot(model, x_test, field_name="u")
>>> export_model(model, "model.onnx", fmt="onnx", example_input=x)
>>> results = run_benchmark({"my_pinn": model}, tasks=["burgers_1d"])
